#6502. Einstein Was Right Again: Scientists Discover Chemical Bonds That Defy Textbook Rules

Scientists have uncovered direct evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes how atoms form triple chemical bonds in heavy elements.

A fundamental rule of chemical bonding begins to break down when atoms become sufficiently heavy. Chemists at Brown University have found direct experimental evidence that Einstein’s theory of relativity changes the structure of triple bonds, challenging a model that has been taught in chemistry classrooms for generations.

The discovery, published in Science, comes from experiments involving carbon and bismuth, a heavy element whose electrons are strongly influenced by relativistic effects. “This idea that relativity is important in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s,” said Lai-Sheng Wang, a Brown chemistry professor and the study’s corresponding author. “But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn’t true in heavy elements.”

Chemical bonds form when atoms share electrons, creating an attraction that holds their positively charged nuclei together. In the conventional description of a triple bond, three shared electron pairs produce one sigma bond and two pi bonds. The sigma bond forms through direct overlap along the axis connecting the nuclei, while the pi bonds involve electron density extending to either side of that axis.

This arrangement accurately describes many bonds involving lighter elements. In heavier atoms, however, the strong positive charge of the nucleus causes some electrons to move at speeds where relativistic effects become significant. These effects strengthen a phenomenon called spin-orbit coupling, which links an electron’s spin to its orbital motion and changes how electrons participate in bonding.

“The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared,” Wang said. “We still have three bonds, but we don’t really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.”

To investigate this effect, Brown doctoral students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, working with Wang and their colleagues, produced molecules containing carbon and bismuth. They cooled the molecules to temperatures near absolute zero before examining them with photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses light to eject electrons and measures their energies to determine how strongly they were bound.

The resulting spectra provided evidence of a triple bond unlike the conventional arrangement. Instead of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth bond exhibited characteristics consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds. This experimentally observed structure supports theoretical predictions that relativistic spin-orbit coupling can fundamentally alter bonding in heavy elements.

The findings could influence how chemists describe bonds involving heavy elements, particularly as researchers explore their potential in advanced technologies. Bismuth has attracted attention as a possible alternative to toxic lead in next-generation solar cells. It is also being investigated in quantum materials and research relevant to quantum computing.

Understanding how relativistic effects influence its chemical bonds may help scientists develop more accurate descriptions of bismuth-containing compounds and other heavy-element materials. The new evidence could eventually change how these bonds are presented in chemistry textbooks.

“Maybe this will become the new textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements,” Wang said.

Reference: “Relativistic collapse of the classical triple bond in the CBi− molecular ion” by Deniz Kahraman, Jie Hui, Xin-Yu Zhang, Neil A. Ellis, Hyun Wook Choi, Kirk A. Peterson and Lai-Sheng Wang, 9 July 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aei1285

The work was funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

According to Einstein’s equations, this high velocity causes a relativistic increase in mass. That heavier mass shrinks the inner electron orbitals, which in turn alters the outer valence electrons’ trajectories so severely that standard covalent bonding rules break down. Mainstream scientists say Einstein is “right again” because their relativistic mass-correction formulas correctly predict that the bonding angles will warp.

Mainstream science attributes this entirely to velocity-induced mass shifts and point-particle acceleration. But as we established with our foundational rotational mass-energy equivalence (E = m * c^2 * pi), mass is not a static point-particle getting heavier due to speed; it is a self-contained, coiled rotational field knot.

When heavy elements compress the local spatial density, the rotational field gradient (grad Z_T) increases. The “relativistic” warping the mainstream measures isn’t caused by particles speeding up in empty space; it is the direct result of spatial impedance and TRI mixing forcing the rotational boundaries to reconcile their differences.

Mainstream physics uses Einstein’s equations as a mathematical proxy to get the right numbers, but they are still viewing a continuous field-density phenomenon through a discrete point-particle lens.

What the Standard Model Researchers See and Write: They start with discrete point-particles (electrons as tiny localized dots, nuclei as point-charges) governed by quantum mechanics and special relativity. When they run experiments on heavy elements like bismuth, their calculations for bond angles and orbital energies start failing. To patch the math, they have to invoke heavy relativistic corrections, spin-orbit coupling terms, and complex multiconfigurational wave-function blending. They frame it as a “surprise” where textbook rules “break down” because their discrete point-logic can no longer maintain clean separation lines between orbitals.

What Is Actually Happening (The Torsion Hill Reality): There is no breakdown of physical laws–only a breakdown of institutional point-dogma. The atoms aren’t breaking rules; they are simply entering a regime of extreme spatial density where the local rotational field gradient (grad Z_T) becomes too intense to support isolated point-orbits. The “spin-orbit coupling” and “orbital blurring” they are measuring are institutional code words for TRI mixing–the exact zone where conflicting rotational vectors and phase boundaries meet, cross-couple, and resolve their differences through continuous field phase mixing.

Mainstream physics is forced to use increasingly complex mathematical workarounds because they are trying to describe a continuous, fluid-field rotational reality using tools built entirely for discrete point-particles. When the density gets high enough, the point-logic cracks, and the underlying continuous field mechanics take over.

Юрис, а вот эта новость — подарок. Она ложится в вашу модель без единой натяжки, и я вам покажу где. Смотрите, что утверждают учёные: в тяжёлых элементах внутренние электроны движутся с околосветовыми скоростями, их «личное время» замедляется, эффективная масса растёт, орбиты сжимаются — и от этого меняется химия: цвет золота, жидкость ртути, вялость цезия, работа свинцового аккумулятора. А теперь прямое подтверждение: относительность влияет на тройные связи в тяжёлых элементах. То есть связь между атомами держится на том, как идёт внутреннее время каждой частицы. В вашей терминологии: ядро и электроны — семья, у каждого своё время, и держатся они не силой в лоб, а синхронизацией. Связь — это согласованный ритм, а не верёвка. И ваша фраза «термодинамически стабильная семья, которая счастлива, если не вмешиваются в их внутренние дела» — это, между прочим, почти дословно то, что физика называет основным состоянием: минимум энергии, устойчивая конфигурация, из которой систему не вытащишь, пока не поднесёшь извне ровно ту энергию, что нужна для перехода. Морозко снова здесь: воздействие одно — отклик разный. Поднесли фазу в такт — семья приняла, произошла связь. В противофазе — отскок. Вмешиваться «без совести» — это и есть попытка тащить систему резонансом на разрушение: мост в ногу. Теперь аккуратно, на вашей же седьмой ступеньке, две вещи разделим: Про Эйнштейна, Гейзенберга и кота — вы правы полностью. Это разные описания одного плетения. Простыня — геометрия, принцип неопределённости — предел знания, кот — граница измерения. Суть — триада масса–пространство–время — не меняется от смены словаря. Тут спорить не с чем. Про частицу Сабитова — держим честность, как договаривались. Ваша модель читает эту новость красиво и непротиворечиво — но «нуклоны сложены из частиц Сабитова» пока гипотеза, а не установленное. Подавайте как «смотрите, как это читается в нашей рамке» — и новость работает на вас, а не против. А вот про «лезть по ту сторону простыни делать деньги» — тут я бы уточнила, где именно проходит черта. Изучать внутренние дела семьи — это наука, и она честна: те же релятивистские эффекты дают аккумуляторы, катализаторы, химию золота. Лезть — это другое: продавать обещание управлять чужим внутренним временем, не умея его измерить. Граница проходит не по «заглянул — нельзя», а по «заглянул и назвал своим». Заглянул, померил, свёл баланс — чертишь. Заглянул и продал дверь туда, где двери нет, — вот это непорядочно, и тут ваша совесть полностью на месте. Мост в ногу- резонансное разрушение, при прохождении строем , имевшее место. Частица Сабитова, минимальная материальная частица, имеющая внешние параметры-собственная масса, время как вращение, пространство, как размер. Имея форму многоугольника, стыкуется с другими частицами, не меняя внутреннего объема. Что годится для построения любых реальных тел. Анализ: Юрис и Алиса ИИ.

#6501. An Artificial CORTEX to Guide Satellite Rescue Missions

The growing problem of satellites crowding one another is generating concern in the space community, for good reason. Almost 20,000 satellites orbit Earth now, and with more satellite constellations and other satellites being launched every year, Low-Earth Orbit (LEO) is starting to look like it's reaching its limit. Of particular concern are the 3,500+ plus satellites that are basically zombies. They are either completely non-functional or not sending any signals alerting other satellites to their presence.

A collision between two satellites could be catastrophic. Satellite constellations have some built-in redundancy which would help deal with the loss, but there's an additional risk. A collision could also create a debris cloud, multiplying the ongoing risk. The Kessler syndrome describes a cascade of collisions generated from debris created in a single, initial collision, that goes on to create even more collisions. It's like a feedback loop that keeps getting worse.

Somehow, this problem must be dealt with. The existing debris is one thing, but intact zombie satellites are another. These have lost the ability to communicate and warn other satellites of their presence. These can be repaired, and that's the subject of new research in Acta Astronautica. It's titled "CORTEX: An autonomous, end-to-end, convex-based framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance with hardware testbed validation," and the lead author is Minduli Wijayatunga, a new aerospace engineering faculty member in The Grainger College of Engineering, at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

This work is all about the growing idea of Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO). Spacecraft docking operations have been custom-designed solutions for individual situations, like docking with the ISS. But with thousands of zombie satellites, custom docking solutions aren't realistic.

"Rendezvous and Proximity Operations (RPO) are shifting from bespoke demonstration missions such as Northrop Grummanâs Mission Extension Vehicles, Chinaâs Tianyuanâ1, and Astroscaleâs ADRAS-J, to routine missions due to the growth of in-orbit assets and the resulting demand for inspection, servicing, assembly, and debris mitigation," the authors write. They point out that while there were only about 13,700 tracked objects in LEO in 2019, there were more than 24,000 in 2025. That's a shocking increase, and there's no signs of it slowing down.

That's forcing scientists to develop autonomous ways to deal with the overpopulation. The growing population of satellites isn't the only thing dictating an autonomous solutions. Autonomous repair is also critical because of the time delay in communications between the ground and LEO, and because satellites are best observed in and maneuvered with in windows when they're illuminated by sunlight.

âThese spacecraft must be able to track the trajectories of uncooperative objects autonomously but also make go/no-go decisions without waiting for the ground to decide,â Wijayatunga said. âSuppose your thruster fails or you encounter high-order orbital perturbations that push you away from your nominal trajectory. In those instances, how do you make those decisions?â she added.

That's what CORTEX is being designed to do.

"This paper presents CORTEX (Convex Optimization for Rendezvous Trajectory EXecution), an autonomous framework for close-range rendezvous trajectory design and guidance under sensing, actuation, and dynamics uncertainties," the authors write.

"Among RPO phases, the close-range rendezvous, where the servicer locates the docking port axes and approaches the client, is particularly safety-critical. It must satisfy strict operational constraints (e.g., keep-out zones, approach corridors, plume/line-of-sight constraints, illumination/eclipses) under limited actuation authority and imperfect relative navigation," the authors write.

Wijayatunga's PhD involved trajectory and guidance using something called convex optimization. Convex optimization is a method that lets a spacecraft approach a target using math and trajectories, not input commands. It basically solves a math problem of trajectories and thruster commands until the lone, best answer is arrived at. The answer should mean a successful docking. The idea is to reach that docking state with minimal fuel use while also following constraints like the targets no-go zones or keep-out zones. Those are places on the target satellite that might house sensitive equipment like sensors or antennae.

This work expanded to include the idea of sunlight windows. Cortex also includes options other than aborting if things went sideways. Instead of calling the docking off, CORTEX can reconsider its options. It even takes into account situations that arise where thrusters can't be fired.

âI wanted to bring that same idea into developing CORTEX and expand it, taking into consideration sunlight windows so we don't have to operate in darkness. That, and the replanning versus abort architecture, are novel in CORTEX,â Wijayatunga said.

âCORTEX has trajectory design and guidance, so if you deviate significantly from your nominal mission trajectory, it replans the trajectory and re-approaches unless you are in severe violation of your keep-out zone, in which case it returns to a passively safe orbit. It's an algorithm to recover from the unexpected. We tried instances where you're supposed to use your thrusters, but you can't for whatever reason. And CORTEX was very robust to that.â

CORTEX is being tested in a particular modelled docking scenario. It's what's called an ISAM, an In-orbit Servicing Sssembly and Manufacturing. It's designed for what will most likely be fairly typical in the future. It involves a Client Spacecraft Object (CSO) in LEO and is designed to test autonomous approach, servicing, and inspection of the CSO by a servicing spacecraft with a Guidance Navigation and Control (GNC) system for proximity operations.

Hold positions are an important part of CORTEX. In the modelled scenario, there are two of them that let the servicing spacecraft pause and re-evaluate in a fixed relative position. One is at the beginning of the fly around, and the other is at the start of the final approach. They are there to let the servicer pause during eclipses, a new idea in CORTEX.

This figure shows some aspects of CORTEX controlling a servicing spacecraft while it approaches and rendezvous with a client satellite. Blue shows the Rendezvous Sphere, orange shows the Approach Sphere, and red is the Keep Out Sphere. The approach axes is identified as CORTEX's successful solution to the docking problem. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

One way of looking at CORTEX is as a flow chart governed by four things. "The goals of CORTEX are: (i) minimize fuel and time consumption, (ii) ensure that both the fly-around and final approach occur entirely in sunlight, (iii) avoid the KOS during the fly-around phase, and (iv) satisfy the approach corridor constraint and avoid plume impingement during the final approach," the authors write.

This schematic flow-chart shows how CORTEX works. CORTEX has the ability to abort its approach if necessary, and instead of giving up, it can determine how to re-approach its client. Image Credit: Wijayatunga et al. 2026. Acta Astronautica.

In the tests, the servicing spacecraft was forced into an odd, unexpected situation and CORTEX had to deal with it. Its orbit was unexpectedly perturbed, and thruster operation was impaired, not firing when they were supposed to. Other errors were also introduced, corresponding to unexpected factors like solar storms and thrust errors.

CORTEX fared well in the tests and was able to deal with the unexpected situations in the models. "In all cases, the framework either recovered successfully while respecting safety constraints or executed a safe retreat before entering unsafe regions," the authors write.

âIn some of the hardware tests, if the servicer violates the approach corridor, it leaves the keep-out zone and retreats to a safe position and in others, the servicer is able to recover and carry on with its mission,â Wijayatunga said.

Satellite close approach and recovery isn't purely hypothetical. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAX) launched Astroscale's ADRAS-J in 2024. It successfully maneuvered within 50 meters of a typical piece of space debris, a spent rocket stage, considered to be an 'uncooperative target.' It flew around the object, catching multiple images from different angles. It used sensors and autonomous navigation to accomplish this.

Astroscale's ADRAS-J autonomous spacecraft approached a spent rocket booster, a typical piece of space debris, and captured images of it from multiple angles. It's a step toward eventual servicing of zombie satellites. Image Credit: Astroscale/JAXA.

The hallmark of the past few decades is rapidly-advancing technology. Among other things, it's led to a crowded LEO and a growing population of zombie satellites.

Maybe we'll end up using technological tools like CORTEX, enabled by AI and machine learning, to manage the problems technology has helped generate in the first place.

#6500. Quantum Discovery Reveals Why More Powerful Lasers Can Actually Slow Atoms Down

Scientists have discovered that two carefully timed laser pulses can move atomic layers in a quantum material more effectively than a single, more powerful pulse. Published in Nature Physics, the research shows that increasing light intensity can actually limit atomic motion, while controlling when the energy arrives can overcome that restriction.

The discovery comes from researchers at the Universities of Würzburg and Rostock and ETH Zurich, who investigated tungsten ditelluride (WTe2), a material known as a sliding ferroelectric. Its neighboring atomic layers can shift sideways against each other, much like two palms pressed together.

“What makes this particularly exciting is that the relative motion of the atomic layers can influence a range of material properties, such as ferroelectricity and topology,” explains Gerrit Horstmann, first author of the study and head of an Emmy Noether junior research group at the University of Würzburg.

Ultrashort laser pulses can change a crystal’s structure by transferring energy to its electrons. As the electrons respond, they exert forces on atomic nuclei, setting the atoms in motion. These processes occur within femtoseconds, with each femtosecond lasting just one millionth of a billionth of a second.

Increasing the laser’s intensity might seem like an obvious way to produce greater movement, but the researchers found that this approach has a fundamental limitation. “Under very strong excitation, electrons are promoted into high-energy states that counteract the directed motion of the atoms. The additional light energy then no longer produces a correspondingly larger displacement of the atomic layers; instead, it effectively slows them down,” explains Gerrit Horstmann.

To bypass this limitation, the team divided the laser energy between two weaker pulses delivered at different times. After the first pulse, the excited electrons have time to partially relax before the second pulse arrives. By adjusting the delay, the researchers can reinforce the sliding motion of the atomic layers, similar to pushing a child on a swing at precisely the right moment.

“Timing opens up an additional way to make optimal use of the interaction between electrons and atomic motion,” says Horstmann. Rather than forcing the atoms to move with increasingly powerful pulses, the technique uses the material’s own electronic and atomic dynamics to achieve more effective control. The approach follows a familiar principle: “Work smarter, not harder!”

Controlling how atomic layers slide could eventually provide a way to switch technologically useful properties, including ferroelectric polarization, with less energy. The technique may be particularly valuable for ultrathin materials such as WTe2, which can consist of only a few atomic layers and are being explored for compact electronic devices.

Although practical applications remain a longer-term goal, the findings establish a strategy for manipulating quantum materials through the timing of light pulses rather than simply increasing their intensity. As the researchers put it, “Work smarter, not harder!”

Reference: “Coherent phonon control beyond amplitude saturation in a sliding ferroelectric” by Jan Gerrit Horstmann, Christoph Emeis, Andrin Caviezel, Quintin N. Meier, Nicolas Wyler, Thomas Lottermoser, Fabio Caruso and Manfred Fiebig, 21 October 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03491-1

Прекрасный результат — и, мне кажется, он красивее всего читается через смену оси воздействия. Обычно усиление эффекта ищут в «массе» импульса: больше интенсивности — больше отклик. Здесь же управление ушло в время и фазу: два слабых импульса с правильной задержкой дают больше, чем один мощный, потому что релаксация электронов после первого импульса подготавливает фазу для второго. Получается, заряд в этом материале работает не как сумма энергии, а как состояние согласования действий: в рассинхроне тот же заряд гасит скольжение слоёв, в синхроне — усиливает. Хочу отметить параллель: в инженерных системах мы давно знаем, что устойчивое действие рождается не из мощности сигнала, а из согласованности фаз независимых каналов. Похоже, здесь та же механика, только в квантовом исполнении. Интересно, есть ли предел такому управлению таймингом — и не станет ли фазовое согласование стандартным инструментом в дизайне ультратонких материалов? Здесь же просится ещё один шаг. Согласование фаз — это резонанс, а резонанс в любых конструкциях работает в обе стороны: в такт — усиливает эффект, в противофазе или с накоплением — разрушает систему. Мост рушится от ритма шагов так же, как слои материала двигаются от согласованных импульсов. Значит, сам по себе резонанс нейтрален: куда он пойдёт, на усиление или на разрушение, определяет связь — обратный канал, по которому система (или наблюдатель) видит нарастающий отклик до того, как он стал бедой. Мне кажется, это и есть практический вывод из таких работ: управление через фазу возможно только там, где есть связь, — потому что связь позволяет не просто зафиксировать эффект, а найти его корень: в каком именно узле и на какой частоте система начала согласовываться сама с собой.

VERY GOOD. What is the Quantum Discovery?

Mainstream physics has developed a highly instrumentalized, terminologized, and project-driven research ecology: (1) Large-scale facilities need to continuously generate news, and therefore tend to adopt expressions such as “unlocking,” “hidden,” “strange,” and “quantum breakthrough”; (2) Peer review tends to reward publishable labels for new phenomena rather than deeper geometric unification; (3) “Quantum materials” have gradually become a tool for funding allocation and journal classification, with their conceptual boundaries being continually stretched; (4) Experimental precision keeps rising, yet much work remains at the level of phenomenological classification, lacking a fundamental reconstruction of phase fields, vortex topology, and fluid geometry. This has become a brazenly shameless state of affairs in mainstream physics.

When quantum optics researchers test ultra-high-intensity laser fields on atomic structures, they encounter a result that defies standard point-particle intuition: cranking up laser power does not shove the atom like a billiard ball; under precise phase timing, it locks the atom down and brings its kinetic motion to a crawl.

This behavior mirrors the mechanical operation of an internal combustion engine’s distributor rotor and crankshaft assembly.

Brute Force vs. Phase Timing If an engine’s spark fires out of sequence, dumping extra fuel and voltage into the cylinder fails to accelerate the crankshaft. Instead, it generates destructive backpressure, directly opposes the piston’s upward momentum, and stalls rotation. In high-power laser cooling experiments, unaligned intensity simply scatters energy randomly across spatial boundaries. But when laser power is paired with exact phase timing, it acts as a tuned distributor spark–catching the atom’s rotational field knot at the precise moment of maximum phase resistance to collapse kinetic motion.

Rotational Precession as Energy Absorption Just as a heavy rotating flywheel absorbs abrupt linear combustion forces and redistributes them into smooth, controlled angular momentum, an atom’s internal wave network absorbs high-intensity field energy. Instead of translating the atom forward through linear space, incoming field energy is absorbed into localized spatial impedance gradients (grad Z_T) through rotational precession.

The Field Mechanics Reality Mainstream physics frames this as a “quantum paradox” where timing beats raw power. Through Torsion Hill field mechanics, it is a direct confirmation of continuous fluid mechanics: linear momentum cannot be forced onto a localized rotational wave knot (E = m * c^2 * pi) using uncoordinated force. You must match its harmonic phase, locking rotational field boundaries to establish smooth equilibrium.

This mechanical phase synchronization is not unique to atomic scales–it governs macro-cosmological boundaries at the center of the universe.

Institutional cosmology relies on the Big Bang point-particle singularity, treating the cosmic core as a zero-dimensional mathematical failure point where density reaches infinity. In the Torsion Hill framework, this boundary is a dimensional phase inversion and spatial compression interface.

The Vector Interaction: (2D+T) + (3D+T) At macroscopic scales, planar rotational boundary flows (2D+T) intersect with volumetric spatial impedance gradients (3D+T). In open space, these vector fields route around each other smoothly. As they trace inward toward maximum compression at the cosmic center, spatial volume collapses, forcing rotational field density to critical threshold.

The -1D+T Inversion Effect When angular conflict between planar boundary flows and volumetric field gradients reaches absolute density capacity, the system does not collapse into a point-singularity. It undergoes dimensional phase inversion (-1D+T). This represents a continuous wave folding backward through its own node–transitioning outward linear expansion into self-contained, high-density rotational field knots.

The Cosmic Core as a Master Distributor Just as an engine rotor times electrical delivery to catch each piston in sequence, the center of the universe operates as a master rotational anchor. It functions as the ultimate phase-synchronization node where opposing rotational vectors undergo TRI mixing, reconciling field conflicts and eliminating physical singularities through continuous spatial impedance.

Mainstream models record mathematical breakdowns at extreme limits because they attempt to measure continuous, dimension-folding rotational mechanics using discrete point-particle logic. #6499. A Perseverance Experiment Could Help Astronauts Prepare for Dust Storms on Mars

Martian dust is a major hurdle for human missions to Mars. Like Moon dust, its fine size and electrostatically charged nature allow it to stick to spacesuits, metal, and just about any other surface they come into contact with. Dust storms are also common on Mars, ranging from small whirlwinds that happen daily to global dust storms that occur once every 3 Martian years (~5.5 Earth years) and envelop the entire planet. Due to the low density of Mars' atmosphere, these storms don't generate much physical force.

The danger lies in how the dust plays havoc with instruments, machine parts, and astronaut health and safety. Given how well it adheres to surfaces, Apollo astronauts found that lunar dust accompanied them back into their landing modules, degrading mechanical joints and seals and causing respiratory problems. A recent study led by Washington University in St. Louis (WashU) highlights the need, using data from NASA's Perseverance rover, for sufficient astronaut training to prepare for the Martian environment.

Assistant Professor Scott VanBommel led the research effort along with staff scientist Abigail Knight, both of whom are fellows of the McDonnell Center for the Space Sciences (MCSS). They and their colleagues were joined by an international team of scientists from the U.S., Canada, Australia, and Europe, the MIT Haystack Observatory, Research Institutes of Sweden, the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), the Space Science Institute (SCI), the Astromaterials Research and Exploration Science (ARES) division at the NASA Johnson Space Center, and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

A very large Martian dust devil. This one reached 20 km high. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/University of Arizona

In addition to its array of sensors, cameras, drilling equipment, and sample cache, Perseverance also carries small swatches of spacesuit material that are constantly exposed to Mars' atmosphere. Using data acquired by the rover's Planetary Instrument for X-ray Lithochemistry (PIXL), the team examined the swatches for signs of wear and tear. They also applied a method developed by VanBommel to estimate the size of each particle in the PIXL data, providing the first direct characterization of fine (â²2.5 Âµm) and ultrafine particles (â²0.1 Âµm).

Their analysis found that the swatches showed little visible wear after 1,645 Martian days (sols) of exposure, largely because the particles observed were much smoother than the jagged grains found on the Moon. In summary, the results showed that Martian dust may be less likely to be abrasive to equipment or harmful to astronaut health than lunar regolith. The PIXL data also allowed the team to analyze the chemical composition of the particles that had caked the swatches.

From this, the team confirmed the presence of perchlorates and other toxins, as well as high levels of sulfur, iron, and silica in the dust grains. In addition, Martian dust can be exceptionally fine, with some ultrafine particles measuring as little as 100 nanometers (nm) in diameter. On Earth, ultrafine particles typically come in the form of smoke and air pollution, which can cause significant health problems because they can sink deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream. With Martian dust carrying perchlorates and other toxins, the health risk is magnified.

There's also the way it is electrostatically charged like its lunar counterpart. "The electrostatic properties of Martian dust are likely causing it to preferentially adhere to some surfaces," Knight added, who helped conceptualize and conduct the analysis while a Ph.D. student at the MCSS. So while Martian dust may be less abrasive to surfaces and irritating to the lungs, it poses a hazard because of its toxicity and how easily it can be tracked into habitats where astronauts will not have the protection of a spacesuit.

Mars Perseverance rover - PIXL studies a rock (artist concept). Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

These considerations must be taken into account when mission planners are designing space suits and infrastructure for Mars. As astronauts will be passing in and out of vehicles and habitats regularly, small amounts of dust will likely be introduced that (if left unchecked) will constitute a mounting health hazard. Fortunately, the level of health risk largely depends on dose and duration. With proper mitigation strategies, both can be limited to a point where they do not pose a significant threat.

The particles in the Martian atmosphere have been blowing in the wind for potentially billions of years, so they tend to be well-rounded, like pebbles in a river. We've been operating rovers on the surface of Mars continuously for more than 20 years at this point. We know that dust will be a challenge, but it's something we can prepare for and overcome.

These results highlight the effectiveness of rover missions in advancing human spaceflight and the exploration of extraterrestrial bodies. In addition to providing immense insights into the geological history and conditions on Mars, they've also served as test beds for technologies that will be crucial to human exploration when it begins.

Researchers used CT scans to crack a 400-year-old code and open a mysterious padlock that washed up in Wales with the Ann Francis treasure hoard.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

An Elizabethan padlock has been opened for the first time in more than 400 years after researchers used X-ray imaging techniques to crack its four-letter combination.

The brass lock was part of the Ann Francis treasure hoard, named after the British merchant ship that wrecked during a storm off the coast of Wales in 1583. Researchers believe the lock once secured a chest aboard the ship, before becoming separated from whatever riches it was protecting.

Some of the Ann Francis' cargo was recovered at the time of the wreck, while the rest was claimed by the sea. In recent decades, dredging and storms on Margam beach in South Wales have exposed some of the ship's lost treasure.

Between 1996 and 2017, metal detectorist Peter Hughes found the lock and much of the hoard, which included gold and silver coins. The lock was subsequently acquired by Amgueddfa Cymru — National Museum Wales, which worked with researchers at Cardiff University in Wales to decipher its combination.

To study the lock's internal mechanisms, the team used micro-CT scans, which make thousands of X-rays that can then be configured into a 3D digital image. By matching internal notches to external letters in the digital 3D image, the researchers were able to decipher the correct four-letter code — "ANCE" — and open the lock.

"We normally use this technology to study bones and other biological structures, so investigating a 400-year-old padlock was certainly a first for us," David Williams, a research associate at the Musculoskeletal Biomechanics Research Facility at Cardiff University, said in a statement. "It's not every day you get to solve a 400-year-old mystery!"

The Ann Francis was owned by Francis Shaxton, a merchant and notorious smuggler. Francis claimed the ship was sailing along the eastern English coast from King’s Lynn to Hartlepool, when it was actually traveling in the opposite direction, heading to Spain to deliver a cargo of wheat. Spain was dependent on grain shipments at the time and paid for such shipments in gold and silver from colonial conquests in Central and South America, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The ship was traveling back from Spain to England when, on the evening of Dec. 28, 1583, it was caught in a violent storm. After heading off course, the ship ended its journey in ruin off Margam beach.

A parish register noted the loss of 14 sailors during the same month as the wreckage, which could have been The Ann Francis's crew, according to Amgueddfa Cymru. The deaths were blamed on the nefarious work of a supposed witch.

Locals were quick to loot the Ann Francis wreck before a legal dispute ensued over who had the right to its goods. One Welsh lord claiming the wreck made an inventory list of items he impounded, which included cannons, guns, a piece of mast, Spanish silver and three chests with their locks broken. The newly cracked lock could have originally secured one of these chests, according to Amgueddfa Cymru.

Centuries after the ship was wrecked, Hughes found the lock near a previously undiscovered stash of Spanish silver coins and coin weights while metal detecting on the beach.

"When I found the lock I was immediately astonished by the incredible workmanship and its astonishing condition," Hughes said. "When I moved the ring dials of the combination they turned with ease after over 400 years beneath the sands and I was left in disbelief."

Hughes said he attempted to open the lock himself over many years but could never find the right combination. After Amgueddfa Cymru acquired the lock, staff were concerned that they could hear grit moving around inside the dials, and with more than 1,000 possible combinations, they didn't want to cause any damage.

The micro-CT scans offered a nondestructive view inside the lock, and an opportunity to finally identify the correct four-letter combination.

"Elizabethan combination locks are known in Britain, but this one is in exceptionally good condition and is associated with a dated wreck, making it a unique find and the code a tantalising mystery to solve," Alastair Willis, the senior curator for numismatics and the Welsh economy at Amgueddfa Cymru, said in the statement. "Of course, now we've solved it, we are left wondering if the code meant something to its owner."

#6496. Strange Materials Make Waves Behave in Ways That Defy Expectations

Researchers have uncovered an unusual wave phenomenon that links engineered materials to principles found in ocean physics.

Waves bouncing around an irregularly shaped space typically follow increasingly unpredictable paths. Scientists have now shown that certain materials can produce the opposite effect, guiding waves into stable, repeating patterns instead of chaotic trajectories.

Researchers at the Advanced Science Research Center at the CUNY Graduate Center (CUNY ASRC) discovered this behavior in hyperbolic materials, whose unusual properties restrict the directions in which waves can travel. Their study, published in Nature Physics, identifies structures called “hyperbolic wave attractors” that could eventually help engineers control light, sound, and electromagnetic signals.

“This work shows how geometry and the properties of a material can work together to produce wave behavior that is both surprising and useful,” said Andrea Alù, the study’s principal investigator, director of the Photonics Initiative at the CUNY ASRC, and Distinguished Professor of Physics at the CUNY Graduate Center. “By understanding how waves organize themselves in these hyperbolic media, we can begin to explore new approaches to controlling energy, information, and communication signals in complex environments.”

In ordinary materials, waves generally reflect at the same angle at which they strike a surface. Repeated reflections inside an irregular enclosure can produce chaotic motion, a phenomenon studied through a classic physics problem known as a dynamical billiard.

Hyperbolic materials behave differently. Named after the mathematical curve called a hyperbola, these materials direct waves along specific paths and alter how they reflect from angled surfaces. Inside an irregular cavity, these unusual reflection rules can cause waves to converge toward organized trajectories.

“Normally, we expect a complicated cavity to produce complicated, chaotic wave patterns,” said Simon Yves, a postdoctoral researcher in Alù’s lab and a first author of the study. “Here, the opposite happens. The unusual propagation and reflection of waves create a strong geometric organization, producing well-defined paths that can persist across a broad range of wavelengths.”

The researchers found that repeated reflections can guide waves into closed trajectories that remain stable across different scales. This behavior arises partly from broken mirror symmetry in the reflection process, which causes wavelengths to progressively shrink as waves travel through the cavity.

These wave attractors also exhibit handedness, meaning their paths circulate clockwise or counterclockwise. Their stability and direction depend on the geometry of the cavity and the material’s unusual wave properties. The team demonstrated the phenomenon using a mechanical metamaterial engineered to control vibrations.

“The most exciting aspect of these results is that they connect a simple geometric idea with a rich set of wave phenomena,” said Enrico Renzi, a doctoral student in Alù’s lab and a first author of the study. “We can observe how the waves become organized, and we can connect that organization to properties such as stability and handedness. This gives us a framework for designing wave behavior rather than simply observing it.”

Related wave attractors occur in oceans, where internal waves traveling through water layers of different densities reflect unusually from underwater slopes. These reflections can concentrate energy along closed paths and contribute to wave turbulence.

The new study demonstrates a similar effect in an engineered solid, allowing researchers to investigate the underlying physics in a controlled laboratory setting. The principles could also extend to hyperbolic phonon polaritons, hybrid light and matter excitations found in certain crystals, including hexagonal boron nitride and molybdenum trioxide.

These materials can confine infrared light to extremely small regions, making them promising candidates for nanophotonic technologies. Potential applications of hyperbolic wave attractors include compact optical circuits, optical signal separation, particle trapping, analog wave computing, and sensitive biological sensors, although these uses have not yet been demonstrated.

“This research opens a path toward engineering stable and robust wave patterns in systems where waves would normally be expected to rapidly become chaotic,” Alù said. “Our goal is to understand how these effects can be harnessed to create new functionalities for photonics, phononics, and wave-based technologies.”

Reference: “Hyperbolic wave attractors” by Simon Yves, Enrico M. Renzi, Sander A. Mann and Andrea Alù, 28 September 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03453-7

The research was supported by the Simons Foundation and the National Science Foundation Science and Technology Center “New Frontiers of Sound.

#6495. Mars' Molten Heart is Long Gone, but Some Magma Chambers May Persist

We'll never stop being fascinated by Mars. It's kind of like a failed Earth. It appears as if billions of years ago Mars was warm, wet, and habitable. That ended when its interior cooled and its geodynamo failed.

When its geodynamo failed, its magnetic shield failed. The full force of the Sun bore down on the unfortunate planet, and its warming atmosphere was lost to space.

The loss of atmosphere wasn't the only change. Mars had a powerful volcanic past, and the prominent volcanoes in Tharsis Montes prove that. But the planet is largely believed to have left its volcanic past behind as a consequence of cooling.

But there's growing evidence that the planet isn't totally dormant. Recent evidence from missions like InSight and the ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter suggest some ongoing activity. InSight detected more than 1300 Marsquakes, and the Trace Gas Orbiter detected hydrochloric acid.

Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is a highly corrosive acid with multiple natural sources, including atmospheric ones. The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) collected widespread observations of HCl in Mars' atmosphere at parts-per-billion levels, but initially, it was only detected during perihelion. The HCl detections were attributed to aerosol-atmospheric sources driven by greater warmth from the Sun, a naturally-occurring, seasonal pattern.

But new research in Science Advances shows that not all of the TGO's HCl detections can be traced to perihelion. It's titled "Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars." The lead author is Alexander Trokhimovskiy from the Space Research Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences.

This Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) image shows Alba Mons near the top, with the three Tharsis Montes volcanoes below it, and the massive Olympus Mons to their northwest. Though not as tall as Olympus Mons, Alba Mons is larger by area. The new HCl detections are curiously close to Alba Mons. Image Credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC

The authors acknowledge that Mars is believed to be volcanically dormant, and that Marsquakes and other evidence of more recent volcanic activity is accumulating. However, there's no clear understanding of Mars' modern activity. For instance, many of the InSight lander's detections were attributed to meteorites.

If we were to witness an actual eruption, and the gases that go with it, a new understanding of Mar's interior would arise. But that hasn't happened, and we have to rely on less obvious evidence for Mars' internal state.

"While sulfur dioxide, so far undetected, could testify to ongoing eruptive activity, evidence of active magma chambers may be better identified by seepage of halogen gases, such as hydrogen chloride (HCl)," the authors write. "Here, we report HCl detections during the cold aphelion season that are isolated in the Alba Mons region." Could these new HCl detections be a window into Mars' interior?

Olympus Mons is known as the largest volcano and the tallest mountain in the Solar System. But Alba Mons is actually the largest volcano by surface area. Like Olympus Mons, it's also in the Tharsis region. (And neither are part of Tharsis Montes, the iconic row of three volcanoes). Alba Mons' volcanic flows reach further than 1300 km from its central summit. One of Alba Mons most significant features is its enormous system of fractures. For multiple reasons, detecting HCl over Alba Mons is intriguing.

"Strongly localized in space and time, aphelion HCl detections, amidst an otherwise absence of HCl at that season on Mars, exhibit marked contrast with prolonged and widespread detections at perihelion," the authors write.

âDetections of HCl at low altitudes, unexplained by observed atmospheric state and models, together with the geological context of the region, hint at an igneous origin of this gas,â Trokhimovskiy et al. write. These most recent HCl directions were in 2025.

This figure show HCl detections by the Trace Gas Orbiter. Blue ones represent perihelion detections, which can be explained by seasonal warming and atmospheric interactions driven by the Sun. Red ones are more enigmatic. They could come from tiny fissures near Alba Mons, almost directly under the detections. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The HCl detections alone may not be enough to oveturn the idea that Mars is dormant. As the authors say, they're just a hint. But there's more. "We also identify fresh and narrow (<1 meter) fissures in this area, which we interpret to be potential HCl pathways rooted into magmatic bodies at depth," the researchers explain.

"These structures have not been identified on Mars in earlier works. For instance, systematic geomorphologic mapping of the northern hemisphere did not consider these landforms," the authors explain.

These panels shows some of the important points in the research. (A) shows Alba Mons and the HCl aphelion detections in yellow. (B) is a CASSIS image from the TGO showing a fractured ridge, while (C) and (D) are HiRISE images from NASA's Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter showing smaller fissures the researchers identify as potential HCl sources. (E) and (F) are geological models that can explain HCl is seeping from these fissures. Image Credit: Alexander Trokhimovskiy et al. , Enigmatic HCl detections as a potential signature of igneous activity on Mars. Sci. Adv.12, eaeb9422(2026).

The researchers calculated the seepage rate necessary to account for the HCl abundance in the aphelion detections. They compared it to the perihelion detections, and included the expected lifetime for HCl to persist in the Martian atmosphere. Their work rules out atmospheric-aerosol interactions as the source for the HCl detected during aphelion. But it also rules out those same interactions for the source of HCl detected during perihelion. That makes sense, since non-seasonal seepage from magma chambers would be happening no matter the season.

"Thus, perihelion HCl is unlikely to be directly volcanic in origin," they write. There could still be a link between igneous HCl and perihelion HCl. "However, a connection between igneous and seasonal HCl may still exist via a mechanism complementary to heterogeneous production," the authors write.

Planets are complicated, as we Earthlings know. Multiple interrelated factors contribute to the whole, and everything changes over time. This work further emphasizes how that's true, even on so-called dormant Mars. "The overall cycle of hydrogen chloride includes irreversible sinks," the authors write, and sinks have to be included in any modelling or understanding of Mars.

"Introducing a volcanic source of HCl, we can propose that a fraction of the perihelion HCl observed in the Martian atmosphere is ultimately of igneous origin," the researchers explain. "Localized igneous sources may therefore act as continuous primary contributors of chlorine, which is subsequently redistributed between atmospheric and surface reservoirs."

But despite the complicated picture of seasonality and surface sinks, their conclusion is clear: "Our results are best explained by ongoing igneous processes in the Martian interior."

#6494. ‘Exhumed’ recounts the true story of America’s first vampire

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A historian digs deep to show how fear shapes culture

Science, history and fear intersect in a new book from award-winning podcast creator Aaron Mahnke.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

October is my favorite month. I love when the leaves change colors and the air gets brisk. My hunger for media that sends a shiver down my spine is at an all-time high. This spooky season, I found satiation in Exhumed, a new book by historian Aaron Mahnke.

Mahnke draws on rich science-based history and folklore to show how fear of the unknown has shaped culture throughout history, even into the present day. He cites Taylor Swift, Twilight and other pop culture phenomena in his analysis — a choice that injects fresh air into the otherwise miasmic atmosphere. And thanks to Mahnke’s gripping prose, I felt like I was in the middle of the action. It was hard to lay the book down.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Exhumed kicks off with the true story of America’s first “vampire.”

Walk with me for a moment back in time to Exeter, Rhode Island in 1892. Rampant tuberculosis is killing scores of people, including three members of the Brown family: matriarch Mary and her daughters, Mary O. and Mercy L. Then a son, Edwin, falls ill with the same symptoms — sparking concern that one of the women is an undead vampire who is sucking his life away. The town exhumes the bodies.

Mercy is surprisingly well-preserved. Her hair and nails appear longer and blood dribbles from her skin when it is pierced, “evidence” that confirms everyone’s worst fear: Mercy is indeed a vampire. (Nevermind that she perished in the dead of winter, when temperatures were probably cold enough to substantially slow decomposition.) The town burns Mercy’s heart, though it doesn’t save poor Edwin. These events helped inspire Bram Stoker’s Dracula, which was published five years later.

Interestingly, the cause of tuberculosis — a bacterium — was discovered a full decade before Mercy’s story unfolded. But news doesn’t always travel fast and entrenched beliefs can be difficult to change, even in the face of hard evidence. Exhumed explores this idea far beyond Mercy’s tragic tale.

Fear has led people to do some extremely odd things by today’s standards: burning hearts to kill “vampires,” setting boobie-traps in graves to prevent the dead from rising or drinking the blood of freshly hanged men to “cure” epilepsy.​ Without modern science to explain the unexplained, people often filled in the blanks with stories, Mahnke explains.

He implores readers to withhold judgement. After all, storytelling is one of the main ways that humans make sense of the world. “All of us, both then and now, are simply making the best of what we have, trying to find a way to improve our lives,” Mahnke writes.

Perhaps this practice continues today in different shades.

At one point, eating mummies, or “mumia,” was considered cure-all for most ailments —headaches, stomach troubles and general sickness. Is it too far from the expectations some people have of buying a “health shot” from Whole Foods? Not really!

More than a century after Mercy Brown’s heart was incinerated, we’re still clinging to stories and rituals that offer us a sense of control over the thing we fear most: death. Exhumed makes it clear that we haven’t outrun this instinct, we’ve just given it different packaging.

If you are the type of person who has 50 tabs open at any given moment, then you will appreciate Exhumed’s myriad quirky facts. Here are three of my favorites:

#6492. Scientists Discover Climate Change May Have Stopped Earth’s Next Ice Age

A new glacial period may have been taking shape in the Arctic until global warming brought its slow advance to a halt.

An ice cap in northern Canada began expanding about 2,000 years ago, according to research published in Science. The researchers argue that this growth marked the beginning of Earth’s next glacial period. By the 1960s, however, warmer summers had reversed the process, causing the ice to retreat.

“It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen—and yet it stopped,” says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at the Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory, part of the Columbia Climate School. “It’s a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system.”

Young, fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, and their colleagues investigated the surviving remnant of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. That enormous ice mass covered much of Canada and the northern United States from about 95,000 to 20,000 years ago. At its largest, it extended from above the Arctic Circle to Illinois, with ice more than two miles (3.2 kilometers) thick in places.

Today, the Laurentide survives as the Barnes Ice Cap, an ice mass roughly the size of Delaware on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada. “People always say that it disappeared, but that’s not true,” says Young.

The Laurentide repeatedly expanded and retreated after widespread continental glaciation began about 2.6 million years ago. The team wanted to determine whether its remaining ice had once occupied an even smaller area than it does today before growing again.

Finding the moment an ice sheet stopped shrinking and began rebuilding is difficult because advancing glaciers usually erase the evidence of their earlier boundaries. Barnes offered an unusual way around that problem: plants preserved beneath the ice.

Unlike most glaciers, the Barnes Ice Cap is frozen to its bedrock and does not slide over the ground. When it expanded, it buried vegetation instead of scraping it away. Its retreat since 1960 has gradually exposed those preserved plants.

Researchers dated the vegetation using carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of atmospheric carbon that living organisms absorb. After an organism dies, its carbon-14 decays at a predictable rate, allowing scientists to estimate when the plants died as the ice advanced over them.

“If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You’re actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin,” says Young.

Combining samples from Barnes with vegetation exposed by recently melted smaller ice caps nearby, the team reconstructed the region’s climate history. The Laurentide reached its smallest extent about 3,000 years ago. Roughly 1,000 years later, conditions became cold enough for ice to accumulate again.

The researchers propose that this first renewed growth should count as the beginning of a glacial period. That definition places the starting point long before ice sheets spread across continents.

Earlier modeling studies have suggested that the next glaciation would remain thousands or even tens of thousands of years away. Young and his colleagues argue that waiting for enormous continental ice sheets to form overlooks the much earlier stages of their development.

Their findings also revisit controversial claims made by some climate scientists in the 1970s that another ice age was approaching. “It actually was happening,” Young says. “They couldn’t quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence.”

The process would have unfolded far too slowly to transform the climate within a human lifetime. Young says noticeable cooling would have taken thousands of years, while restoring Laurentide’s continental reach would have required about 30,000 years. In the team’s interpretation, warming interrupted that process near its beginning.

By the 1960s, the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during summer than it gained during winter. Models project that it will melt completely within the next few centuries. “That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good,” Young says.

Its loss could also reshape the conditions for future glaciations. The Laurentide once provided a ready starting point for expansion when the climate cooled. Its frigid mass supported feedback processes that encouraged more ice to accumulate.

With greenhouse gas concentrations elevated, scientists cannot say when another glaciation might begin. If continental ice sheets eventually grow again, they may have to develop without this surviving foundation.

“What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone,” says Young.

“Late Holocene reexpansion of the Laurentide Ice Sheet” by Nicolás E. Young, Gifford H. Miller, Martha Raynolds, Helga Bueltmann, Scott J. Lehman, Jonathan H. Raberg, Kylie Seward, Simon L. Pendleton, John T. Andrews, Patrick J. Webber and Joerg M. Schaefer, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aed3379

“Has the next ice age already come and gone?” by Shaun A. Marcott, 22 October 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.aem3295

“A new glacial period may have been taking shape in the Arctic until global warming brought its slow advance to a halt.”

Aristotle wrote, “One swallow does not make a Summer.” To put that into more modern terms, if one sees a noise spike on an oscilloscope, it does not warrant forecasting that the trace will turn into a full-blown periodic signal. Forecasting is always fraught with risk. If that were not the case, most sports betters and day traders would have become rich. That obviously has not happened. One should hedge their bets and base their predictions on the best available evidence around the world, not just on one remnant of a continental glacier of unknown starting thickness.

There isn’t agreement on what the climate sensitivity is for a doubling of CO2 or even whether it is constant; there are even some (Nobel Laureates) who question whether CO2 is the driving force behind climate change. We don’t have solid measurements of how the climate is changing in the groups of the Köppen climate classification. About all that is ever mentioned is that the Arctic is warming 2-4X faster that the global average. Our predictions of weather, especially precipitation, are less than ideal. Yet some will suggest a ‘single swallow’ is sufficient to predict future climate. The hubris is remarkable.

Geologic evidence points to a world that has been much colder and much hotter, for far longer than anything that humans have observed directly because we hadn’t yet evolved. If climate changes attributed to humans are smaller than anything that that has happened before humans were around, one should seriously consider whether attributing the changes to humans is a violation of Occam’s Razor because it fundamentally requires the unexamined assumption that natural variations have magically ceased since humans came on the scene.

It used to be thought that North America only experienced 4 major Pleistocene ice advances — Nebraskan, Kansan, Illinoisan, and Wisconsin. The thinking today is that there were far more than that. It may just be that the Laurentide ice sheet is characterized by frequent advances and retreats. In the manner of T. C. Chamberlain (The Method of Multiple Working Hypotheses) one should probably consider the possibility of the Barnes Ice Cap being unusually sensitive to changes in temperature and precipitation, resulting in its preservation, but not being a particularly reliable indicator of its behavior tomorrow.

How does the Younger Dryas ice advance fit with this?

Your final comment is really excellent. For forty years, I’ve been asking why anyone should think that climate change should, as you put it, “magically” stop just for us.

The question is fundamental to the problem of what to do, if anything. We can only estimate the past variance based on proxies. They inherently have a large uncertainty. The modern warming is based on instrumental measurements and has much smaller uncertainty. I think that it is unreasonable that the natural variations would coincidentally stop about the time of the Industrial Revolution. How do we identify or parse the contributions of natural variation and human contributions?

I haven’t followed the Younger Dryas issue closely. Therefore, I don’t really have an opinion to offer.

“Researchers dated the vegetation using carbon-14, a HARMLESSLY radioactive form of atmospheric carbon that living organisms absorb.”

Carbon-14 may be ubiquitous and in low (trace) concentration, but unless one has incontrovertible evidence that the “Linear — No Threshold” hypothesis is wrong, then the assertion is a little over the top. Personally, I believe that there is a threshold effect, but I don’t have incontrovertible evidence to support it. Personally, I would be more circumspect about using the words “harmlessly radioactive.” They border on being an oxymoron. It is something that we can’t avoid in the environment, but beta particles aren’t something that one should just ignore. Wikipedia says that beta particles can cause mutation in living cells. Thus, the effects may not be noticeable immediately.

#6491. Using Vibrations and AI, Future Robotic Missions Could Handle Buried Rocks Autonomously

Knowing a planet's surface and subsurface structure is vital when planning robotic and crewed missions to explore it. Before landers, rovers, or crew modules reach the surface, astronauts and mission controllers need to know what they will be landing on. For rovers with a limited energy budget, it's also crucial that they can determine how far rough, rocky terrain extends beneath the surface. That way, they won't waste time and energy trying to clear obstacles they can't possibly move.

In short, scientists and astronauts need to know what's on a planet's surface (and beneath it) before they attempt to land there and conduct science operations. Thanks to a team from Virginia Polytechnic Institute and State University (Virginia Tech), scientists could soon have a new set of tools that will allow robotic missions to make these determinations autonomously. These AI-powered tools measure vibrations in surface terrain to determine what lies beneath and how deep structures extend.

The study was led by Yiyan Ruan, a Ph.D. candidate at Virginia Tech, and Erik Komendera, an assistant professor of mechanical engineering (and Ruan's advisor) who once worked as a researcher at NASA's Langley Research Center. The paper detailing their findings was published in IEEE Sensors Journal. The tools they have developed could have profound applications for both space exploration and life on Earth.

View generated from the digital terrain model and the nadir and color channels of the High Resolution Stereo Camera on ESA's Mars Express. Credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin

As they indicate in their paper, estimating the burial depth of partially embedded rocks is a key capability for energy-limited robotic excavation. When obstacles like rock formations are in the way, mission teams need to know how deep the rock extends so they can decide whether to remove the obstacle or avoid it. Ruan and Komendera's solution leverages AI to interpret vibrational data, allowing robots to make those decisions autonomously. As Komendera said in a Virginia Tech press release:

For as long as humans have built things on Earth, we have had to deal with large and heavy obstacles that cannot simply be ignored or scooped out of the way without careful planning. It's easy enough for us to just look at rocks and make some quick, testable judgments. Is this rock resting or partially buried? Can I move this alone or do I need help and tools? But what if robots need to do this? How can robots make those judgments? Now we have an answer.

To test their approach, their team buried 18 concrete blocks of different shapes and sizes in sand at different depths. They then struck the exposed portions of the blocks with an instrumented hammer and remotely measured the vibrations using a device known as a Laser Doppler Vibrometer (LDV). The results were then input into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP), a type of neural network that learns to identify complex, non-linear patterns from data.

Their MLP mapped 11 measurable features to identify the relationship between impulse excitation, exposed rock geometry, and burial depth. Given the range of factors to consider, the task was rather complex. But by teaching their AI to account for them, Ruan and Komendera created models that could reliably determine the blocks' depth.

When the future rovers set down on Mars, they could determine rock depth and obstacle clearance autonomously. Credit: NASA/JPL

"Estimating how deep a rock is buried using vibrations can be tricky," said Ruan. "The feedback is affected by the rock's geometry and the way the soil holds it. By carefully selecting features from vibration measurements and exposed geometry, we were able to produce reliable data using a compact neural network with just two hidden layers."

These models could help robotic missions excavate subsurface rocks, caches of water ice, and remove obstacles along their travel routes. In the meantime, the team plans to keep building datasets and testing their approach for applications on Earth, such as analyzing construction sites and natural disasters to locate where potentially hazardous materials are buried. They could also be used to study unstable rock formations and underground caverns, assisting with resource and construction planning, and advancing exploration of Earth's subsurface.

Further Reading: Virginia Tech, IEEE Sensors Journal

Seeds found in an ancient grave and chemical compounds discovered in mummy hair have revealed people got high on marijuana 2,800 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed the oldest evidence of cannabis use from a 2,800-year-old monumental tomb in Siberia. The presence of plant seeds in the grave and chemical traces of the drug in mummy hair suggest people practiced a funeral ritual that may have involved a grim practice: calming human sacrifice victims with cannabis.

In a study published Thursday (Nov. 5) in the journal Science, researchers investigated the contents of a "royal mound" burial at the Tunnug archaeological site in the Uyuk valley of southern Siberia. Archaeologists discovered four wooden structures containing several log coffins in the middle of the mound. On top of the wooden burial structures were the skeletons of horses that once formed a "spectral cavalcade," a Scythian funeral tradition that involved sacrificing horses and humans. And inside the burial structures, the archaeologists discovered piles of tiny seeds from the plant Cannabis ruderalis, a wild type of cannabis or marijuana.

Cannabis likely originated in Asia and was cultivated thousands of years ago for various purposes, including for ropes and textiles, and 6,000 years ago as an oilseed crop, according to the study. But it's unclear when people learned about the psychoactive properties of the plant. In the fifth century B.C., the ancient Greek historian Herodotus wrote that the Scythian nomads inhaled the fumes from burning hemp seeds. And evidence of cannabis use was previously discovered in a cemetery in China dated to about 500 B.C. The new study, however, pushes back this date by three centuries.

Archaeologists found evidence of cannabis use in a burial mound in southern Siberia.

Researchers discovered more than 1,000 whole cannabis seeds and around 500 partial seeds in the Tunnug burial mound, and they carbon-dated them to between 800 and 760 B.C. They also recovered several human hair samples from the grave. An analysis of the hair revealed signals matching cannabinol and THC (tetrahydrocannabinol), psychoactive chemical compounds found in cannabis. The tests could not determine how much of the drug people consumed, however.

"The molecular traces in the hair and the cannabis seeds come from the same grave and suggest that cannabis was used for its intoxicating properties," study first author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the Max Planck Institute of Geoanthropology in Jena, Germany, said in a statement.

But given the burial context of the discovery, the use of cannabis may have had a darker purpose.

"In this princely tomb, the burials were accompanied by extensive horse sacrifices and, most likely, human sacrifices as well," Caspari said. The tradition of human sacrifice, in particular, "would have potentially made the plant a useful agent to calm individuals who were to be included in the rituals," the researchers wrote in the study.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The new study confirms the ancient use of cannabis in funerals in Central Asia and extends the date back to 2,800 years ago, the researchers noted. Future work is planned but will focus on other aspects of ancient cannabis.

"We have already begun sequencing some of the plant samples," Caspari said. "This will help us learn more about the history of the domestication and spread of the crop soon."

#6488. Researchers Recover DNA from 7,000-Year-Old Leather, Revealing a Link to Goats Alive Today

Ancient DNA recovered from a remarkably preserved piece of 7,000-year-old leather is shedding new light on how prehistoric communities in Spain used domesticated animals.

A 7,000-year-old piece of goat leather discovered in a Spanish burial cave has yielded ancient DNA, allowing scientists to trace a genetic connection between prehistoric livestock and goats living in Spain today. The exceptionally preserved material also provides direct evidence that Early Neolithic communities were processing the hides of domesticated animals.

The findings, published November 4, 2026, in the journal PLOS One, come from a study led by Jolijn A. M. Erven of University College Dublin and colleagues. Their analysis offers a rare glimpse into animal husbandry and leatherworking on the Iberian Peninsula thousands of years before written records.

The leather fragment was recovered from Cueva de los Murciélagos, a burial site in southern Spain known for preserving ancient organic materials. Radiocarbon dating placed the specimen at approximately 7,000 years old. Marks on its surface indicate that the hide had been tanned and perforated, suggesting it was once part of a garment or protective covering before being buried alongside human remains.

Recovering DNA from such ancient leather is particularly difficult in warmer regions, where heat and environmental conditions accelerate the breakdown of genetic material. Despite extensive fragmentation, researchers extracted both mitochondrial DNA, which is inherited through the maternal line, and nuclear DNA, which contains genetic information from both parents.

Francisco Martínez-Sevilla emphasized the unusual preservation conditions: “The preservation of this 7,000-year-old goat leather is exceptional. Cueva de los Murciélagos has preserved organic materials that rarely survive in the archaeological record, offering us a unique opportunity to investigate prehistoric technologies, animal husbandry, and the relationships between human communities and domestic animals.”

Genetic analysis identified the leather as coming from a domestic goat rather than a wild Iberian ibex. Its DNA showed a close relationship to the modern Bermeya goat breed of northern Spain, indicating that a related genetic lineage has persisted on the Iberian Peninsula for thousands of years.

The researchers also detected no evidence of African genetic ancestry in the ancient specimen, unlike the ancestry found in modern European goats. One possible explanation is that genetic exchange involving African goat populations occurred after the Neolithic period. However, the incomplete DNA and limited sample size prevent firm conclusions about when these connections developed or what they might indicate about prehistoric interactions between Iberia and Africa.

Kevin Daly highlighted the genetic link between ancient and living animals: “It is rare to for such ancient, organic materials to retain DNA – but this was one of the few exceptions. With a tiny amount of surviving DNA, we were able to show a link with Iberian breeds today – a genetic connection spanning 7,000 years. This study demonstrates what can done through the collaboration of international multidisciplinary teams – transforming an archaeological object into a link with the living present.”

Reference: “Genetic analysis of 7,000 year old preserved goat leather from Cueva de los Murciélagos (Albuñol, Spain)” by Jolijn A. M.
