#6463. Smithsonian Scientists Built a Virtual Universe 1.5 Billion Light-Years Across

Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in a record-breaking simulation that could reveal new secrets about the Big Bang and the birth of galaxies.

Scientists have recreated the universe’s first 2 billion years in extraordinary detail using one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers. The enormous simulation, called “Lumina,” allows researchers to explore how the earliest stars and galaxies formed, how dark matter influenced their development, and how radiation transformed the young cosmos.

Developed by researchers at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, Lumina is among the largest and most sophisticated simulations of the early universe ever produced. It provides a virtual record of cosmic evolution that scientists can compare with observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) and the Nancy Roman Space Telescope.

The research, published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, could help answer fundamental questions about what happened after the Big Bang. By recreating the interactions between ordinary matter, dark matter, and radiation, scientists can test whether their current theories accurately describe the early universe or whether surprising telescope discoveries point to physics that remains unexplained.

Astronomers have spent centuries studying the sky and developing theories to explain the origins of stars, galaxies, and the enormous structures that fill the universe. Modern supercomputers have added a powerful new approach by allowing scientists to simulate how the cosmos should develop if those theories are correct.

These simulations act as virtual laboratories. Researchers can start with conditions in the young universe, apply the known laws of physics, and calculate how matter and energy evolve over billions of years. The results can then be compared with actual telescope observations.

If the simulated universe resembles what astronomers observe, it strengthens confidence in the underlying models. But if important differences emerge, those discrepancies could reveal missing pieces in our understanding of cosmic history.

“With JWST, the early universe has become an exciting new frontier in astrophysics,” said lead author Oliver Zier, an ITC Fellow at the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian. “To understand what we are seeing with this telescope, we need to translate our theories into detailed predictions. After several years of work, with plenty of ups and downs, it is incredibly rewarding to see the simulation results and watch our predictions come to life in video.”

Lumina sets a new benchmark for a particular class of cosmological simulations known as radiation hydrodynamics simulations. These models calculate how gas, dark matter, and radiation influence one another as the universe develops, making it possible to investigate the processes responsible for creating the earliest galaxies.

Dark matter is an invisible form of matter whose gravitational influence helps shape galaxies and other cosmic structures. Meanwhile, radiation from stars and other luminous objects affects the surrounding gas, changing its temperature and physical state. Capturing these interactions is essential for understanding how the early universe evolved.

Lumina follows these processes across the first 2 billion years of cosmic history, revealing how young galaxies formed and how their light gradually altered the enormous clouds of gas that filled the space between them.

The simulation’s scale is particularly remarkable. It encompasses a cube of space approximately 1.5 billion light-years along each side, representing more than 100 times the volume covered by previous comparable simulations. That enormous region is similar in scale to the volumes of the universe astronomers can investigate with today’s most advanced telescopes.

One of Lumina’s most important advances involves a process called reionization, which fundamentally changed the gas that filled the early universe.

As the first generations of luminous objects emerged, their radiation stripped electrons from atoms of hydrogen and helium, transforming much of the surrounding gas into an ionized state. This transition helped establish the conditions found throughout the universe today.

Lumina is the first simulation of its kind to model helium reionization as it happened while allowing the resulting changes to immediately affect other processes unfolding within the simulated cosmos.

“We feel incredibly fortunate to be building simulations like Lumina,” said Aaron Smith, an assistant professor of physics at the University of Texas at Dallas and an author on the paper. “For the first time, we can follow along as both hydrogen and helium changed into their modern form across such an enormous volume of the universe, while still resolving the galaxies and other luminous objects driving that transformation.”

By capturing both the large-scale evolution of cosmic gas and the smaller structures responsible for transforming it, Lumina gives scientists an unusually comprehensive view of how the young universe developed.

Building such an enormous and detailed virtual universe required extraordinary computing power.

The team used Frontier, a supercomputer at Oak Ridge National Laboratory in Tennessee that ranks among the fastest machines in the world. More than 15,000 graphics processing units worked together to perform the immense number of calculations needed to produce Lumina.

That processing power made it possible to simulate a much larger region of the early universe than previously comparable models while preserving enough detail to investigate individual galaxies, stars, and black holes.

This combination of scale and precision is especially valuable because cosmic evolution involves processes operating across vastly different distances. Changes occurring around individual galaxies can influence the gas between them, while the overall distribution of matter helps determine where galaxies form.

Lumina is designed to do more than recreate the past. It gives astronomers a way to investigate competing explanations for how the universe developed and to make predictions that can be tested against real observations.

Future research will examine how gas travels between galaxies, how radiation left over from the Big Bang influenced cosmic evolution, and how regions of particularly intense star formation emerged and changed over time.

As observations from JWST, Roman, and other telescopes provide increasingly detailed views of the distant universe, Lumina will help researchers interpret what they find.

By comparing the simulated cosmos with the real one, scientists may discover where existing theories succeed, where they fall short, and what new physics might be needed to explain the universe’s earliest chapters.

Reference: “Introducing the lumina project: large-volume radiation-hydrodynamic simulations of the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization” by Oliver Zier, Aaron Smith, Xuejian Shen, Rongrong Liu, Rahul Kannan, Sonja M Koehler, Volker Springel, Rüdiger Pakmor, Mark Vogelsberger, Teodora-Elena Bulichi and Lars Hernquist, 26 October 2026, Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. DOI: 10.1093/mnras/stag1469

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6459. Hidden Brain Signals Could Predict Alzheimer’s Years Before Symptoms Appear

Subtle differences in brain activity may reveal who is most vulnerable to Alzheimer’s disease and who could remain mentally sharp well into old age.

Distinct patterns of brain activity may predict Alzheimer’s disease years before memory problems or hallmark brain changes appear. Stanford Medicine researchers have developed a scoring system that identifies people at greater risk of cognitive decline while also recognizing those whose brains show unusual resilience to aging.

The study, published November 4 in Science Advances, found that these patterns could predict future cognitive decline more effectively than several established risk indicators, including genetics and Alzheimer’s biomarkers.

Researchers analyzed resting-state functional MRI scans from 180 “super agers,” adults aged 75 and older with memory abilities comparable to those of typical 45-year-olds, and 110 similarly aged people diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease.

“Normal, cognitively unimpaired individuals are pretty heterogeneous in terms of their biological abnormalities,” said Yu Zhang, PhD, assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine. “Simply comparing super agers with such a heterogeneous population makes it challenging to define what is critical in terms of resilient or vulnerable brain patterns.”

The team identified distinct patterns of activity across brain networks and developed the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome (ARC) score. The system distinguished super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with approximately 85% accuracy.

The researchers tested the ARC score in more than 1,300 cognitively healthy adults aged 55 to 70. Although participants initially showed no clear differences in cognitive performance, their brain activity patterns predicted different outcomes over follow-up periods extending as long as 12 years.

People with more Alzheimer’s-like activity experienced faster cognitive decline and were more likely to develop amyloid-beta plaques or receive an Alzheimer’s diagnosis. Those with super-ager-like patterns generally maintained stronger cognitive abilities.

“We used the ARC score to make a prediction of how likely this patient will convert into mild cognitive impairment or Alzheimer’s disease,” said Kanhao (Alex) Zhao, PhD, a Stanford postdoctoral scholar and lead author.

“We want to address a major challenge in the Alzheimer’s field nowadays — most studies are looking at well-known Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers, such as amyloid-beta or tau. But those are observable at relatively late stages of the disease,” Zhang said. “What we really care about is defining early markers that can detect earlier signs of cognitive decline and potentially help us deliver timely interventions to people.”

The ARC score performed as well as or better than existing biomarkers at predicting progression toward Alzheimer’s, while offering information at an earlier stage. Combining the score with traditional biomarkers improved predictions further.

“We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer’s disease,” Zhao said. “Our model shows comparable or better prediction ability, and it can do so at an earlier time point. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves.”

The researchers also found a relationship between ARC scores and brain age, a broader measure of aging derived from functional MRI data.

“I’m excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline,” Zhang said.

ARC scores are not diagnostic, and they do not determine a person’s future. Brain activity can change with aging, injuries, and neuropsychiatric conditions. Researchers hope that targeted interventions might eventually shift vulnerable brain patterns toward greater resilience.

Potential approaches include cognitive training and transcranial magnetic stimulation, which uses magnetic pulses to influence brain activity. However, these interventions have not been shown to prevent cognitive decline by changing ARC patterns.

“There are two main components: One is to know which part of the brain to target, the other is how we should change it,” Zhang said. “That’s why identifying the super-ager brain resilience pattern is a critical component — so we know what a good pattern should be.”

Zhang’s team is planning a trial to examine whether cognitive training can alter ARC scores.

“But the critical part is that we have to intervene at an early stage,” Zhang said. “That’s why we focus on the cognitively unimpaired population to identify super-ager-like versus Alzheimer’s-like individuals. If we can precisely identify such as early indicator, I’m optimistic that we can reverse or prevent this process through advanced intervention technologies.”

Reference: “A functional connectome identifies vulnerability to cognitive decline and Alzheimer’s disease progression” by Kanhao Zhao, Hua Xie, Gregory A. Fonzo, Nancy B. Carlisle, Tovia Jacobs, Ricardo S. Osorio, Arpana Church, Feng Vankee Lin, Yu Zhang and Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, 4 November 2026, Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed9351

The study received funding from the National Institutes of Health (grants R21AG080425, R01MH129694 and R01AG081768), a joint Rosenkranz Foundation-Knight Initiative program, an Alzheimer’s Association grant and a Lehigh University CORE grant.

#6457. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Laura Sanders: What’s a voice you like to listen to?

Kate Nilson: That is a great question. I hope my students don’t listen to this. I was having Snoop Dogg read their assignments to me the other day, just because I thought it was funny. But I don’t know if I would say that’s my favorite.

Sanders: That’s speech language pathologist and professor Kate Nilson. And if you’re wondering, this is a real, legitimate thing that anyone can do.

Snoop Dogg audio: Vector mathematics. Think about a car trip. Your displacement from your starting point is a vector.

Snoop Dogg: I’m glad to be the voice of reason so you can focus better, understand more, and enjoy listening to the internet in the voice of Snoop Dogg.

Sanders: Welcome to The Deep End, Talk To Me. In this episode, we’re stepping out of the lab and into the new digital world we all live in. We’re going to get into some of the good, bad and strange scenarios that come up when voices can be cloned and let loose in the world. Let’s talk about it.

[voices] Hey mom, can I tell you something? Hi. Do you want to talk? That added layer of it being you. Hello? Your voice. Hi. Your voice is you.

Sanders: As we’ve heard in earlier episodes, ultra-realistic voice clones can be extremely meaningful to people who can no longer speak.

Jules Rodriguez: So when I first heard my cloned voice, it felt like I reappeared. When my wife first heard it, she cried because of how close it sounded like me before I lost my voice. I knew of the potential of this technology at that moment.

Sanders: These digital copies of voices have restored connections to their loved ones.

MA Fernandez: You know, the first thing he played for me, I was like chills all over.

Patrick Darling: The first time I performed with the AI voice, I was surprised how physically connected I felt with it.

Sanders: These voice clones have been transformative for people who have lost the ability to talk. But the existence of realistic digital copies of voices has effects that ripple farther out into society.

Hany Farid: So here’s where sort of state of the art is. Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, anybody doing or saying anything.

Sanders: That’s Hany Farid. He’s a computer scientist at Dartmouth College and cofounder of Get Real Security, a firm that sorts real from fake. I called him to ask how these voice clones have changed our world.

Farid: If you had asked me, I don’t know, five years ago, is this possible? I would say, yeah, maybe, but not anytime soon. And then all of a sudden, boom, it just came out of nowhere.

Farid: It’s essentially like they’re flipping a coin.

Sanders: But there’s another, even higher bar for voice clones to pass. That’s whether they can mimic a specific person well enough to slip by undetected.

Farid: The other question too is what if I, for example, play a real voice sample of your voice, Laura, and then I clone your voice using my favorite AI cloning technology, and then I type something and I get you to say something, and I play those two samples to somebody, and I don’t ask them if it’s real/fake. I say, is this the same person? Is the AI not only able to make something that is natural, but is it identity preserving?

In many cases, that good comes because these voices are both extremely realistic and extremely good at sounding like a specific person. People want their voice to sound like theirs.

Farid: People with ALS can speak with what sounds like their voice. We’ve seen beautiful examples of that. Translation, right? We can now translate things in real time from any language and it’ll sound like you. I’ve made videos of myself speaking any language I want and it sounds like me, and it’s amazing. It’s really cool.

Sanders: These new ways to connect are very impressive, but as with any technology, these powerful realistic auditory dupes can be repurposed to cause harm.

Farid: My voice was cloned by an attacker. I was working a very sensitive case with an attorney. Not many people knew about it. And he got a call from my phone number in my voice talking about the case. And after about three minutes, got suspicious, hung up, called me back. Wasn’t me.

Sanders: Bigger picture, we’ve reached a point where it’s safe to say we can no longer automatically trust digital versions of other people. That applies to the images and sounds on my computer screen as I talked with Farid. Maybe this 2-D picture and sound coming from my laptop is a fake.

Farid: So this two-dimensional version that you and I are sharing now, all right, I can’t control that. That can be stolen. The three-dimensional is right now still me, right? We don’t have the robots that can mimic us. Yet is the end of that sentence.

Sanders: So my interview with Farid was alarming. There are parallels here to any new technology, though. Today, people talk about brain rot from junk online. But remember that television was also going to rot our brains.

[Audio] Its content affects us. So does the sheer weight of the hours we watch.

Sanders: Phones today are the downfall of society, but actual wired telephones encountered really similar resistance when they first started appearing in homes.

[Audio] In Chicago, Sharon Krall’s 15-year-old daughter Angie got so addicted to one teen talk line, she ran up an $850 bill in one month.

Sanders: No big technological advance has escaped this fear.

[Audio] We need teachers who are deeply concerned about how the modern media of communication are changing education.

Sanders: Electricity, bicycles, railways, novels, even the printing press all had their skeptics. So this fear of the new thing has been around a long time. Are synthetic voices created by AI any different? Here’s Karina Nagin from Bridging Voice.

Nagin: Taking off my Bridging Voice hat and just as like a human being in the world, I think there’s a lot of things about AI that I’m very concerned. Deepfakes, the ability to make videos and audio that sound and look just like someone saying something that they’re not saying, I think is a huge, huge concern to our news and public information.

Sanders: Nagin then pivots back to the good, the possibilities here.

Nagin: And then I put on my little hat in my space that I am like, this is how we can harness this to impact people’s lives in our space right now. And I think both conversations need to happen.

Sanders: It occurs to me that I’m seeing the ends of the spectrum here. The stories Farid told me were awful. And the stories that Jules and Casey and others have told me were really, really life-changingly good. Yet these ends of the spectrum are the easy ones. The ones you can look at and say, that’s a horrible way to use this technology. Or that is a powerful and good way to use a voice clone. Between those two poles is the middle ground. That’s the place where Snoop explains cell biology.

[Audio] The membrane separates the material outside the cell.

Sanders: Good, because it’s helping people learn more about mitochondria and who couldn’t use more of that in their lives. Bad, because Snoop never actually said those words, and it’s weird to pretend otherwise.

[Audio] The artists of the Renaissance said that man’s main concern should be for man.

Sanders: There are deepfakes of the late great physicist Richard Feynman delivering famous lectures.

[Audio] The problem is the laws of physics themselves. Let me start with something basic. The next star over from us is called Proxima Centauri.

Sanders: Good because it introduces some amazing physics to people who would otherwise scroll past? Bad because it’s somewhat disrespectful and possibly inaccurate? There aren’t easy answers here. This murky middle gets even murkier with the invention of griefbots. Those are digital versions of people who have passed away. And that means that special voices can keep talking to us long after the body that created them is gone.

I read a poignant post online written by a guy who had lost his dad after years of dementia. He missed his dad’s voice, he wrote, so he cloned it. He paid for the starter pack, submitted three minutes of his dad’s audio, and he wrote, quote, a few minutes later, I had a scarily accurate clone of my dead father’s voice. He goes on to write, quote, my family and I had a good cathartic cry upon hearing the results. I had his cloned voice read the Lord’s Prayer as well as ‘Twas the Night before Christmas. Just hearing his simulated voice again is such a blessing and is helping me in the grief process. End quote.

There are lots of companies now offering this exact thing. A casual search online gets me to a company that sells chats with dead loved ones. There’s a big orange button to click that says bring them back to life. A 2024 documentary called “Eternal You” follows the stories of people as they grapple with this idea. Here’s a little bit of the trailer.

[Audio] We are on the verge of a new era. Hi. It’s like, it’s the funniest thing. It’s like, what’s the first thing you say to someone that’s dead? Like, welcome back.

Sanders: Griefbots or digital avatars of loved ones offer a bridge from the past to the present, a way to remember vividly. But they are also a denial, of sorts, that all life must come to an end.

[Audio] And what I can tell you is that AI really is changing the way that we interact with death.

Sanders: That’s from a 2025 TEDx talk from Dylan Thomas Doyle. He’s a former hospital chaplain, current academic researcher at Northwestern University and self-described philosophy bro. His work explores death and AI.

[Audio] Imagine that you are at a funeral, and you’re sitting there in silent reflection, and all of a sudden, on the back screen in the auditorium, a woman’s face appears. And it’s the face of a woman named Marina. And her hologram, she starts talking to you, and she starts asking you how you’re doing today. And you answer her, and then you ask her a question back. And she responds as if she is still there.

Sanders: I called Doyle to ask about the implications of using technology this way.

Doyle: It was on my radar as a chaplain and a technology researcher, I started thinking through, well, what is the actual impact of this technology on people? So what is it like to hear the voice, in the context of this podcast, the voice of, say, your father who’s passed away while you’re actively grieving their death? And they’re not just repeating what they said or a journal entry in their voice, but like, creating new stories and new relationships through their voice. It gives a lot of people existential ick, is what I’ve heard. And that’s something that I really, I’m curious about.

Sanders: There’s tension here, Doyle tells me.

Doyle: So there’s this push force where you’re like, this is not right. We don’t have the narrative or cultural script to understand what’s going on there. But then as people are beginning to use it, there’s a comfort that comes out of it. So we’re working in that tension space between this comfort that comes, then you’re still dealing with this push away from this technology of it just being weird in a way that people are still grappling with language, I think, to describe.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.

#6455. A New Approach Could Eliminate “Zombie” Cancer Cells That Survive Chemotherapy

Some cancer cells survive chemotherapy by blocking their own self-destruct system, but researchers have found a way to switch it back on and kill those cells.

Chemotherapy can leave behind cancer cells that have stopped dividing but remain alive and capable of helping a tumor recover. These survivors can draw support from an unexpected source, the immune system, by activating responses that normally help the body repair damaged tissue.

This “zombie-like state,” called “premature senescence,” involves dramatic changes. Within a few days of exposure to chemotherapy, senescent cells can grow to almost ten times the size of a normal cell and increase the activity of genes associated with wound healing. Their ability to release inflammatory mediators, molecules that attract immune cells, also increases greatly.

The danger lies in the range of jobs the immune system performs. Alongside protecting against infection, it coordinates the repair and replacement of damaged tissue. During wound healing, it stimulates cell division to replace cells lost through injury and triggers the growth of blood vessels that deliver extra oxygen and nutrients. Normally, this complex, carefully coordinated process ensures that new cells appear only where and when they are needed.

Cancers can exploit those repair functions by masquerading as damaged tissue. Instead of destroying malignant cells, the immune system can then help them divide and obtain more oxygen and nutrients. That behavior has led cancers to be described as “wounds that do not heal,” although how they activate the immune system’s wound-healing capabilities remains poorly understood.

Research newly published in Science Advances identifies a mechanism that helps cancer cells survive chemotherapy and enter senescence. Scientists at the Smurfit Institute of Genetics at Trinity College Dublin found that molecules called Inhibitor of Apoptosis Proteins, or IAPs, can protect tumor cells from the killing effects of commonly used chemotherapy drugs. The team was led by Professor Seamus Martin, Smurfit Professor of Medical Genetics, and Dr. Gokhan Gunay, a postdoctoral research fellow.

The researchers found that DNA damage caused by chemotherapy switched on molecules called “Death Receptors,” which can trigger a cell’s self-destruct program. IAPs neutralized their cell-killing effects. That protection allowed surviving tumor cells to enter senescence, where they could coordinate wound-healing responses that benefit the tumor and help it recover after treatment.

But the cells’ continued survival also depended heavily on IAPs, creating a vulnerability. In the study, compounds called IAP antagonists neutralized these proteins and reactivated the Death Receptor self-destruct program, selectively eliminating the senescent cells. The same proteins that helped the cells escape chemotherapy thus remained essential to keeping them alive afterward.

Senescent cells are also relevant beyond cancer treatment. They accumulate in tissues as people age, and that buildup is thought to contribute to age-related inflammation and declining normal function in many tissues.

For cancer treatment, the findings identify both an escape mechanism and a possible way to target the cells that use it. Tumors that evade chemotherapy remain a major challenge for clinicians, and improved treatments could offer patients better survival and quality of life.

Professor Martin said, “Discovering how tumors can evade the cell-killing effects of chemotherapy and enter senescence is an important and challenging problem.

“These new findings suggest ways in which we may be able to lower the defenses of tumors by neutralizing IAPs after the delivery of chemotherapeutic drugs, which should block their entry to senescence and kill more cells of the tumor.”

Reference: “Death receptors regulate entry to therapy-induced senescence and orchestrate addiction to IAPs” by Gokhan Gunay, Seren Hamsici, Vaishnavi Venugopalan, Aoife Costigan, Melanie Fritsch, Aislinn Gallagher Aldave, Anne Huber, Brianna Fernandez, Hande Efe-Cicek, Pavel Davidovich, Pavitha Parathan, Akash Srivaths, Natalie Hudson, Eleanor Noone, Jeffrey O’Callaghan, Lisa A. Mielke, Sarah L. Doyle, Sabrina L. Spencer, Matthew Campbell, Conor J. Kearney, Hamid Kashkar and Seamus J. Martin, 23 October 2026, Science Advances. DOI: 10.1126/sciadv.aed4541

Work in The Martin laboratory at Trinity is supported by the European Research Council (Project DESTRESS) and Research Ireland.

Live Science readers respond to a recent poll about whether they'd visit the Red Planet even with potential health risks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For centuries, Mars has been seen as a potential place for future human settlements. But long-duration space travel comes with serious risks to astronauts' health, including those resulting from cosmic radiation and the effects of microgravity.

A new study found that rats that were exposed to radiation similar to what astronauts might encounter during a Mars mission developed more scar tissue around their hearts' small blood vessels compared with a control group. Although the findings haven't been validated in humans, the results contribute to growing concerns about the potential effects of long-haul space missions on astronauts' health.

Given these new findings, Live Science asked its readers whether they'd travel to the Red Planet, despite these potential health risks. Over 240 readers weighed in, with 65% picking "No, I don't think the risks are worth it."

Interestingly enough, the comments reflect a slightly different trend. One reader wrote, "Any pioneers who travel to Mars will be facing the prospect of death and never coming back. Even if they make it back, there are any number of health issues that could come up. These risks have not stopped people from exploring throughout human history. The bigger question is who to send?"

Other commenters echoed this sentiment, with another reader posting, "Explorers in the past have always been exposed to unusual risks; without the risk takers we would still believe the world is flat."

Beyond the feelings that Mars will be explored anyway, despite the health risks, other commenters highlighted the cost of these missions, with one reader stating, "Sending flesh water balloons to Mars is ridiculous. For the cost of one human on Mars, we could literally probe the entire solar system and map/sample/rove every planet and every major Moon."

Others highlighted the mental and emotional cost of a trip to Mars. "As a devoted sci-fi fan for decades, I always wished I could go into space," another reader noted. "Now that I am 77 years old, I realize I would miss the outdoors. The wind and trees, the birdsong and sweet grass under my feet would be a devastating loss. Let the brave explorers go instead. Life is too brief to leave this planet for the uncertainty and dangers of space travel."

Do you agree with these readers? Let us know your thoughts in the comments!

Kenna Hughes-Castleberry is the Content Manager at Live Science. Formerly, she was the Content Manager at Space.com and before that the Science Communicator at JILA, a physics research institute. Her beats include physics, health, environmental science, technology, AI, animal intelligence, corvids, and cephalopods.

#6452. Scientists Discover a Hidden Weakness in Prostate Cancer That Could Transform Treatment

A newly identified vulnerability in a cancer-driving protein could pave the way for a different approach to treating prostate cancer.

Researchers at the University of Michigan have identified a potential way to target a protein that helps drive prostate cancer but has long been considered beyond the reach of drugs. Their experimental compound, PBITE-1, interfered with the protein’s cancer-promoting activity in laboratory models, offering a possible starting point for more targeted treatments.

The protein, known as ERG, becomes abnormally active when two genes, TMPRSS2 and ERG, fuse together. This genetic rearrangement occurs in roughly half of prostate cancer cases among patients of European ancestry and promotes tumor cell growth and migration.

For years, ERG has been considered “undruggable” because it appeared to lack the molecular pockets where medications typically attach. In the new study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, researchers discovered an accessible pocket in a region called the PNT domain, which helps regulate ERG’s interactions with other proteins.

After screening more than 1,600 compounds, the team identified a promising molecule and refined it into PBITE-1. In experiments involving prostate cancer cell lines and laboratory models of human and mouse prostate tissue, the compound inhibited ERG activity, triggered cancer cell death, and reduced the ability of cancer cells to invade surrounding tissue.

“Although we were the first to identify the gene fusion as a driver of prostate cancer, it was challenging to find a drug target for ERG,” said Arul Chinnaiyan, M.D., Ph.D., S.P. Hicks Professor of Pathology and member of the Rogel Cancer Center.

Most existing prostate cancer therapies focus on androgen receptors, proteins that respond to hormones such as testosterone. These receptors can activate the TMPRSS2-ERG fusion, helping fuel tumor growth. Drugs that block androgen signaling can slow the disease, but tumors often develop resistance, and treatment can cause side effects that affect quality of life.

Targeting ERG directly could provide an alternative approach for patients whose tumors carry the gene fusion, rather than relying exclusively on treatments that interfere with hormone signaling.

“This work shows that instead of treating all prostate cancer as one disease, we have the potential to personalize therapy for subtypes of prostate cancer.”

PBITE-1 remains an experimental research tool, and its effects have not been established in patients. Further research will be needed to determine whether compounds targeting ERG can be developed into safe and effective medicines.

“Although it is unlikely that PBITE-1 is ready to become a drug any time soon, this study shows that ERG is a druggable target,” Chinnaiyan said.

“It is exciting that we now have a path forward to target ERG in prostate cancer.”

Reference: “A ligandable PNT domain establishes ERG as a directly targetable oncogenic driver in prostate cancer” by Xiaoju Wang, Wenyan Liu, Jiehao Yang, Jean Ching-Yi Tien, Yu Chang, Rahul Mannan, Somnath Mahapatra, Yang Zhou, Lihao Gan, Xuhong Cao, Jiayi Zhou, Yuping Zhang, Sharpkate Shaker, Yichao Huang, Hang Qiao, Rudana Hamadeh, Grafton Ervine, Cynthia Wang, Fengyun Su, Rui Wang, Lanbo Xiao, Raghunath Ranga Sudharshan, Arvind Rao, Zaneta Nikolovska-Coleska, Cole Stephens, Lifeng Pan, James J. Chou, Debashish Sahu, Jeanne Stuckey, Zhen Wang, Ke Ding and Arul M. Chinnaiyan, 7 July 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2537437123

#6451. How hawkmoths turned their genitals into bat-busting weapons

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Hawkmoths can create ultrasonic bursts that thwart the sonar of predatory bats

The pink-spotted hawkmoth (Agrius cingulata) is one of many species whose males make ultrasound by scraping specialized genital scales against spines along the abdomen.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

When a bat closes in, some hawkmoths fight back with their genitalia. By rasping specialized scales on their sex organs against structures on their abdomens, the moths unleash bursts of ultrasound that can scramble the sonar a hungry bat uses to lock onto prey.

But this acoustic counterattack is no evolutionary one-off. Relentless pressure from predators has pushed these otherwise tasty insects to reinvent this defensive tactic up to seven times throughout their evolution, with separate lineages arriving at distinct anatomical solutions to the same threat, researchers report November 4 in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The findings suggest that the high-frequency acoustic skirmishes playing out overhead each night, beyond the range of human hearing, may be far more varied than scientists realized.

“Clearly the hawkmoths as a whole have more tricks up their sleeve,” says Marc Holderied, a sensory biologist and bioacoustics researcher at the University of Bristol in England who was not involved in the study.

The discovery builds on more than a decade of research by sensory ecologist Jesse Barber, now at the American Museum of Natural History in New York City, and entomologist Akito Kawahara of the Florida Museum of Natural History in Gainesville. Those scientists’ earlier work showed that moths across multiple families, from tiger moths and fruit-piercing moths to geometer moths and jewel caterpillar moths, produce ultrasound in response to bat attacks. Other insects, including some beetles and fireflies, do too.

But among the most striking defenders are hawkmoths, a family of some 1,600 mostly nocturnal, torpedo-shaped speedsters, also known as sphinx moths, that hover at flowers like hummingbirds. Many fend off bats by scraping their genitalia like a fingernail dragged along a comb, producing ultrasonic clicks that can disrupt the predators’ sonar.

The anatomical diversity of these sound-producing systems, however, and how they evolved remained poorly understood. So Barber, Kawahara and their team, including Florida museum colleague and evolutionary biologist Paul Masonick, combined audio recordings of male hawkmoths responding to bat calls with high-resolution imaging of preserved specimens from overlapping species. Although some females also produce ultrasound, the researchers focused on males because female sound creation remains too poorly documented for systematic analysis.

Among the 143 species tested, 77 produced ultrasound. They did so in three distinct ways. All three rely on a patch of enlarged, football-shaped scales on the male’s genital valves, which are paired structures used to clasp females during mating. But what those scales scrape against varies.

Some rub the scales against a row of corresponding scales near the rear of the abdomen. Others drag them across stiff spines jutting from the abdomen’s edge. Still others rasp them over a field of microscopic bumps on the insect’s underside, a previously unidentified part of the sound-making apparatus.

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

Paul Masonick/Florida Museum of Natural History

These mechanical differences are reflected in the sounds themselves. Moths that scrape their genital scales against spines or tiny bumps tend to make more continuous noise, with greater potential to jam bat sonar. Those that scrape scales against other scales produce irregular bursts, which may startle attackers or mimic the warning calls of foul-tasting prey.

Notably, moths that scrape against the newly identified bumpy surface have the broadest acoustic repertoire, with even close relatives sounding quite different. That flexibility could give them more options for evolving new defenses against bats, notes Nick Dowdy, an evolutionary biologist at the Milwaukee Public Museum who was not involved in the research. Other groups, by comparison, may be more constrained by their anatomy, he says, leaving them “locked into certain strategies.”

The authors estimate that genitalia-enabled ultrasound production evolved independently at least four and as many as seven times between roughly 5 million and 30 million years ago. According to Masonick, it is a vivid example of convergent evolution in which the same predatory menace repeatedly drove the moths to adapt similar behaviors through different anatomical routes.

But the evolutionary arms race was not a one-way street, he points out. Several hawkmoth lineages that shifted toward twilight or daytime activity subsequently lost their specialized sound-producing machinery.

“It goes to show how intense bat predation is on insects,” Masonick says. “It’s been a major driver of insect evolution.”

#6446. Is Einstein Wrong? Deep-Sea Neutrinos Put the Laws of Physics to the Test

Scientists are testing whether one of Einstein’s most fundamental principles holds true throughout the Universe.

A neutrino telescope deep in the Mediterranean Sea has put one of Einstein’s fundamental principles to a new test. After analyzing 5,828 atmospheric neutrino candidate events, scientists found no evidence that Lorentz invariance, a cornerstone of relativity, had been violated. Their findings place new restrictions on theories suggesting that the laws of physics might behave differently under certain conditions.

The international KM3NeT collaboration conducted the study using KM3NeT/ORCA, an underwater detector designed to investigate neutrinos and their unusual behavior. Published in the Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics (JCAP), the research establishes the first direct experimental limits on certain possible violations involving muon and tau neutrinos, two types of these elusive particles.

Lorentz invariance requires the fundamental laws of physics to remain unchanged for observers moving at different constant velocities or facing different directions. Some theories of quantum gravity, which attempt to unite general relativity with quantum physics, suggest that this principle might not hold perfectly at extremely small scales.

One possibility is that spacetime is not truly continuous but consists of tiny, discrete units. If such a structure exists, it could produce subtle deviations from the predictions of relativity.

“We still don’t know whether our spacetime is continuous or might be discrete,” explains Alba Domi, a researcher at the Erlangen Center for Astroparticle Physics (ECAP), Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, and one of the study’s corresponding authors. “Looking for violations of Lorentz invariance is one way to investigate this possibility.”

Neutrinos are exceptionally difficult to detect because they interact so weakly with matter. Vast numbers pass through Earth without leaving a trace, allowing them to travel enormous distances with little interference.

These particles also possess an unusual ability: they can transform between different types, or “flavor” (this is the term used by scientists), as they travel. Known as neutrino oscillation, this phenomenon follows mathematical predictions that scientists can test against observations. Unexpected changes in these oscillations could indicate previously unknown physical effects, including violations of Lorentz invariance.

To search for such discrepancies, the researchers examined 1.4 years of observations collected by KM3NeT/ORCA. At the time, the telescope was operating with only six detection units. The team compared the neutrinos’ measured energies and arrival directions with theoretical predictions to identify potential departures from established physics.

The analysis revealed no evidence of Lorentz invariance violation. However, it established tighter constraints on certain possible effects, including those that could influence oscillations between muon and tau neutrinos.

Despite relying on an early version of the detector, the results were competitive with measurements from established experiments such as IceCube and Super-Kamiokande, which have collected neutrino data over much longer periods.

“These results show the potential of KM3NeT/ORCA to test fundamental principles of physics, even with a relatively small detector,” says Lukas Hennig, a PhD student at ECAP and the study’s other corresponding author. “With more data and an expanding detector, we will be able to search for even smaller effects.”

As KM3NeT/ORCA expands toward its full planned configuration, researchers expect to improve their sensitivity to possible deviations from relativity. They also hope to extend these investigations to KM3NeT/ARCA, a detector designed to study much higher-energy neutrinos originating from distant astrophysical sources.

Some proposed violations of Lorentz invariance could become more pronounced as neutrino energy increases or as particles travel across greater distances. Neutrinos arriving from distant cosmic sources may therefore offer a way to test effects too small to detect with atmospheric neutrinos.

“ARCA could be particularly well suited to this kind of research, but we don’t yet have enough astrophysical neutrino events to perform such an analysis,” explains Domi.

Reference: “Atmospheric neutrino constraints on Lorentz invariance violation with the first six detection units of KM3NeT/ORCA” by O. Adriani et al., 4 November 2026, Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics. DOI: 10.1088/1475-7516/2026/11/012

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6444. A New Iron Age? Scientists Uncover a Potential Game Changer for Clean Energy

Scientists are exploring how iron powder could transform renewable energy storage and transportation while giving aging coal power plants a new purpose.

Iron powder could help transform old coal power plants into a source of climate-neutral electricity, according to a new study from the Karlsruhe Institute of Technology (KIT). Researchers found that this recyclable fuel could help keep Europe’s power supply stable during extended periods of weak wind and sunlight, particularly in regions where other forms of energy storage are limited.

The process relies on a cycle in which iron powder is burned to generate heat, producing iron oxide, commonly known as rust. Hydrogen produced using renewable energy can then remove the oxygen from the iron oxide, restoring the metal so it can be used again. “This works in a cycle that emits no carbon dioxide or environmentally harmful substances,” said Julia Schuler from KIT’s Institute for Industrial Production (IIP).

One potential advantage is that iron powder could be used in existing coal power plants without replacing all their equipment. “When burned, iron powder behaves very much like coal. We wanted to find out whether it was possible to repurpose existing coal power plants to iron-firing,” said Schuler.

According to Schuler, most modifications would involve the equipment responsible for generating heat. Other major components, including steam turbines, generators, and connections to the electricity grid, could remain in service. Germany may be particularly well suited to this approach because of its large fleet of coal power plants and the possibility of retaining existing heating networks and other infrastructure.

Iron powder could also provide a practical way to move renewable energy across long distances. Electricity generated by coastal wind farms or solar facilities in desert regions could be used to produce hydrogen, which would convert iron oxide into iron. The resulting powder could then be transported to another location and burned to recover the stored energy.

Unlike hydrogen, which requires specialized pipelines, import terminals, and underground storage facilities, iron powder is relatively straightforward to transport and store for extended periods. This could reduce the infrastructure investment needed to move renewable energy between regions. Surplus renewable electricity generated within Europe could also be used to regenerate iron locally through an intermediate hydrogen production step.

To investigate the technology’s potential, KIT scientists built on findings from the Clean Circles research project. In a study funded by Stiftung Energieforschung Baden-Württemberg (Baden-Württemberg energy-research foundation), they expanded the established PERSEUS energy model to include iron-fueled power plants, facilities for regenerating iron, and the infrastructure needed for storage and transportation.

The researchers then simulated the development of a climate-neutral European energy system through 2050, comparing iron with competing technologies such as batteries, hydrogen storage, and hydrogen power plants. Iron-fired power plants appeared in the lowest-cost energy system across every scenario examined, although the results did not suggest that iron would replace hydrogen.

The greatest benefits emerged in countries with limited hydropower resources or few suitable locations for underground hydrogen storage. In these regions, iron could help maintain electricity supplies during prolonged shortages of wind and solar generation. It could also reduce demand on hydrogen pipelines and import facilities when their capacity becomes constrained.

“Iron might play a very special, but economically meaningful role for reaching climate-neutrality and in reliably making renewables available,” said Schuler.

Whether a new “iron age” emerges in electricity generation will depend largely on two unresolved technical and economic questions: how extensively existing coal power plants must be modified and how efficiently iron oxide can be converted back into reusable iron. The simulations indicate that iron could complement hydrogen in a climate-neutral energy system, but its practical competitiveness will depend on how these processes perform outside the model.

Reference: “A new iron age? The potential role of iron fuel in Europe’s clean energy transition” by Julia Schuler, Armin Ardone, Viktor Slednev and Wolf Fichtner, 8 June 2026, Chem Circularity. DOI: 10.1016/j.checir.2026.100047

The weakest links in this proposal for eliminating CO2 are mining, beneficiating the ore, pelletizing, smelting, and then converting the iron to powder. Next is transporting the burned iron to the hydrogen facility, crushing to make a powder, and then back to the burner. Make no mistake, these are energy intensive operations. Where is that energy going to come from?

A plus is that the iron is not consumed, it’s continually reused. Basically it’s just a transport vehicle for oxygen.

The whole point of a battery system is that we don’t care where the electricity comes from. So, if you could have a system where you plug some containers, or a small building, into a wind farm (or just off the grid, to soak up the excess solar during the day), then you convert thee iron oxide back into iron powder.

Then you ‘burn it’ (oxidise it), to extract the energy, and have the same iron left over to process back into iron powder.

At some point you don’t need any more iron. Not like we don’t already have plenty around.

#6441. Dinosaurs May Have Eaten Far More Fruit Than Scientists Ever Thought

An exceptionally preserved 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico is revealing unexpected details about ancient plant life.

Dinosaurs may have been eating a much wider variety of fruits than scientists once believed. Fossils from a 74-million-year-old forest in New Mexico show that some flowering plants were already producing surprisingly large fruits millions of years before the asteroid impact that ended the age of non-avian dinosaurs.

The findings, published in the journal Science, challenge the longstanding theory that larger fruits and more complex seed dispersal strategies evolved primarily after the extinction event 66 million years ago. They also suggest that dinosaurs and other prehistoric animals may have helped spread the seeds of flowering plants much earlier than previously thought.

The research centers on an exceptionally preserved fossil forest near Truth or Consequences, New Mexico. James Saulsbury, a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Kansas Biodiversity Institute and Natural History Museum, helped collect, classify, and analyze the plant fossils discovered there.

“This paper focuses on a fossil forest in New Mexico and the preserved fruits, seeds and other reproductive structures of the plants that lived there,” Saulsbury said. “These fossils change how we understand the way flowering plants became modern in terms of their reproductive ecology.”

The forest was buried beneath volcanic ash that eventually hardened into rock. The preserved deposit stretches more than a kilometer (about 0.6 miles), capturing plants from approximately the same period and retaining evidence of how they were arranged across the ancient landscape.

“The New Mexico fossil site is exceptional,” Saulsbury said. “My co-authors have referred to it as a ‘botanical Pompeii’ because of its remarkable preservation. The site contains a layer of volcanic ash preserved as rock, known as tuff, that stretches for more than a kilometer. The deposits formed at essentially the same time, preserving many plants where they lived and died. It provides a snapshot of a forest from about 74 million years ago and even preserves aspects of its spatial arrangement.”

Flowering plants first appeared approximately 136 million years ago, but researchers have traditionally believed that their reproductive strategies remained relatively simple throughout much of the Cretaceous Period. Early flowering plants generally produced small seeds and fruits, with wind and other non-animal mechanisms thought to play major roles in seed dispersal.

“For much of their early history, they were relatively small, weedy plants that did not dominate forest canopies,” Saulsbury said. “Although they gradually diversified and occupied more ecological niches, it was thought their seeds and dispersal structures remained small and were primarily dispersed by wind or without fleshy fruit.”

Many early flowering plant seeds were thought to have ranged from dust-sized particles to roughly the size of poppy seeds. By contrast, the New Mexico fossils include fruits approximately as large as modern grapes. Such fruits are much larger than those previously expected from flowering plants of that age.

“The prevailing view has been that this more diverse reproductive ecology emerged only after the end-Cretaceous extinction,” Saulsbury said. “Our study suggests that transition began much earlier. The largest fruits in our fossil flora are about the size of a grape. That may not sound especially large today, but it is remarkably large for flowering plants of that period.”

The team examined hundreds of fossilized seeds, sorting them according to their physical characteristics. Because fossil material often lacks the features necessary to identify an exact species, researchers organized specimens into groups based on their shapes and structures.

“We sorted hundreds of fossil seeds into what we call morphotypes,” Saulsbury said. “These are groupings based on form rather than confirmed species because it is often impossible to determine whether similar-looking fossils represent one species or several.”

The fossil assemblage contains an unusual diversity of fruits, seeds, and reproductive structures. Although the exceptional preservation helped researchers recover this material, Saulsbury believes the forest itself differed from many other known Cretaceous environments.

“However, we don’t believe these findings are simply the result of preservation bias,” he said. “It appears to represent a genuinely unusual forest.”

Fruit size can provide information about the environments in which plants evolved and how their seeds may have spread. Today, many flowering plants produce fleshy fruits that attract animals, which can transport seeds away from the parent plant after eating the fruit.

“Large fruits tend to occur in moist environments with densely packed forests,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings indicate that modern-looking forest structure and reproductive ecology were developing earlier than previously believed. The diversification of flowering plant reproductive strategies did not have to wait until after the end-of-Cretaceous extinction.”

The discovery also complicates an established explanation for the evolution of fruit-bearing plants. Scientists had proposed that large, fleshy fruits became more widespread as mammals diversified following the extinction of non-avian dinosaurs, creating new opportunities for plants to disperse their seeds through animals.

“As mammals expanded into newly available ecological niches, flowering plants were thought to have diversified their seed dispersal strategies in response,” Saulsbury said. “Our findings suggest that story began earlier. If diverse, large fruits already existed in Cretaceous forests, they were likely being dispersed not only by early mammals but also by large dinosaurs and other animals.”

Reference: “Diversification of angiosperm reproductive strategies predated the end-Cretaceous extinction” by Jaemin Lee, Dori L. Contreras, James G. Saulsbury, Garland R. Upchurch and Cindy V. Looy, 25 June 2026, Science. DOI: 10.1126/science.adw9457

#6440. Food contains thousands of overlooked chemicals. This physicist is mapping them

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

By Tina Hesman Saey, Mandana Tadayon and Anna Mattson

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Computational physicist Giulia Menichetti is looking for “dark matter” in our food. In addition to known macronutrients, vitamins and minerals, the things we eat contain a whole world of natural chemicals we have no idea about. And those chemicals may affect our health.

“They have the ability to interact, to bind to human proteins, to modulate our microbiome,” says Menichetti of Harvard Medical School. “We want to leverage this to talk more and more about the role of food and nutrition in human health.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Menichetti leads Foodome, a project to map our food’s full chemical complexity. Her team uses AI to mine scientific papers for every chemical compound that has ever been linked to a food. She singles out ones that haven’t been tracked by epidemiological studies — the “nutritional dark matter.” So far, her team has cataloged about 140,000 molecules.

When one hears about chemicals in food, they might initially think of artificial additives. Her team addresses those, but she’s also interested in naturally occurring chemicals. Take garlic, for example. Foodome has cataloged almost 7,000 different molecules in raw garlic alone. Some of these compounds have been investigated for health effects, but some are entirely new.

Foodome is still mining the scientific literature for these molecules and building out databases. Eventually, Menichetti would like AI to be able to predict how all these food molecules interact together and in the human body.

“There is a legacy of chemical complexity that comes from organisms that are all around us,” she says. “Food is part of that. It is actually our way to interact with our environment. We need to study it better.”
