#6414. Scientists learn how colorblind cuttlefish constantly adjust their skin patterns to perfectly match the ocean floor

A new study reveals that cuttlefish camouflage is a complex, multi-step process. Rather than an instant match, cuttlefish continuously check and adjust their skin to blend into the seafloor.

On the seafloor, a cuttlefish can make its skin look so much like the sand and pebbles around it that the animal disappears.

Earlier experiments made the trick look simple: the eyes read the background, and the brain sends out the matching pattern with no checking afterward. Up close, the change is slower and busier than that.

The skin reaches its match in steps. The change slows down, speeds up again and slows once more, and each step brings the pattern closer to the background. The animal seems to be checking its own work as it goes.

Sam Reiter at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) in Japan co-led the study of cuttlefish camouflage. He shared the lead with Gilles Laurent at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research in Germany, and the study came out in Nature in June 2023.

Reiter and Laurent’s team filmed a dozen young common European cuttlefish, Sepia officinalis, in a lab tank. The animals had hatched from eggs collected in the English Channel and the North Atlantic, and their main bodies measured 1.7 to 3.5 inches (42 to 90 mm) long.

“Prior research suggested that cuttlefish only had a limited selection of pattern components that they would use to achieve the best match against the environment,” said Reiter, who heads the Computational Neuroethology Unit at OIST.

“But our latest research has shown that their camouflaging response is much more complicated and flexible – we just hadn’t been able to detect it as previous approaches were not as detailed or quantitative.”

Cuttlefish are cephalopods, the group that also includes squid and octopuses. They change their skin color with millions of tiny sacs of pigment. A set of muscles surrounds each sac, and nerve cells in the brain control those muscles directly.

When the muscles pull, the sac stretches wide and shows its color. When they relax, it shrinks back and the color is hidden. Expand some and shrink others, and a new pattern appears, the way dots on a screen make a picture.

Biologists call these sacs chromatophores. To build one pattern, the brain controls tens of thousands of nerve cells at once, and the whole routine runs on instinct. Cuttlefish branched off from the line that led to humans more than 550 million years ago.

The skin can also raise small bumps to change its texture, but this study looked only at the flat pattern of light and dark.

The filming tank was about 28 inches (70 cm) on a side. Printed photos of pebbles and rock ran across the tank floor on a roll of fabric. Every 5 to 10 minutes, a researcher turned a hand crank to change the scene.

Above the tank, 17 high-resolution cameras filmed the skin at 25 frames a second. At that magnification, a single pigment sac covered about 54 pixels. A separate wide-angle camera filmed the whole animal at the same time.

From the wide-angle footage of a single animal, the team collected more than 200,000 images. They came from 27 hours of video.

A neural network, a kind of artificial intelligence, turned each image into a list of numbers describing the pattern, with a supercomputer at OIST doing the processing.

With the patterns written as numbers, the team could ask how many independent ways a cuttlefish pattern can vary. Earlier studies had sorted the patterns into three basic types.

For these animals, the number of independent ways came out close to 60, and the method the team used usually underestimates.

Next, the team swapped one background for another and watched the skin change. A change typically took around a minute, and it didn’t happen at a steady pace.

The skin changed quickly, then almost stopped changing, then sped up again, and it settled only after several of these pauses.

In 85 such changes across three animals, the team checked which way the pattern changed each time the change restarted after a pause.

Each time, it moved toward where it would finally end up, rather than continuing in the direction it had started out in.

The closer the pattern got to its final form, the more often the change paused and the longer each pause lasted. Each step improved the match with the background.

“The cuttlefish would often overshoot their target skin pattern, pause, and then come back,” said Theodosia Woo, a graduate student at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research and one of the study’s two first authors.

“In other words, cuttlefish don’t simply detect the background and go straight to a set pattern, instead, it is likely that they continuously receive feedback about their skin pattern and use it to adjust their camouflage.”

The authors compared the process to a hand correcting its path as it reaches for something, rather than a throw that can’t be corrected once it leaves the hand.

Even repeats weren’t exact repeats. When the same animal faced the same background change again, the final patterns looked identical to a person.

Underneath, though, different sets of pigment sacs expanded and shrank together each time. In one case, about 1,100 sacs that changed size as one group during the first change split into 15 separate groups during the second.

The team also looked at a different skin change. When something threatens a cuttlefish, it turns pale, a response called blanching.

In the lab, the threat was a researcher’s hand reaching toward the animal and stopping 8 inches (20 cm) away. In other trials, it was a dark circle growing larger on a screen beside the tank.

“Unlike camouflaging, blanching was fast and direct, suggesting it uses a different and repeatable control system,” said Dominic Evans, a postdoctoral fellow at the Max Planck Institute for Brain Research.

The pale skin wasn’t blank, though. Up close, faint traces of the camouflage pattern the animal had been showing were still there. And in 16 of 17 threat trials in one animal, the skin went back to nearly the same pattern afterward.

“This suggests that information about the initial camouflage somehow remains,” said Xitong Liang, the study’s other first author, who did the work as a postdoctoral researcher at the Max Planck Institute and is now at Peking University.

“The blanching is more like a response that temporarily overrides the camouflage signals from the brain and might be controlled by a completely different neural circuit in the brain.”

If a cuttlefish adjusts its pattern by checking the result, something has to tell its brain what the skin currently looks like. The study can’t say what.

“Exactly how they receive that feedback – whether they use their eyes, or whether they have a sense of how contracted the muscles around each chromatophore are – we don’t yet know,” Woo said.

So far, nothing like a muscle-position sensor has been found around a cuttlefish’s pigment sacs. The authors also raised a third possibility: the brain might keep a copy of the commands it just sent out and use that copy to judge the result.

The authors suggested a way to test whether the eyes are involved. Cover the animal’s skin while it camouflages, so it can’t see its own pattern, and watch whether the pauses and corrections still happen.

Liang said the next step is to record activity from cuttlefish brains while the animals change pattern, to work out how they control the skin.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6413. How octopuses squeeze through tiny openings, step by step

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The cephalopod how-to guide involves three or four moves, depending on a hole’s size

Octopuses are famous for fleeing tanks by squeezing through narrow slits and impossibly tiny holes. Now scientists have studied the sequences some cephalopods like this Mayan octopus use to make such great escapes.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Octopuses have made many a great escape. Remember Inky, who fled from New Zealand’s national aquarium?

The cephalopods can Houdini their way out of tanks and off boats by squeezing through narrow slits and incredibly tiny holes. Now researchers know exactly how some octopuses pull it off. These masterful getaways involve a consistent, step-by-step game plan, researchers report November 5 in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Octopuses are mostly squishy muscle, allowing them to shape-shift, though they do have some rigid body parts. Not many scientists have studied how these animals squirm through small openings, says Robyn Crook, an evolutionary biologist at San Francisco State University who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the most characteristic behaviors of octopuses in popular awareness, but the strategies octopuses use have not really been examined systematically.”

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Sneaking through small spaces isn’t just a party trick for octopuses, says Michael Kuba, a biologist at the University of Naples Federico II in Italy. The animals use that skill to find hidden food and to avoid becoming food themselves.

Kuba and his colleagues observed how three common octopuses (Octopus vulgaris) and four Mayan octopuses (Octopus maya) approached small holes. For each individual, the team measured the distance between the octopus’s eyes as an indicator of the size of their most rigid cartilage around their brain. Then the researchers designed acrylic boxes with holes that were slightly smaller or larger than that eye-to-eye measurement. They plopped the octopuses inside and watched what happened.

Octopuses have slightly different escape how-tos, depending on the size of the hole they are squeezing through. Here, a common octopus (Octopus vulgaris) wriggles through a space just a little bit bigger than their most rigid body parts. It takes just three steps for the octopus to free itself from the acrylic box.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Common octopuses used one of two escape strategies depending on the hole’s size. When the hole was wider than the distance between their eyes, the octopuses pushed themselves through it in three steps. First, they snuck one or two arms through the hole and then threaded a couple more arms through. Finally, they used the arms that they had already snaked through the hole to push against the box and yank their head and the rest of their arms through in one fell swoop. The whole operation took a few seconds.

When the hole was narrower, common octopuses added a fourth step. They shoved all of their arms through the hole first and then squished their head and bulbous mantle through.

When a hole is smaller than their most rigid body parts, common octopuses add a fourth step to wrestle their bodies through an opening.

W. Xin et al/J. of Experimental Biology 2026, reproduced with permission of The Company of Biologists

Mayan octopuses behaved more cautiously than the common octopuses. When confronted with the narrower hole, Mayan octopuses didn’t even attempt to fit inside of it. They usually ignored it. This difference between the species could stem from their biology or how they’ve adapted to their environments, Kuba says. Mayan octopuses live in sandy, rocky areas, so while they might disappear under rocks, they don’t often need to cram through holes, he says.

The team hopes these escape artists will inspire new soft robots that can morph their shape to fit through tiny spaces, says Wenci Xin, a robotics researcher at the National University of Singapore. “This incredible capability could enable robots to overcome environmental limitations and enter spaces that are difficult to reach.”

Studying how octopuses navigate different types of holes may provide additional clues for robots, Crook says. For instance, the cephalopods may take a different tack for openings that are more like slits or tubes than holes.

Currently, robots built to fit through tiny holes tend to be snake-shaped, but further research on these eight-armed contortionists could unlock other configurations.

#6412. Scientists reach record-low temperature aboard China’s space station

Physicists on China's Tiangong station cooled 20,000 atoms to the coldest temperature in space: 9.7 trillionths of a degree above zero.

For 30 years, physicists have pushed clouds of atoms toward ever lower temperatures, with Earth’s gravity limiting how far they could go.

Now, a speck of gas aboard China’s Tiangong space station has reached what its creators report is a record-low temperature.

There, physicists chilled about 20,000 rubidium atoms to an equivalent temperature of 9.7 trillionths of a degree above absolute zero, which is minus 459.67°F (minus 273.15°C).

The previous record for a cloud like this was 38 trillionths, set in a drop tower on Earth.

The temperature here is a measure of how fast the cloud spreads once released, not a reading from a thermometer. The authors wrote that the result is the lowest they know of.

Xiaoji Zhou and Xuzong Chen of Peking University led the work with Weibiao Chen of the Shanghai Institute of Optics and Fine Mechanics and colleagues at Fudan University.

Their apparatus has been running on the station since October 2022. When they released the atoms, they could still see the cloud seven seconds later.

The usual way to make atoms this cold is to hold them in a trap and let the hottest ones escape, the way steam leaving a cup cools the coffee.

The looser the trap, the colder the atoms that remain. On Earth, though, a trap that is too loose simply drops its atoms. Gravity sets a floor.

That is why laboratories on the ground have stalled around 350 trillionths of a degree in three dimensions.

Drop towers and sounding rockets buy a few seconds of free fall.

NASA’s Cold Atom Laboratory on the International Space Station, which holds atoms with magnetic fields, has reached 52 trillionths and watched clouds for about a second.

The Chinese team used light instead of magnets. Two crossed laser beams make a trap that can hold atoms whatever their magnetic state, which opens up experiments a magnetic trap can’t run.

No one had made a quantum gas this way in orbit before.

The experiment lives in the Cold Atom Physics Rack aboard the space station‘s Mengtian module.

About two million rubidium atoms were loaded into the first trap and the laser power was eased down over about 20 seconds.

As the trap weakened, the gas formed a Bose-Einstein condensate, a state in which many atoms share a single quantum state and behave collectively.

Weightlessness turned out to have a cost. On Earth, gravity tilts the trap and helps the hottest atoms spill out.

Without that tilt, evaporation in orbit was slower and less complete, and only about 65% of the atoms joined the condensate, against 89% in an identical setup on the ground.

The team’s fix was a stand-in for gravity. A magnetic field gradient pulled on the atoms whose spins made them magnetic, speeding their escape and pushing the rest into a single, magnetically neutral state.

The fraction in the condensate climbed to 89%, about 23,000 atoms.

Even a condensate isn’t finished cooling. The atoms still push on one another, and when the trap opens that pressure becomes motion.

So the team handed the atoms to a second, wider pair of beams, let the trap relax for just over a second, and then switched it off.

Released, the cloud drifted outward at about 70 to 88 micrometers a second, a few thousandths of an inch per second.

Translated into temperature, that is 9.7 trillionths of a degree, with an uncertainty of roughly three trillionths either way. The atoms were, for practical purposes, barely moving.

The team’s computer simulation of the same steps predicted 7.4 trillionths of a degree, and the authors attributed the difference to jitter in the laser beams.

A cloud that expands this slowly could improve atom interferometers, whose sensitivity can increase with the square of the atoms’ time in free flight.

Seven seconds of free fall in orbit is a very long time by that standard.

The temperature estimate rests on the first two seconds of expansion. Although the cloud remained visible afterward, the later images were too faint to use in the calculation.

The condensate is also small. The authors wrote that a trap whose volume can be tuned should let them hold more atoms.

Their stated goals are to study exotic quantum phases that only appear at these temperatures, and to build an atom interferometer in orbit.

That is a device that could test whether all objects really fall at the same rate.

Both goals would benefit from more atoms and longer free flight. The experiment marks a step toward creating those conditions in orbit.

The full study was published in the journal Science.

#6411. Amazon’s New Kindle Paperwhite Is Here. Here’s What’s Different From the Last Version.

From slimmer designs to updated displays and charging features, here's what's changed with Amazon's latest e-readers.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Amazon has refreshed its Kindle lineup for 2026, introducing new versions of the popular Kindle Paperwhite and Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition. Both e-readers have notable design updates, but if you already own a previous model, you might wonder whether it's worth upgrading.

The short answer? It depends on which Kindle you're using. Compared to the 2024 models, the latest Paperwhites offer a sleeker design, updated display technology, and some welcome improvements to everyday usability. The Signature Edition, in particular, gets a few extras that make it feel more like a premium device. Here's what's changed and what's stayed the same.

Amazon Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition

The most noticeable upgrade is the design and appearance. Amazon has made the standard Paperwhite thinner and slightly lighter, reducing its thickness from 7.8 millimeters to 6.8 millimeters. It also weighs approximately 204 grams, compared to the previous model's 211 grams. That might not sound like much, but a slimmer e-reader is always welcome when you're holding it for hours or slipping it into a bag.

The redesigned display construction also creates a more seamless, edge-to-edge look. Amazon uses a new display stack with an oxide thin-film transistor backplane, designed to deliver excellent contrast, deeper blacks, and crisp text. The screen is still 7 inches with a 300-ppi resolution, so don't expect a dramatic jump in sharpness over the 2024 model.

Another small but genuinely useful change is the power button's placement. Instead of sitting along the bottom edge, where it was easy to press accidentally, it's now positioned on the upper-right side.

And if battery life is your biggest concern, there's good news: Amazon still promises up to 12 weeks on a single charge, just like the previous generation. The new model also maintains its IPX8 waterproof rating and adjustable warm lighting.

The Signature Edition receives the same thinner design and updated screen construction, but Amazon has made a few additional changes to distinguish it from the standard Paperwhite.

For starters, it now has an aluminum back instead of the previous model's plastic construction, giving it a more premium look and feel. That upgrade comes with a trade-off, though: At approximately 229 grams, the new Signature Edition is actually a little heavier than its 214-gram predecessor.

The new model also introduces pogo-pin connectors for charging and accessories. These let the Kindle connect to Amazon's new charging stand and a magnetic Page-Turn Cover with physical buttons, which could appeal to readers who miss the page-turn buttons on older e-readers.

One important difference is that the 2024 Signature Edition supported conventional Qi wireless charging, while the 2026 model switches to the new contact-based pogo-pin system.

Amazon also highlights a double-tap feature that lets you advance pages by tapping the side or back of the device, making one-handed reading a little easier.

Otherwise, you'll still get 32GB of storage, an auto-adjusting front light, and up to 12 weeks of battery life. Both generations are waterproof, too.

If you're shopping for a new Kindle rather than replacing an older one, the decision mostly comes down to whether the Signature Edition's premium features are worth an additional $50.

The standard Paperwhite starts at $199.99 and includes 16GB of storage, adjustable warm lighting, and a 7-inch glare-free display.

For $249.99, the Signature Edition doubles the storage to 32GB, adds an aluminum back and automatic brightness adjustment, and supports the new pogo-pin charging accessories. It's also available in Seaglass Green, whereas the regular Paperwhite comes in Graphite.

Both deliver essentially the same core reading experience, so casual readers probably won't miss much by sticking with the less expensive version.

If you already own a 2024 Kindle Paperwhite or Signature Edition and it's working perfectly fine, you probably don't need to replace it. You're still getting the same screen size and resolution, excellent battery life, waterproofing, and access to Amazon's massive Kindle library.

However, if you're upgrading from an older 2021 Paperwhite—or you're shopping for your first e-reader—the 2026 models are worth considering. The thinner design, improved screen construction, and updated controls make the latest lineup more appealing.

For most readers, the regular Paperwhite will be more than enough. But if you read every day, want the premium aluminum design, or like the idea of a case with physical page-turn buttons, the Signature Edition is a worthwhile step up.

#6410. Crystals reveal what pushed seven very different volcanoes to erupt

Crystals from seven Andean volcanoes share one chemical fingerprint, tying each volcano eruption trigger to a pulse of hot magma from below.

A volcano that erupts once and goes quiet forever seems like a different animal from one that has blown up again and again.

A study of seven Andean volcanoes suggests that, despite their different histories, their eruptions shared a trigger.

The last crystals to grow before each eruption carry the same chemical fingerprint, and it points to a pulse of hotter magma pushing up from below.

Daniela Parra-Encalada, a doctoral student in the School of the Environment at the University of Queensland, read that fingerprint out of plagioclase.

That’s the common white mineral that makes up most of the crystals in volcanic rock.

Parra-Encalada worked with senior author Teresa Ubide and colleagues from Australia, the Universidad de Chile, Spain and Argentina.

Together they collected lava and ash from seven volcanoes along 143 miles (230 kilometers) of the Central Andes.

The work rests on 28 rock samples. Whether the same signal could ever help forecast an eruption is a question the team has only begun to test.

“Plagioclase grows in magma only a few kilometers below the surface, reacting to changes in temperature, water content and magma composition,” Parra-Encalada said.

One of those reactions is a swap of calcium for sodium, so each crystal keeps a record of the melt it grew from.

Two kinds of crystal turned up in every rock the team cut open. Large ones, up to about a twelfth of an inch (2 millimeters) long, grew slowly while the magma was stored underground.

Tiny ones, shorter than about a hundredth of an inch (300 micrometers), grew during the final rise to the surface.

The tiny crystals are the only ones that formed entirely from the magma that erupted.

Across all seven volcanoes, they held nearly the same calcium-to-sodium balance, and the outer rims of the large crystals matched them.

The team named that narrow band the plagioclase eruptibility field. The volcanoes couldn’t have been much more different.

Lascar, the most active volcano in the region, has neighbors that erupted only once, some as long as 3 million years ago.

Some lie on the main volcanic arc and others far behind it, where the crust is half as thick.

In an interview with Earth.com, Parra-Encalada was asked what surprised her most about the match.

“What surprised us most was discovering that this similarity was related to the textures and shapes of plagioclase crystals,” she said.

The cores of the large crystals told a different story. About half of all the plagioclase in these rocks didn’t grow from the erupted magma at all.

Its chemistry points to a silica-rich melt that cooled and crystallized for a long time a few miles down. Along the way it soaked up material from the surrounding crust.

Volcanologists call that kind of sluggish, crystal-packed body a mush.

In the Andean rocks, pieces of it arrived as clusters of interlocking crystals and as chunks of fully solidified rock, pulled loose and carried up when the eruption came.

The trapped crystals share their chemistry with crystals in the region’s ancient super-eruption deposits, which Parra-Encalada told Earth.com was one of the two findings that excited her most.

The same stalled magma systems may also matter for how copper and gold collect underground, she said.

The team is now comparing Andean crystals with those from large ore deposits.

To work out what the fingerprint means, the researchers ran computer simulations of magma cooling and crystallizing at different depths.

The trapped crystals formed at about 1,380°F to 1,560°F (750°C to 850°C), within 7 miles (11 kilometers) of the surface.

The eruptibility-field crystals formed hotter, at roughly 1,650°F to 1,790°F (900°C to 975°C). Their magma had just been reheated by a fresh injection from deeper down.

The fresh injection also carried more dissolved water. As the mixture rose, the water began bubbling out and building pressure in the shallow magma chamber.

Strontium isotopes told the same story: crystal cores carried the signature of melt that had digested old crust, while the rims matched the fresh carrier magma.

The team’s reading is that a volcano on this arc needs a shove from below to erupt, and the shove is what the newest crystals record.

Parra-Encalada then pulled plagioclase data from a public geochemistry database covering 26 volcanic arcs.

The average crystal composition worldwide fell inside the Andean eruptibility field. So did the averages for the Cascades and for Kamchatka.

“And this was not just in the Andes!” she said.

In the Aleutians and in Indonesia, the crust changes from continental to oceanic. There too, the crystal rims fell in the field while the cores scattered.

The result also speaks to an old puzzle. Lavas with intermediate silica levels commonly erupt along these arcs, yet the silica-rich and silica-poor magmas that mix to produce them rarely reach the surface on their own.

The crystals suggest the crust works as a filter: the thick, silica-rich mush and the dense, iron-rich mush both stay trapped, and only the reheated blend in between gets out.

Two of the samples came from an ancient deposit beneath Lascar. It was left by one of the caldera-forming explosive eruptions that buried the region about 4 million years ago.

Those crystals showed almost none of the reheating signature. In a chemical map of an entire rock slice, 97% of the crystals had grown steadily without disturbance.

So the shove that sets off an ordinary Andean eruption may not be what sets off the giant ones.

The authors suggest those huge silica-rich reservoirs can destabilize and empty on their own once enough magma has piled in.

Using crystal chemistry to identify volcanoes more likely to erupt remains an untested idea.

The idea, Parra-Encalada said, is that a volcano whose large crystals also fall near the eruptibility field may hold magma already close to erupting conditions.

Some crystal interiors at Lascar do. Lascar last erupted in the year 2022, two weeks after the team finished fieldwork there.

“If we observe a similar pattern in other polygenetic volcanoes, where most plagioclase crystals have compositions within the eruptibility field, it could indicate a volcanic system that deserves closer attention,” Parra-Encalada noted.

Polygenetic means a volcano that erupts more than once.

Nothing in this study links the fingerprint to how often a volcano erupts or how soon, and the team’s next paper takes up that question.

The samples also come from one slice of one continental arc. The global comparison relies on other researchers’ data, most of it without the crystal-by-crystal sorting this study depended on.

The team is expanding its work to Tonga to test whether the pattern also holds in an oceanic setting.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Communications.

#6408. Teen messaging and well-being: Who is on the other end matters

A study of Swedish teens links messaging with offline friends to higher well-being and contact with online-only friends to lower scores.

The usual question about a teenager’s phone is how many hours. A survey of 3,034 Swedish 15-year-olds asked a different one: who is on the other end?

Teens who messaged close friends or their wider circle several times a day or more scored higher on a well-being test than teens who rarely did.

Teens who kept up with friends they had only ever met online, even just weekly, scored lower.

Viviane Straatmann of Stockholm University is the study’s senior author.

She conducted the study with first author Madeleine Björnsdotter Orfanidou, also at Stockholm, and Kenisha Russell Jonsson of the University of Gothenburg.

The survey was taken at one moment in each teen’s life, so it can show a pattern and not a cause.

In an interview with Earth.com, Straatmann said parents should take an interest not only in how much time teens spend messaging but in whom they message.

“Online communication can be a valuable way to maintain and strengthen friendships with people adolescents know offline,” she said.

The teens came from two rounds of the Health Behaviour in School-aged Children survey, a long-running study of young people’s health across many countries.

One round ran in the 2017 to 2018 school year, the other in 2021 to 2022, and the team pooled them.

Each teen was asked how often they sent and received texts, emojis, photos, videos or voice messages, or made video calls, with three kinds of people.

One was a close friend. One was a larger group of friends. The third was friends they had met through the internet and never in person.

The answers were sorted into three levels: rarely, weekly to daily, and several times a day up to almost all the time. Two-thirds of the teens were in that top band with their close friends.

Well-being was measured using seven questions about the past two weeks, including feeling optimistic, useful, relaxed and close to other people. Higher scores mean better well-being.

Teens who messaged a close friend several times a day scored about 1.6 points higher than teens who rarely did.

Once the team accounted for gender, family finances, family situation and survey year, that gap shrank to about one point and was no longer statistically significant.

Frequent messaging with a larger friend group remained associated with higher well-being after the same adjustments, with a gap of nearly one point.

Straatmann called that an important finding, because it means online communication was not uniformly negative.

Digital contact, she said, can be a positive tool when it complements a teen’s everyday offline relationships.

The pattern reversed for friends a teen knew only online. Teens who messaged such friends weekly to daily scored about 0.9 points lower than teens who rarely did.

Teens who did so several times a day scored about 0.7 points lower. Both gaps survived the adjustments.

The split is not new. The authors wrote that studies in the United Kingdom and Finland found the same thing.

Teens in touch online with friends they knew offline reported higher well-being, and teens communicating mostly with online-only friends reported lower.

Those are small differences on the scale. For comparison, girls scored almost three points lower than boys.

Teens from families they described as well off scored almost three points higher than teens who said their family was not.

The association with online-only contact remained after adjustment, but the differences by gender and family finances were larger.

“This does not mean that all online-only friendships are harmful, but it underlines the importance of open conversations, age-appropriate guidance, and a safe digital environment,” Straatmann told Earth.com.

Girls were more likely than boys to message a close friend several times a day or more: 77% compared with 65%.

Teens from the most affluent families were far more likely to do so than teens from the least, 82% to 62%.

Boys were slightly more likely than girls to be in frequent contact with online-only friends, though the gap was not clearly beyond chance.

The team adjusted for those differences. But the authors wrote that their models did not test whether the link between online-only friends and well-being differs for girls or for lower-income teens.

The study could not establish which way the relationship runs.

“As this was a cross-sectional study, we cannot say whether these online relationships contribute to poorer well-being, whether adolescents with lower well-being are more likely to seek such relationships, or whether both processes are involved,” Straatmann said.

The study also measured only Swedish 15-year-olds, couldn’t apply the survey’s population weights, and didn’t ask about cyberbullying or how good the friendships were.

Teens surveyed in the 2021–2022 round scored almost two points lower than those in the earlier round, and the design can’t separate the pandemic from everything else that changed between the rounds.

Sweden’s public health agency recently issued its first screen guidance for teenagers, built around a daily limit of two to three hours for ages 13 to 18.

The authors wrote that the nature of online contact, not only its length, might belong in future updates of that advice.

Straatmann said the next step is following the same teens over time, to watch how messaging and well-being shape each other.

She also wants to know whether the pattern holds for neurodivergent teens, including those with ADHD or autism, for whom online contact may offer an unusually important route to connection.

The full study was published in the journal Child and Adolescent Mental Health.

The Vikings are famous for being warriors, but how frequently did Viking women take part in battles?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The Vikings were explorers, farmers, merchants and, most famously, warriors who launched raids across large parts of Europe.

Stereotypes of Vikings usually conjure up images of muscular men. But over the past few decades, researchers have turned their attention to women of the Viking Age (roughly A.D. 793 to 1066) and the roles they held. For instance, there are stories of "shield maidens" who fought alongside men, and some of these texts mention Viking women who fought in battle. The archaeological record also holds evidence, including graves of Viking Age women who were buried with war-grade weapons and shields.

It's still a matter of debate whether women who lived during the Viking Age could be warriors, but this discussion raises another question: It's one thing to have texts describing female fighters and archaeological records of women buried with weapons, but what can the evidence tell us about how frequently Viking women fought in battle?

The answer, experts told Live Science, largely depends on our interpretation of texts, artifacts, and burials of Viking Age women, which often face higher scrutiny than burials of men who were buried with similar (or even fewer) weapons.

The Vikings used a runic system of writing, but they left precious few texts behind. Instead, much of what we know about the Vikings was written about them by people from other cultures or by their Norse descendants.

One of the most evocative texts was written in the 12th century by the Danish historian and theologian Saxo Grammaticus. In "Gesta Danorum" (Latin for "History of the Danes" and translated by Jenny Jochens), he wrote that "there were once women in Denmark who dressed themselves to look like men and spent almost every minute cultivating [combat] skills." As "if they were forgetful of their true selves they put toughness before allure, aimed at conflicts instead of kisses, tasted blood, not lips, sought the clash of arms rather than the arm's embrace, fitted to weapons hands what should have been weaving, desired not the couch but the kill, and those they could have appeased with looks they attacked with lances."

Another text about the Vikings, the medieval Irish "Cogadh Gaedhelre Gallaibh" ("War of the Irish with the Foreigners"), refers to a woman known as the "Red Lady" leading a Viking fleet in a raid on Belfast in the 10th century.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

There's a lot of uncertainty, said Neil Price, an archaeology professor at Uppsala University in Sweden who has written extensively about the Vikings. The text in the "Cogadh Gaedhel re Gallaibh" that refers to the Red Lady is of debatable accuracy, Price told Live Science in an email.

He suspects that Viking women fought in battle but not frequently. In addition, "female warriors were probably a very small minority," Price said.

A modern-day reenactment depicting Viking warriors.

The account written by Saxo Grammaticus is also contentious. Thomas Kristian Heebøll-Holm, a history professor at the University of Southern Denmark, said Saxo Grammaticus is not a reliable source.

"Saxo Grammaticus does write about female warriors, but only in the parts of his work concerned [with] the legendary past of Denmark," Heebøll-Holm told Live Science in an email. "Furthermore, these writings are not accurate, but moral and fictitious," Heebøll-Holm said, noting that, in some instances, Saxo Grammaticus seemed to be drawing on the stories of the Amazons, a group of legendary female warriors whom the ancient Greeks believed in with stories about them dating back more than 2,500 years.

Archaeological evidence can also be challenging to interpret. Archaeologists know of about 30 Viking Age female burials containing weapons, including three with swords in Scandinavia. Even more Viking Age women's graves have items that could have been used as weapons ‪—‬ including spears, axes and knives ‪—‬ although these tools also could have been used for hunting or tending to farms. Either way, we can't be sure if these women fought in battle.

"The first concern is that the weapons were really used by the deceased and were not merely included as signs of special status or social rank acquired through inheritance," Deborah Shepherd, an independent researcher who holds a doctorate in archaeology and has studied the Vikings extensively, told Live Science in an email. She noted that graves are often not well preserved, making it difficult to gather information.

This 1889 illustration shows a grave at Birka in Sweden. It is now known that the person buried with war-grade weapons and riding gear is a woman.

There were likely "some few female warriors, but they were probably only found in the highest ranking families, and their warrior career was probably short-lived," Shepherd said. "They wouldn't have fought in the great armies of later centuries but possibly did fight in pre-Christian skirmishes." (The Vikings began gradually converting to Christianity between the ninth and 12th centuries.)

There is at least one known case of a Viking woman found with what may be combat-related injuries. A Viking woman found in Solør, Norway, had a head injury consistent with a sword strike. She was 18 or 19 at the time she died, was buried with weapons and lived around 900.

Ole Kastholm, a curator and senior researcher at the Roskilde Museum in Denmark, said there is a lot of uncertainty regarding how frequently Viking Age women fought in battle.

Weapons "do occur as a grave good in a handful of graves with female human remains," Kastholm told Live Science in an email. "Often it is just a single weapon [such] as a spear or [a] battle axe. But we know of at least one example of a female grave with a full set of weapons as well as riding equipment," which is located in Birka, Sweden.

"If this was a man's grave, researchers would have no doubt that it was a warrior grave, and this explanation must necessarily also apply when the interred is a woman," Kastholm said.

That said, there were female warriors in other cultures. "One can also note in passing that female warriors were an almost common feature of central Asian societies for at least a millennium before the Viking Age," Price wrote in his book, "The Sea-King and the Sorceress: Life and Death in the Viking Age" (Basic Books, 2026).

For instance the Scythians are a people who flourished in eastern Europe and Asia and Scythian women have been found buried with horses and weapons. In some cases, the Scythian women suffered combat wounds such as arrowheads and it's been speculated that they may have been an inspiration for stories of the Amazons.

Owen Jarus is a regular contributor to Live Science who writes about archaeology and humans' past. He has also written for The Independent (UK), The Canadian Press (CP) and The Associated Press (AP), among others. Owen has a bachelor of arts degree from the University of Toronto and a journalism degree from Ryerson University.

#6406. TCL A400U Designer Series TV Review: An Art TV That Puts Movie Night First

TCL's slim art TV gives you deep blacks and bright HDR, but its art mode isn’t quite as mesmerizing.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Frame TVs are built to look good when you’re not watching them. They’re designed to look like a painting, rather than a TV, with thin designs, wood frames, and a rotating set of digital art that lets it fade into the background of your home, unlike home theaters that often dominate the living room.

While appealing conceptually, most of these TVs do not provide the same performance as an equally expensive conventional TV. Specifically, very few of the models we’ve seen or tested have a feature called full-array local dimming, which allows the TV to brighten or darken different parts of the screen to optimize color and contrast. Without it, the whole backlight stays lit, so dark scenes look more gray than true black.

TCL's A400U Designer Series doesn't have that problem. Its QD-Mini LED panel has 836 local dimming zones, making the dark scenes actually look dark and moody instead of a faded gray. It also hits a claimed 2,500 nits at peak brightness, so HDR highlights, like explosions, really pop. And it still has that art TV look and feel: The body is just 1.57 inches thick, so it sits flush against the wall like a picture frame. Those are far better core specs than most Frame TVs, and at $1,600 for a 75-inch set, it costs far less than Samsung's Frame Pro ($2,800 for a 75-inch), the best-known art TV with a Mini-LED backlight.

While the A400U has the power to deliver a better picture when you’re watching, it also isn’t exactly an “art TV” as we’ve come to understand it. In fact, it’s missing a couple of the hallmarks. First of all, it doesn’t actually have a physical frame: It opts for a stylishly thin bezel that one might describe as artful. And the screen features a semi-glossy, low-reflection coating instead of the matte anti-reflection coating that has become a signature across most of the best art TVs, including Samsung’s Frame and Frame Pro, the Amazon Ember Artline, and the Hisense S7SG. Even TCL’s own A300L, a lesser version of this TV, has it. The matte coating is the X factor for art TVs: It makes digital art (especially paintings) look real at a glance. Without it, the A400U falls from possibly the perfect art TV to one that offers a different type of compromise: It’s a great set for folks who want the Frame aesthetic for an attainable price without compromising on TV image quality, at the expense of that “Frame TV” magic.

The A400U’s QD-mini-LED display panel combines two technologies that are fairly common in conventional TVs, quantum dots (that’s the “QD”) and mini-LED, which is a form of LED backlighting that puts thousands of tiny LEDs behind every inch of the screen. Since the TV supports local dimming, those lights are broken up into 836 groups or “zones,” which the TV can independently control, making them brighter or dimmer to more precisely produce whatever’s on screen. You’ll notice the difference most in dark scenes: Local dimming can accurately produce the lighting of a darkly candle-lit room, or even show what it’s like to see in the dark.

I watched Zach Cregger's Resident Evil, which is set entirely at night, and you can see right away how the Mini-LED’s local dimming zones come in clutch. When Bryan is driving through the snowy mountain roads, the night sky and surrounding forest stay black while the headlights and snow stay bright, so you only see what his headlights catch, which is exactly how a horror movie should look. When I watched the same scene on the Ember Artline, which does not have the tech, the whole backlight stayed lit, and the night sky turned a dull gray.

Quantum dots, which you may know best from “QLED” TVs that introduced them, enhance the screen’s color. There’s a layer of tiny nanoparticles in the display that glow a specific color when light hits them. When the backlight passes through the dots, the blue LED light turns into red and green. This allows the TV to produce deeper reds and greens than a standard LED TV, such as the red of Darth Vader's lightsaber or the green of the Hulk in Spider-Man: Brand New Day. TCL says the A400U covers 93 percent of the DCI-P3 color gamut, the color space where most movies and shows are mastered. That’s a respectable figure, though a step behind top-tier TVs. Top OLEDs like LG’s C6 cover 99 percent or more. Still, the colors on the A400U look rich and vibrant.

While the A400U’s display performance is impressive among Frame TVs, its performance does not compare to an elite mini-LED TV. I’ve praised the A400U for having 836 zones, but there are more than 2,000 in the 75-inch TCL QM8K, for example. With fewer, larger zones, excess light from bright spots on the screen can cloud the darker ones around them. (It’s no different from resolution or frame rate, really: Having more dimming zones creates a smoother gradient for the TV’s lighting.) That glow, called blooming, is pretty easy to spot around white subtitles on a black background, but it's a much smaller problem than the gray haze you get on a TV without full-array local dimming.

TCL claims the A400U hits 2,500 nits at peak brightness. That’s much, much better than the roughly 680 nits we measured on Hisense's S7SG. Most streaming content maxes out at 1,000 nits, so the A400U can show HDR highlights, like the flash of an explosion, at full intensity instead of dimming them.

The A400U has the build of an art TV. It comes with a flush wall mount that holds its incredibly slim body right up against the wall. The mount is fixed, though, so you can't tilt the screen down or swivel it toward a different seat. It also leaves no room behind the TV to reach the ports, so plugging in a new HDMI cable is a hassle. The A400U also has a center pedestal stand for setting it on a media console, but given its size, it looks much better on the wall.

But, as I mentioned at the outset, this TV doesn’t have a physical frame. Instead, the edge is a flat edge of black metal, which is closer to a minimalist frame than a chunky TV bezel. I like the look, and it suits the modern vibe TCL is going for, but it doesn’t quite give you that framed picture look. TK. Removing the frame is a strange omission: TCL makes a more affordable version of this TV, the A300L, which comes with a light-wood magnetic frame that snaps onto the edges of the screen.

In the same vein, TCL omits the ultra-matte anti-reflection coating found on most frame TVs, in favor of what the brand refers to as an “ultra-low-reflection coating.” The matte coating is the secret sauce for art TVs: It scatters light that hits the screen instead of bouncing it straight back at you, which cuts out any glare. In most cases, it does a pretty amazing job of making digital images look like a physical piece of art hanging on a wall. The A400U's finish is somewhere between glossy and matte, but closer to glossy. Combined with the bright backlight, that gives paintings a sheen and a glow that a print on the wall wouldn't have.

I put the A400U in the brightest room in my house, on the west wall. There's a small window right next to it and a huge window on the north wall, plus a door with a big glass pane directly across from the TV. The vaulted ceiling goes up about two stories and has more windows along the top. It's the worst spot in the house for a TV, but also the only space that could accommodate its size, which made it a good test.

The low-reflection coating and high brightness kept most of that light from washing out the picture, and glare was rarely bad enough to make me close the blinds. It can't block every reflection, though. When the screen is mostly dark, there isn't much light coming from the picture to cover up reflections, so the windows around the room show up more. During the day, that makes a movie like Resident Evil harder to enjoy. Brighter shows and movies look fine, and dark ones look much better after sunset or with the blinds closed.

When you aren't watching anything, the A400U can show pieces from TCL's Art Library, artificial intelligence–generated art, or your own photos uploaded through the TCL Home app, and none of it requires a subscription. Samsung's Frame TVs give you 30 free artworks a month and charge $5 a month for the full Art Store. TCL’s TV also has an Ambient Mode that plays moving scenes, similar to the looping landscape videos on the Ember Artline.

An ambient light sensor adjusts the screen's brightness to match the room, so a painting doesn't glow too brightly after dark. Unlike the Ember Artline, the A400U doesn't have a motion sensor, so it won't wake up and switch to art when you walk into the room. I usually turn art mode on whenever I'm done watching something, and I set it up to stay on for a few hours before shutting off.

The A400U runs at a native 144Hz and supports variable refresh rate (VRR) and AMD FreeSync Premium Pro. VRR matches the TV's refresh rate to the frames a console or gaming PC is putting out, which prevents tearing when a game's frame rate dips. I played Control Resonant and Marvel's Wolverine on my PS5. The detailed worlds in Control Resonant looked incredible, with sharp textures on the warped buildings and bright effects. In Wolverine, the fast action stayed smooth and clear, without the blur or stutter you'd see on a slower 60Hz screen.

Only HDMI 1 and 2 support 4K at 144Hz, while HDMI 3 and 4 top out at 4K at 60Hz. HDMI 1 is also the eARC port, which you need to send full-quality Dolby Atmos audio to a soundbar. If you plug a soundbar in there without passthrough, you’ll be left with one fast port, so a second console or a gaming PC would run at 60Hz. Since the flush mount makes swapping cables a pain, it’s worth figuring out which device goes in which port before you hang the TV.

The A400U runs Google TV and supports both Chromecast and AirPlay 2, so you can stream video from an Android phone or an iPhone. Google has added more ads over the years, but it's still faster than the Fire TV software on the Ember Artline, which lagged while scrolling through menus.

The built-in speakers are a pair of 10-watt drivers tuned by Onkyo, with Dolby Atmos and DTS Virtual:X processing that simulates surround and height effects. When I fired up Top Gun: Maverick, I was impressed by how clear and detailed they sound for TV speakers. Dialogue was easy to follow without raising the volume, and the rumble of the jets filled the room. In other words, I wouldn't rush out to buy a soundbar.

With the A400U, TCL kind of wants to have its cake and eat it too. Its performance, design, and overall vibe are clearly meant to appeal to the art TV crowd, but it doesn’t have a frame or the matte coating, which are arguably the two defining qualities of the category. That isn’t necessarily a problem, though: It just makes this set a niche choice. This is a TV for people who want the aesthetics of art TV, but care enough about how movies and video games look that the standard Frame and other models like it may not live up to their expectations.

Ultimately, the Samsung Frame Pro still comes closer to letting you have it all—great performance and the true, matte-coated “frame” experience. It also has a Mini-LED backlight, along with the matte screen and a frame-style bezel that make art look like it’s actually hanging on your wall. But it costs $2,800 for a 75-inch model on Samsung’s site, compared with $1,600 for the 74-inch A400U.

If the Frame Pro’s price tag is a little too high, there are plenty of affordable alternatives with matte screens and magnetic wood frames that come much closer to looking like real paintings, including TCL’s own A300L and the Amazon Ember Artline. If you want an art TV you’ll also use every night for movies and games, the A400U gets you that for less than the Frame Pro, as long as you can live with art mode looking more like a TV.

Brandon Russell is a freelance writer covering gear and technology. He started his journey as a news writer at a small newspaper and later began reviewing smartphones, movies, and video games. #6405. People with early-onset Alzheimer’s often face depression and dizziness before their diagnosis, but not high blood pressure

Before early-onset Alzheimer's was diagnosed, depression, dizziness and brain injuries became more common, but high blood pressure did not.

High blood pressure and high cholesterol are two of the best-known risk factors for Alzheimer’s disease in older people.

In people diagnosed at 65 or younger, researchers in Finland found these two were no more common than in people of the same age without the disease.

What did rise was a scattered set of other problems.

In the five years before diagnosis, people who went on to develop early-onset Alzheimer’s were more often diagnosed with dizziness, depression, headaches, delirium, epilepsy, and brain injuries.

“Our findings support the view that early-onset Alzheimer’s disease is not simply a younger-age version of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease,” said Johanna Krüger, an adjunct professor at the University of Oulu and the study’s lead investigator.

“Rather than the familiar cardiovascular risk factors, we observed a range of other health problems becoming more common as diagnosis approached.”

Early-onset Alzheimer’s accounts for up to 10% of all Alzheimer’s cases. It tends to move faster than the late-onset kind, and it more often starts in unusual ways.

The early-onset disease is also slower to diagnose.

Earlier studies cited by the team put the average time to diagnosis at about 42 months, compared to about 31 months for the late-onset disease.

Diagnosis is often delayed by several years after the first symptoms appear.

The researchers wanted to know whether the years before diagnosis leave a trail in medical records.

The team came from the University of Oulu and the University of Eastern Finland. It started with every patient sent to the memory clinics at Oulu and Kuopio university hospitals from 2010 to 2021.

In Finland, suspected early-onset cases in those regions are sent to those two hospitals.

The team re-checked each record against standard criteria for Alzheimer’s. That left 407 people diagnosed at age 65 or younger, with an average age at diagnosis of about 61.

For comparison, a national agency randomly picked 4,035 people matched to the patients by age, sex, and region. None had a neurodegenerative disease.

Next, the team pulled every diagnosis for both groups from Finland’s national health records. Finnish doctors must record a diagnosis code after every visit, public or private.

The team compared the groups at three stretches of time before diagnosis: one to five years, six to 10, and 11 to 15.

Eleven to 15 years before diagnosis, none of the conditions the team examined differed between the groups. Six to 10 years out, one did.

Tinnitus and hearing loss were recorded in 4.7% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

The bigger change came in the last five years. Dizziness was recorded in 5.9% of future patients compared to 2.1% of the comparison group.

Depression appeared in 5.7% compared to 2.3%, and headache in 4.9% compared to 1.6%.

Brain injuries, strokes, epilepsy, thyroid disorders, alcohol-related disorders, and delirium were all more common too.

Delirium is a sudden state of confusion, and it was recorded in 1.5% of future patients compared to 0.1% of the others.

Each of these conditions was still uncommon, recorded in no more than about 6% of future patients.

High blood pressure or high cholesterol was recorded in 10.6% of future patients in the last five years, compared to 9.3% of the comparison group.

That gap was too small to rule out chance, and the two groups were close at every earlier stretch as well.

In late-onset Alzheimer’s, those heart and blood vessel risks have been linked to the disease in earlier research.

The authors wrote that only one earlier, smaller study had reported a similar result for the early-onset disease. They suggested that the causes of the two forms may differ, at least in part.

Health care visits rose only near the end. In the year before diagnosis, future patients had an average of 3.3 recorded care episodes, compared to 1.9 for the comparison group.

In the year of diagnosis it was 6.3 compared to 2.0. Two or more years out, the groups did not differ.

“Of course, no single disease or symptom predicts Alzheimer’s disease,” said Laura Leppänen, a doctoral researcher at the University of Oulu and the study’s first author.

“Our results suggest that, in the years before diagnosis, patients may accumulate a variety of seemingly unrelated symptoms and healthcare encounters. Recognizing this overall pattern could help raise suspicion of a neurodegenerative disease earlier than is currently the case.”

The study compares records, so it can’t say whether any of these conditions helps cause the disease.

Depression, delirium, or alcohol-related disorders may be early signs of brain changes already under way, and the authors wrote that the design cannot tell those possibilities apart.

The registers held no information on social and economic background, lifestyle, or genes, and diagnoses in them could not be checked independently.

Only people who lived through each stretch were counted. People in the comparison group could also have had early brain changes that had not been diagnosed.

Early onset was defined by age at diagnosis, not at first symptoms, which may have left out people whose symptoms began just before 65.

The results come from one country’s health system, and the authors wrote that they need to be checked in other datasets.

Researchers at the same universities have reported that early-onset dementia is more common than earlier international studies suggested.

Other teams are working on blood tests that might flag the disease years before symptoms.

The full study was published in the journal Alzheimer’s & Dementia.

#6404. This armored amphibian once lived and hunted on the seafloor

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The ancient creature differs from all other known amphibians in its ability to tolerate saltwater

A Gerrothorax maritimus fossil unearthed in China was discovered in an ancient seabed, suggesting it's the first and only amphibian known to have lived in the ocean.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Most amphibians shrivel or suffocate in saltwater. But long ago, an oddball armored amphibian may have dwelled deep in the ocean.

Scientists have found evidence that an ancient amphibian with a flattened body and upturned eyes may have once stalked the seafloor. The animal, Gerrothorax maritimus, is the first ever amphibian known to have lived without access to land or freshwater, researchers report October 26 in Nature Ecology & Evolution.

G. maritimus, which lived 237 million years ago, was rather unlike today’s amphibians, which breathe and drink through their porous skin. The creature’s lifestyle was unimaginable for an amphibian, says Ryosuke Motani, a paleobiologist at the University of California, Davis. Of the more than 8,000 amphibians known today, none live solely in saltwater.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Motani and his colleagues inspected two well-preserved G. maritimus fossils from the late Triassic Period, which spanned roughly 237 million to 201 million years ago. Each creature measured around 70 centimeters, about as long as a skateboard, and was swathed in armor made of bony plates. The specimens appeared nearly identical to their closest relatives, other amphibians that dwelled in freshwater, Motani says. But the fossils’ location was unusual: They were found in what was once a seabed, roughly 30 kilometers from any ancient land.

It wasn’t clear whether the creatures lived in the ocean or were landlubbers that got buried there after they perished. So the team performed a chemical analysis. Levels of different forms of strontium in the fossil bones matched those of the Triassic ocean. This telltale sign revealed that G. maritimus ate seafood and drank seawater. “That means it lived there,” Motani says.

For amphibians, “this is the first time that that we have hard evidence that they were actually adapted for long-term life in the sea,” says Lachlan Hart, a paleobiologist at the University of New South Wales in Sydney who was not involved with the new study. Hart and his colleagues previously suggested that a different ancient amphibian may have been seafaring but probably did not dwell in the ocean.

Scientists have long searched for a marine amphibian. The fossil record is littered with skeletal fragments revealing how some mammals, reptiles and birds have adapted to a salty lifestyle. “Amphibians were always the problem because they did not really follow the rule,” Motani says.

The same skin that makes today’s amphibians vulnerable to disease and toxins also makes saltwater fearsome. Key adaptations allowed G. maritimus to skirt these issues. G. maritimus and its relatives evolved bony body armor, probably for defense. But these hard plates would have helped the seafloor dwellers prevent water loss. And unlike modern amphibians, which typically lose their internal gills after the larval stage, this creature and its close relatives retained a fishy breathing strategy suitable for life in the depths.

G. maritimus fossils hint that the animal lurked on the seafloor as an ambush predator. Its jaw lifted upward like a toilet seat so that it could unleash a suction attack on fish and other small creatures.

There may yet be other amphibians hiding in ancient oceans, environments ignored by paleontologists studying these creatures. “Because they’re amphibians, we would be looking for them in terrestrial freshwater environments,” Hart says. Perhaps there are more amphibians that have gotten their sea legs.

#6403. Adding limestone to farmland is helping to store more carbon dioxide than it releases

Agricultural liming in the Mississippi Basin removed more carbon dioxide than it released, after accounting for acid from fertilizer and pollution.

Limestone is rock made partly of carbon, so spreading it on farm fields sounds like a way to put carbon dioxide into the air. Climate accounting rules treat it that way.

However, a new study finds that, over the past century in the Mississippi River Basin, the limestone that farmers spread has removed more carbon dioxide than it released.

The old math leaves out the acid. Fertilizer and air pollution add acid to soil and water. That acid releases carbon dioxide, whether or not anyone spreads lime.

Measured against a basin with the same acid and no limestone, the lime has worked as a carbon sink.

Geochemist Tim Jesper Suhrhoff of the Yale Center for Natural Carbon Capture led the work with colleagues at Georgia Tech and elsewhere.

The team paired a computer model of soil chemistry with a century of river records from one giant watershed.

In an interview with Earth.com, Suhrhoff said the result adds to what farmers already gain from lime.

“Liming may provide a public climate benefit on top of the benefits farmers already get from healthier soils and better yields,” he said.

Many farm soils slowly turn acidic, and crops grown in acidic soil tend to yield less. Farmers fix that by spreading finely ground limestone or a similar rock called dolomite, a practice known as agricultural liming.

Between 1935 and 1950, lime use in the U.S. rose from about 1.1 million tons (1 million metric tons) a year to about 22 million tons (20 million metric tons).

Most of it went to the Mississippi River Basin, the land drained by the Mississippi and its tributaries. It holds about 65 percent of the cropland in the contiguous U.S.

When limestone dissolves in acidic soil, it gives off carbon dioxide. So the default method from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) treats all the carbon in applied lime as emitted.

The U.S. national inventory assumes about half of it escapes.

When nitrogen fertilizer and manure break down in soil, they produce acid. Burning coal and oil sends sulfur and nitrogen pollution into the sky, and it comes back down as acid.

Rivers carry carbon dissolved in a form called bicarbonate. When acid reaches that water, it turns some of the bicarbonate back into carbon dioxide, which escapes into the air.

Across the basin, acid from farming and pollution far outpaced the lime. By 2015, about half of all the acid added since 1900 hadn’t been offset by lime, mostly on land that sees little liming.

In parts of the Corn Belt, though, decades of liming matched or exceeded the acid.

In 1980, the team’s model estimated, acid alone would have released about 22 million tons (20 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide.

Adding lime cut that to about 17 million tons (15 million metric tons). The IPCC and U.S. methods came in lower, at roughly 8 million and 4 million tons (7 million and 3.5 million metric tons) respectively.

So the standard methods assign the emissions to the lime and miss most of what the acid does.

“I was also struck by how much excess acidity has been added to the system over the last century, implying that agricultural CO₂ emissions from acidification may have been substantially larger than we usually account for,” Suhrhoff told Earth.com.

To check the model, researchers pulled more than seven decades of water chemistry from five U.S. Geological Survey stations between Vicksburg, Mississippi, and Belle Chasse, Louisiana. Samples from the early 1900s filled in the start.

The team compared the bicarbonate that the river carried once liming took off with what it carried before. They traced the extra to about 440 million tons (400 million metric tons) of carbon dioxide. This was removed between 1900 and 2015.

That’s roughly 90 percent of what the lime could have removed if all of it had reacted in the ideal way.

The soil model, built up from conditions across the basin, estimated about 240 million to 410 million tons (220 million to 370 million metric tons). Two different methods reached nearly the same answer.

“I was surprised by how well the bottom-up modeling and top-down river data converged, and that we could actually see these trends at the scale of the entire Mississippi River Basin,” Suhrhoff said.

When liming first ramped up in the late 1930s, the model shows a brief burst of carbon dioxide before removal began. Calcium from dissolved lime attaches to soil particles and releases acid stored there.

That stored acid has to be neutralized before much of the lime’s effect reaches the river.

In the river records, carbon left the basin decades after the limestone went down. The authors warn that carbon removal programs that credit lime as soon as it’s spread could overstate the near-term benefit.

Liming is a close relative of enhanced weathering, which means spreading crushed rock on fields to draw carbon dioxide out of the air.

“This is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to trace more than 120 years of historical records that can tell us whether enhanced weathering works,” said Noah Planavsky, a corresponding author at Yale University.

“I would caution against assuming that the Mississippi result translates directly everywhere,” Suhrhoff said.

The early emissions, the delay and the amount of carbon removed all vary, he added. They depend on how much lime is used, the local soils and how water moves.

Where acidic soils hold back harvests and farmers can’t afford lime, he said, subsidies or pay-for-practice programs could widen access. Three of the authors advise CREW Carbon, a company that adds lime in wastewater treatment plants rather than on farm fields.

For most of the Mississippi’s own tributaries, the records aren’t long or continuous enough to separate lime’s effect from everything else.

The authors call for more regional studies wherever long, detailed records exist. Spreading more lime than the basin’s farmers did would need its own look at local soils, water and that early burst of emissions.

The full study was published in the journal Nature.

#6402. The ReelCharge ReelPro 200W Power Bank Is a Travel-Ready Charging Beast

This laptop charger has everything you could want in a travel power backup solution and only costs $120.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

ReelCharge, a relative newcomer to the portable battery pack market, has caught our eye this year with a few interesting options. Most notable among them is the ReelPro 200W, a compact but massively powerful laptop charger that can keep up with your travel charging needs better than any pack we’ve tested. It features an ample 27,000 milliampere-hour (mAh) battery capacity—about as much as you can get while staying under the FAA’s 100-watt-hour limit—and a maximum power output of 200 watts (W), including up to 140-watt charging on a single device. That beats most laptop wall chargers on speed. Best of all, it costs only $120, substantially undercutting flagship battery packs from legacy brands such as Anker and EcoFlow.

Throw in some premium features and a three-year warranty, and you have a power bank that truly feels like it's setting a new gold standard for high-end power banks that the competition will need to meet.

The ReelPro 200W looks like a bougie battery pack. It has a sleek housing with a matte finish, a glossy front panel, and a color LED display. A display is definitely a must for a high-capacity battery pack in the mid-2020s. It shows the battery’s remaining charge and the wattage going into each outlet, plus status checks on temperature and health. It’s neatly integrated into the pack’s glossy front panel, so it fades into it when turned off, giving it a pleasantly minimalist look.

The ReelPro can charge up to three devices—more than a little, but not the most we’ve seen. It has an integrated, retractable USB-C cable, which can loop around to become a wrist strap. There are also USB-C and USB-A ports for when you want to charge up multiple devices (and to charge the pack itself). Personally, I prefer a battery pack with an external cable to one with a retractable cord because this leaves more interior space for battery cells and allows for a larger capacity.

Having plenty of ports means little if the pack can’t power them properly, and that’s where the ReelPro 200 watts really impresses. As the name suggests, it has a total power output of 200W and can charge a single device at up to 140 watts. That’s as much as we’ve ever seen in a battery pack, and more than you’ll get out of premium wall chargers for laptops and other devices. Case in point: the official charger for the 16-inch MacBook Pro delivers the same amount of power.

Having that extra 60 watts of output means that when you plug in multiple devices, you’re less likely to see a slowdown in charging. I was able to charge my MacBook Pro and an iPhone 18 Pro Max at the same time at full speed. If you were to plug in three large devices (like laptops) at the same time, there would be a substantial drop-off in power going to the first device, but it can handle most common travel setups without that happening.

The result is a backup power solution that works just as well as plugging your devices into the wall, even when you need to charge multiple devices. On a recent weekend trip, I used it to charge a 14-inch MacBook Pro faster than its included 70-watt adapter, without exceeding 140 watts. It’s the kind of performance we all wish we could get from a battery pack, but never actually do.

This is a secondary concern, but I think it’s worth pointing out that ReelCharge offers a best-in-class three-year warranty on the ReelPro 200W. That’s a lot of protection for any piece of tech, and far longer than most competitors: Anker, for example, backs battery packs with an 18-month warranty, which is better than average. Standing by its products for so long shows the brand has strong faith in them.

If you are a frequent traveler, or a mobile worker who lives and dies by having constant access to a laptop, this is the best high-capacity battery pack I’ve tested to date. It’s definitely too big to fit in your pocket, so it’s overkill if you just need to top up a phone or tablet occasionally, but this is the ReelPro 200W, a big battery backup that you can depend on, and it costs far less than the Anker Prime, our previous laptop charger of choice.
