#6401. A fossil pygmy sperm whale discovered in Peru might hold the record for the most uneven, lopsided face of any mammal ever recorded

A 6-million-year-old pygmy sperm whale from Peru had both nostrils on the left, a snout angled 31 degrees down and a face unlike any other whale.

In 2015, Aldo Benites-Palomino was working on his bachelor’s thesis at the Museo de Historia Natural in Lima, Peru, when he examined a fossil sperm whale skull that looked twisted.

The skull had been found in the mid-1990s in the Pisco Formation of southern Peru. It stayed unnamed until this month.

Benites-Palomino and 10 colleagues have now described it as Scaphokogia huachafo, a pygmy sperm whale about 9 feet (2.7 meters) long.

According to the University of Zurich, it shows the most extreme facial asymmetry known in any cetacean and possibly in any mammal, though that claim rests on a single skull.

The holotype, the specimen that defines a species, carries the catalog number MUSM 972. It came from Aguada de Lomas in the Sacaco basin of Arequipa, from rock laid down between 6.3 and 5.6 million years ago.

Toothed whales already have uneven skulls, because the fatty organs they use to make sound sit in the forehead. In this animal, both bony nostrils lie left of the midline and the left one is much larger than the right.

The right premaxilla, a bone of the upper face, grew thick and heavy, while the two sides around the eyes differ in shape and reach.

Benites-Palomino, who studied the fossil for his doctorate at the University of Zurich and now teaches at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg, gave the university a blunt summary. “The skull looks completely crooked,” he said.

The first worry was damage. Sediment can flatten or twist a skull over millions of years, so the team checked the bones for signs of it.

The sutures were fully closed, and the paper reports no deformation elsewhere on the skull. Benites-Palomino called the shape “genuine biology, not a result of poor preservation.”

The drawing of the fossil in the paper also marks shark bite marks along the snout. Sharks left similar traces on other Pisco fossils, and a separate study found that megalodons went after the fatty noses of sperm whales in the same formation.

The team placed 37 points on the facial bones of 3D skull models with a program called MorphoDig, then ran the statistics in R.

The sample held 31 taxa, among them 11 sperm whales, 4 early toothed whales and 16 members of the group that includes modern dolphins.

Francesco Nobile produced the 3D scans of MUSM 171, according to the acknowledgements, which describe the paper as the end of nearly a decade of work on Peruvian fossil sperm whales.

S. huachafo sat at the extreme of the pygmy sperm whales in the first whole-face analysis and again in a second one that corrected for family relationships.

Other strange skulls sat near the edges too, including the walrus-like dolphin Odobenocetops, also known from Peru. The analysis placed Pebanista, the giant freshwater dolphin from the Peruvian Amazon described by Zurich paleontologists, close to some sperm whales.

The authors listed flatfish, with both eyes on one side, and owls, with offset ears, as the better-known cases of uneven heads in vertebrates.

The species name comes from a term that Peruvians use for something flashy, bizarre or tacky. Benites-Palomino said the proportions of the whale “broke every rule of symmetry and elegance seen in living cetaceans.”

“Its anatomy is so extravagant and odd that huachafo seemed the perfect name for it,” he said.

The snout of S. huachafo tilted 31 degrees below the main axis of the skull. Its relatives had less of a bend, with about 16 to 21 degrees in S. cochlearis and 27 degrees in S. totajpe.

Dense bone and ossified cartilage filled out the snout, which would have moved the center of gravity forward. Heavy bone often goes with bottom feeding in sea mammals, as in sea cows and walruses, and the dense skeleton of Perucetus colossus is another Peruvian example of a whale built with extra bone.

A second skull, MUSM 171, kept the atlas, the first bone of the neck. With the neck raised as far as it could go, the snout still pointed 22 degrees downward. With the neck lowered fully, the angle reached 55 degrees.

Gabriel Aguirre-Fernández, a co-author and doctoral advisor at the University of Zurich, said the whole arrangement served one purpose. “The entire cranio-cervical complex is modified to point the snout directly toward the bottom,” he said.

Living sperm whales hunt squid in deep ocean water, the university said. The paper describes S. huachafo as a bottom feeder in the shallow coastal seas of the late Miocene.

Most bottom-feeding marine mammals find food by sight or with specialized structures around the mouth, the authors wrote. Scaphokogia appears to lack those structures, and they proposed that it used echolocation to find prey in soft sediment.

Eight large tooth sockets mark the underside of the upper jaw, and spongy bone had filled them in. The authors suggested that the animal may have had teeth earlier in life and lost them.

The paper states that the size of the nasal organs in Scaphokogia cannot be assessed, because soft tissue rarely fossilizes. The authors based the sonar idea on the attachment sites those organs left on the bone.

MUSM 171 is identified only as Scaphokogia sp., and it is the one specimen of the genus with an atlas. The range of motion given for S. huachafo is therefore a reconstruction from a related animal.

When the team compared only the left and right premaxillae, the most extreme animal was S. totajpe, a species Benites-Palomino helped name in 2020, and not S. huachafo.

That test ranked Scaphokogia as the most asymmetric whale genus in the sample. A separate comparison between groups gave a p-value of 0.076, which the authors called marginal.

The university said this way of feeding disappeared as ocean conditions changed at the end of the Miocene. Surface scans of the skull are public through Morphomuseum. The catalog number MUSM 972 still ties the original to the Lima museum where Benites-Palomino first saw it in 2015.

The full study was published in the journal Communications Biology.

NASA's Swift Observatory went out in a blaze of glory this week, but it left behind millions of images of the universe that could fuel discoveries for decades.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Early Wednesday (Nov. 4), NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory fell out of space, burning up in the sky over Sumatra. It was a fitting, fiery end for a telescope that spent 22 years studying the most powerful explosions in the universe — and, even with Swift gone, its observations will continue to feed scientific curiosity for years to come.

Swift's most important contributions to astronomy are not exactly eye candy. Designed to swivel toward deep-space explosions at a moment's notice, Swift excelled at capturing bright, fleeting and faraway specks of light. The multiwavelength observatory was equipped with optical, ultraviolet (UV) and X-ray instruments, allowing it to catch cosmic bursts of energy across the electromagnetic spectrum, zeroing in on flares of light that other telescopes might miss.

One of its most significant detections was a gamma-ray burst — an incredibly bright blast, likely emitted by a giant star as it exploded in a supernova before collapsing into a black hole. Swift's famous image of GRB 221009A, or the BOAT ‪—‬ short for "brightest of all time" ‪—‬ looks like a speckled orange bull's-eye, caused by waves from the explosion rippling across space.

How the Swift Observatory saw the gamma-ray burst GRB 221009A, which may be the most energetic emission of this kind ever seen.

But Swift also took millions of observations of the nearby universe, including galaxies in our backyard. One of its most jaw-dropping images is this 24-hour exposure of the Andromeda galaxy (M31), located about 2.5 million light-years from Earth.

Andromeda is the closest major galaxy to ours, and it may be destined for a shared fate. Scientists suspect that Andromeda and the Milky Way are drawing closer together and might eventually collide. The merger would add Andromeda's roughly 1 trillion stars to our sky, though there probably wouldn't be any life left on Earth to appreciate it.

In Swift's view of our encroaching neighbor, captured with the observatory's ultraviolet instrument, tens of thousands of Andromeda's stars shine like sapphires set in a sparkling ring.

According to NASA, the observatory detected some 20,000 ultraviolet light sources in this image, captured over two months from May to July 2008. These sources include thousands of dense, hot star clusters scattered across Andromeda's 150,000-light-year-wide ring, as well as the distant galaxy M32 (seen as a bright orb of light to the bottom right of Andromeda's center).

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

In visible-light images of Andromeda taken with ground-based telescopes, the galaxy's bright center bleaches out many of the fiery young stars that emerge in Swift's view. While Swift likely won't be remembered best for shimmering starscapes like this one, it's a powerful reminder that looking at familiar structures in a new light can change everything.

#6399. A new genetic discovery points to how sloths manage to survive while using so little energy

Scientists mapped the two-toed sloth genome and found a record number of extra gene copies. These unique energy-linked genes may explain how sloths survive on so little daily energy.

Hanging motionless in trees, sloths are doing something no other mammal on record does. They can run their entire bodies on less than half the energy expected for animals their size, and biologists still can’t explain how.

A new genome of the two-toed sloth points to one possible part of the answer. The sloth carries dozens of extra gene copies that it shares only with other sloths, and many of them are tied to how cells make and manage energy.

The researchers think those copies may be part of what lets a sloth live on so little, though that idea hasn’t been tested in living cells yet.

“Evolution has already run billions of experiments,” said Marcela Uliano-Silva, a bioinformatician at the Wellcome Sanger Institute in Cambridge, England, who co-led the work. “By studying unusual animals like sloths, we sometimes uncover biological solutions that humans never evolved.”

The sequenced sloth was Lama Su, a two-toed sloth from Tierpark Berlin. When zoo veterinarians euthanized the animal for reasons unrelated to the study, the team collected its spleen, blood, brain, lung and liver and froze them at once.

DNA from the spleen became the finished genome, about 3.2 billion letters long, with almost every letter placed on a chromosome.

A southern anteater named Anton, from the same zoo, supplied a second new genome. Sloths, anteaters and armadillos make up Xenarthra, the only major branch of placental mammals that arose in South America.

The team compared the two new genomes with three published ones, from a maned sloth, a second species of two-toed sloth and the nine-banded armadillo. A catalog of mammal genomes, 41 species in all, from mice to people, supplied the wider comparison.

A big share of any mammal’s genome is DNA that can copy itself and insert the copy somewhere else. Biologists call them jumping genes, and in people most of them are old and no longer active.

The machinery a jumping gene uses to copy itself doesn’t only copy the jumping gene. Sometimes it copies the message a cell has just read off an ordinary gene and writes that message back into the DNA as a new copy of the gene.

The copy lands without the switches that turn a gene on, so some geneticists have classed these copies as genes that don’t work.

The two-toed sloth’s genome has 15,898 of them, nearly twice as many as a human genome, which has around 8,000. Other mammals typically carry between 2,000 and 8,000 such copies. No mammal, and no other animal, has been reported with more.

The other four xenarthrans all had more than 10,000. And in the two-toed sloth, some single genes had been copied more than 100 times each.

About a third of the two-toed sloth’s copies, 32%, also exist in at least one of the other two sloths and in no other animal the team checked.

That puts their origin on the branch leading to the ancestor of all living sloths, roughly 30 million years ago, after sloths had split from anteaters and armadillos.

The copying didn’t stop there. Of the copies found in the two-toed sloth and nowhere else, nearly 16% are so close to their parent gene that they were made recently or are still being made.

The jumping genes that do the copying are themselves switched on in the sloth’s tissues, especially in blood.

The anteater and the armadillo show neither sign. Their jumping genes are old, and their gene copies show no sign of recent copying.

To find copies that might be doing a job, the team started with the 5,123 copies the two-toed sloth shares only with other sloths and kept narrowing.

A copy had to be switched on in at least one of the five tissues sampled, and 2,347 were. It had to keep at least 70% of the instructions for its parent protein, and 525 did.

The third test looked at the DNA itself. Mutations that change the protein had to be less than half as common as mutations that don’t, which is the mark of a gene that natural selection is protecting. That left 123.

The team then checked each one by hand and kept only copies with sequencing reads that could have come from the copy alone, not from its parent gene. Thirty-eight remained.

Many of the 38 are copies of genes that work in mitochondria, the parts of a cell that produce its energy. Others come from genes that handle fats or help a cell respond to stress. The energy-related copies are most active in blood, brain or liver, and the stress-response copies in blood.

Why a sloth would keep spare copies of energy genes is the question the team raises next. Some of the same researchers have early, unpublished results on the DNA inside sloth mitochondria.

Those results suggest that mitochondrial DNA in sloths is under less pressure than usual to stay intact, possibly because so little energy is demanded of it.

If that’s right, the extra copies might be compensating for mitochondria that have picked up more mutations than they otherwise would.

“Our findings suggest that sloths might have evolved genetic ‘backup systems’ that help compensate for their ‘relaxed mitochondria’ and support their unique lifestyle,” said Camila Mazzoni, who co-led the study at the Leibniz Institute for Zoo and Wildlife Research in Berlin.

The researchers describe the link between the 38 copies and a sloth’s metabolism as a hypothesis, not a result. They haven’t yet tested what any of these copies does inside a living cell, and the mitochondrial finding behind the idea isn’t published yet.

The team also had only one anteater and one armadillo to compare against, out of 11 anteater species and 25 armadillo species alive today.

More genomes will be needed to tell whether what the team saw in those two animals holds across their whole groups.

Uliano-Silva’s team plans to grow sloth cells in the lab next and test what the copies do there.

For now, the 38 copies are candidates. Whether any of them helps a sloth live on so little energy is the question those cell experiments are meant to answer.

The full study was published in the journal BMC Biology.

#6398. This may be the best evidence yet that dinosaur blood can fossilize

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Minerals may have preserved remnants of ancient blood in a dinosaur bone, but some are skeptical

Using a technique called scanning electron microscopy to peer inside an 115 million-year-old dinosaur limb bone, researchers captured images of tiny ellipsoid structures, about 20 micrometers in diameter, that may be fossilized red blood cells. Molecular analyses found preserved heme — the oxygen-carrying component of hemoglobin — in the bone.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

The life and times of a dinosaur may be written in its blood — if blood can be preserved in bone.

Tiny microstructures found in the limb bones of a fossilized 115-million-year-old specimen are the remnants of red blood cells, researchers report November 2 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. The team says these are both the oldest red blood cell structures yet identified and the first to be chemically proven. But not everyone is as sanguine about that conclusion.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

The ability to identify such structures could offer a powerful molecular window into the physiology of long-extinct animals, including their metabolism and even activity levels, says paleontologist Kliti Grice of Curtin University in Bentley, Australia.

The bone, from a fossil-rich site in northeastern Brazil called Mina Pedra Branca, belonged to the dinosaur Aratasaurus museunacionali. Grice and her colleagues used a variety of chemical and imaging analyses to study the Cretaceous Period specimen.

Maurilio Oliveira/Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 4.0)

The team prepared thin cross-sectional slices of bone and imaged details of the limb bone’s internal structure with focused electron beams. That revealed ellipse-shaped microstructures within the limb’s fossilized network of blood vessels.

A map of the ellipsoids’ chemical element composition revealed that they were full of iron, carbon and nitrogen, all components of a biomolecule called heme. Heme is an iron-bearing, ring-shaped molecule found in hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen throughout the body.

Then, the researchers used a technique that identifies molecules by how they scatter laser light. Those analyses suggested the presence of porphyrins, ringlike organic compounds found in blood — and the precursors of heme. Finally, they ruled out contamination from other porphyrins, such as the pigment chlorophyll, by separating and identifying the molecular contents of a bone extract. That experiment also suggested heme.

Taken together, these findings point unequivocally to the preservation of molecular traces of ancient blood, the team says. They also offer a clue to a novel pathway that might preserve those traces for so many millions of years.

Blood cells decompose within days of the death of an organism. Only unusual and fast-acting environmental and biochemical conditions could have stopped decay and held those tissues in place as the organism fossilizes.

In this fossil, the secret ingredient was a manganese oxide mineral called hausmannite, the researchers say. The team’s analyses had found the mineral within the ellipsoid structures. That mineral, they propose, may have acted as a time capsule, preserving the cellular structures and protecting the molecules within, including collagen amino acids.

Distinguishing fossilized blood cells from nonorganic minerals that formed within a fossil after the organism’s death is a tricky task. During fossilization, mineral-rich fluids seep in and around the bones, and the minerals that form within the fossil can bear a strong resemblance to bodily structures.

In a 1997 study, two paleontologists analyzed tiny spheres found inside the limb of a fossil, possibly a pterosaur. The spheres were once thought to be the fossilized remnants of ancient blood cells, but the duo determined that the spheres were instead pyrite, an iron mineral that had been deposited in the bones after death.

Those paleontologists suggested that, going forward, several criteria should be met before proposing a blood cell origin for fossilized structures, including comparing the shape of the structures with that of living related organisms and identifying certain biomarkers in the structures. One of those biomarkers is heme compounds.

Grice and her colleagues say that their study meets these criteria. Unlike the pyrite, hausmannite was crucial to preservation, “rather than simply a mineral that replaced biological material after it had disappeared,” she says. The close spatial relationship between the hausmannite, the blood cell-like structures and the chemical signatures of heme “raises the possibility that mineralization helped stabilize, entomb and protect components of the original biological material during fossilization.”

But Mary Schweitzer, a paleontologist at North Carolina State University in Raleigh who was not involved in the new study, says she doesn’t think these findings do fully meet those criteria.

The heme biomarkers, for example, don’t appear to be localized to the round structures alone, as would be expected in fossilized blood cells, but come from analysis of the entire bone. The proposed red blood cells also differ in size and shape compared with red blood cells from living birds and reptiles, she says.

Schweitzer is no stranger to skepticism over the discovery of ephemeral tissues in fossils. In 2005, she and her colleagues reported the first recovery of flexible, soft-tissue blood vessels from the 68-million-year-old fossilized leg bone of a Tyrannosaurus rex. It was a landmark study that sparked debate, including over how it would even be possible to preserve such tissues through deep time, as well as the most surefire way to detect them in the present.

“I am not convinced” that the research team has definitively identified heme compounds, Schweitzer says. “I do applaud them for bringing a plethora of methods to the study. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, and that does require state-of-the-art technology.”

No one really knows what a dinosaur’s red blood cell shape would be, let alone how the process of fossilization might distort the original shape of the structures, or allow heme-related molecules to escape their cellular confines over time, Grice says.

And, she says, her team’s interpretation of the evidence doesn’t just rely on the observations of those structures. “[It] rests on the convergence of anatomy, morphology, mineralogy, elemental analysis and molecular chemistry,” she says. “That combination is critical.”

As for whether other fossils might have molecular traces that have been preserved by hausmannite, “we simply don’t know yet,” Grice says. “But this type of preservation may not be quite as rare as we currently think.”

#6397. I’m a Tape Measure Guy. But This Laser Measuring Tool is Testing My Loyalty.

Measuring long walls, gauging ceiling heights, and handling the awkward math are where the Mileseey S50C shines.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Look, I’m a tape measure guy. Always have been. Always will be. That red Milwaukee 25-footer rides on my hip like Wyatt Earp’s six-shooter, ready to draw when I need fast dimensions across a 2x4 or sheet of plywood. I ask a lot of it, and it always delivers. That is, until I ask it to stretch across a long wall and maintain its rigidity.

But I got my hands on Mileseey’s S50C Laser Measure and it has me reconsidering how often I reach for my trusty tape—especially when my foe is notably larger than normal and physically out of my league. No one ever said I had to fight fair, so lately I find myself reaching for a more technologically advanced weapon of choice. And in that moment before I grab, I always have the same thought: Why am I working so hard?

What’s won me over about the S50C is how easily it takes over the measurements I least enjoy making with a tape. Long distances. Wall-to-wall dimensions. Floor-to-ceiling heights. The sort of thing that usually has me looking around for another person to whom I need to say “Hey, could you hold this for a second?” Aim, press the button, read the measurement. Nobody has to put down what they’re doing and walk over.

The S50C has been impressively accurate and simple to operate. It’s also handy as heck, which matters to me more than a long list of functions. A tool can have enough computing power to figure out a Mars landing, but if taking basic measurements becomes a small administrative project, I’m going straight back to the tape. With this one, I’ve found myself grabbing it as soon as a measurement starts feeling like it’s going to give me a fight, which is exactly how any new tool tends to earn a home in my usual routine.

The S50C also goes way beyond telling you how far away the opposite wall is. You can easily toggle through its measurement modes on the touch screen display to select area, volume, and wall area calculations, along with more specialized functions for awkward dimensions. For something like a basement renovation, that means you can gather room dimensions and calculate floor area without balancing a notebook on your knee or pulling up the calculator app on your phone. For painting, wall-area calculations give you a useful starting point for estimating coverage. You still have to account for multiple coats, product coverage, and waste—I mean, this device isn’t going to manage your entire renovation. But it can take a welcome chunk of arithmetic off your plate.

The trick is choosing the proper mode and taking the measurements it requests. It isn’t one magical button that automatically understands your basement. You supply the dimensions by placing the green laser dot on the opposing wall or ceiling, press the button, and record the measurement. The S50C handles the rest of the calculations.

The S50C has a built-in camera with up to 8x zoom—but it’s for helping you aim at distant targets. A 2.4-inch AMOLED touch screen displays the targeting view, measurements, and menus. That gives the camera a practical reason to exist. Finding a little laser dot at a distance—especially outdoors measuring distances for a fence installation—can become its own project and a huge source of frustration. The camera is there to help you see where you’re aiming, which is great for me and my ever-flagging eyesight.

Mileseey lists a maximum measuring range of 670 feet. I’ve yet to verify that distance without putting the laser on my neighbor’s home five houses away from me, but it does give you some semblance of the work this device is designed to accommodate. It also charges through USB-C and carries an IP65 dust- and water-resistance rating.

There are plenty of measurements for which I’ll keep pulling my tape. Most, come to think of it. Marking a board for a miter saw cut, checking a short dimension, laying something out directly on a workpiece. That familiar steel blade is like an extension of my hand most times.

But the S50C is worth grabbing when distance, access, or a shortage of available hands suddenly turns that tape measure into a nuisance. Its more advanced functions expand the possibilities, I suppose, but its quick convenience is what brings me back in those moments of need. On that note, if you think your measuring needs are more basic in nature, Mileseey’s S50 PrecisionX model is an ideal alternative to all of those extra features of the S50C.

I really didn’t expect to become attached to a laser measure, let alone one with so many bells and whistles. But then my tape buckled halfway across my ceiling, and the S50C gadget was sitting right there waiting.

#6396. Scientists found two tiny new fish species deep in the Red Sea, but they have completely disappeared from the wild since the discovery

Two gobies under an inch long, netted at 98 feet off Saudi Arabia in May 2023, remain the only known specimens of Trimma charon.

On May 15, 2023, Viktor Nunes Peinemann and Matthew Tietbohl Talas of King Abdullah University of Science and Technology (KAUST) collected fish during a scuba dive outside a Red Sea cave off Walih Island, Saudi Arabia. The depth was roughly 98 feet (30 meters).

The team nabbed two small gobies at the bottom of the cave entrance, where the fish had been moving over dead carbonate rock.

A paper from September 2026 names them Trimma charon. Other surveys done after 2023 found no other specimens, and the authors can think of only two possible explanations: a truly rare fish, or it has a home on deeper reefs.

The methods section lists clove oil, a fish anesthetic, and hand nets as the only collecting gear.

The site sits in the northern Red Sea at 27.7897°N, 35.1630°E. The reef there is a steep slope that drops past 328 feet (100 meters).

The authors described the bottom as hard carbonate with little structure and few living or recently dead corals, which they called unusual for the Red Sea. The region’s corals are better known for recovering from heat stress that bleaches reefs farther south.

Peinemann photographed the paratype fresh from the water in an upright photo tank, using a Nikon Z7 body, a 105 mm macro lens and a Godox flash. Almost all the body color faded later in preservative, the paper says, and only the eye kept a faint trace of its pattern.

Both fish went to the ichthyology collection of the Royal Ontario Museum, under catalog numbers ROMI118236 and ROMI118237. The larger one, 0.66 inch (16.8 millimeters) long without its tail fin, is the holotype, the specimen that formally defines the species. The second, the paratype, measures 0.48 inch (12.1 millimeters).

The paper also thanks the captain and crew of the research vessel R/V Al-Azizi for support during field operations.

In life the goby is translucent, with a broad orange-red stripe running from the eye to the base of the tail. Three narrow pale bars interrupt the stripe, and each iris is split into four uneven sectors of white and orange.

The tail carries the feature that gave the fish its name. Peinemann described the golden spots in a statement from the publisher Pensoft. “They cover most of the fin and resemble small gold coins,” he said.

Charon is the ferryman of Greek mythology, who carried the souls of the dead across the river Styx in exchange for coins. The acknowledgements credit Jesse Cochran with suggesting the name.

Peinemann also connected the name to the reefs below the dive limit, saying those dark, deeper and unexplored reefs could be seen as a kind of underworld.

Before this description, scientists recognized 10 species of Trimma in the Red Sea. The new fish raises that count to 11, and at least nine appear to live only in that region.

That makes Trimma the most species-rich goby genus in the Red Sea, the authors wrote, though Gobiodon, Eviota and Hetereleotris are close behind. Peinemann and his colleagues also built an illustrated identification key to all 11 species, with photographs of each.

Three other members of the group have been named since 2015. One is Trimma berumeni, a yellow goby known from large caves in the Farasan Banks, also collected near 98 feet (30 meters).

KAUST scientists also described the grumpy dwarfgoby on Red Sea reefs, and small bottom-dwelling species of this kind supply nearly 60 percent of the food eaten by other reef fish.

The closest look-alike is Trimma anaima, a pygmygoby recorded from the Comoros to Fiji but never from the Red Sea. The two share the orange-red stripe, but T. charon has 14 rays in each pectoral fin, while T. anaima usually has 16.

The genetic comparison used COI, a mitochondrial gene often used as a barcode for animal species. Among 93 described Trimma species with available sequences, T. anaima came closest, at 85 to 86 percent identity.

The authors used that gap for a rough calculation. Modern reefs have existed in the Red Sea for only about 5.5 million years, so a split inside that window would need at least about 3 percent COI change per million years.

That pace falls within rates estimated for other small reef gobies. The authors noted that it would still imply a long presence in the Red Sea, and that the fish could instead be more widespread or related to an unsampled lineage.

The size of the record is the main limit of the study. “So far, the entire species is known from only a single encounter and two specimens,” Peinemann said in the Pensoft statement.

The team surveyed comparable habitats at similar depths on other Red Sea reefs and found no more. The fish also never appeared in the rotenone sampling stations of two earlier reef studies, or in a survey that identified fish larvae by their DNA.

Depth complicates that absence. The authors’ surveys ran mostly between the surface and 98 feet (30 meters), along the Saudi coast from the Gulf of Aqaba to the Farasan Banks, and 98 feet was the deepest the team dived for science, according to Pensoft.

The steep wall at Walih Island continues far below that line. The paper raises the possibility that 98 feet is only the shallow edge of the species’ range, with more of the fish on mesophotic reefs, the dim coral zone below normal diving depth.

The paper offers no deep-reef collections to test that idea. Deep work elsewhere has turned up a new reef fish about 400 feet down off Brazil, and the authors called the Red Sea and wider Indian Ocean particularly undersampled at these depths.

The catalog entry for both specimens still gives one locality and one date, outside a cave off Walih Island on May 15, 2023.

The full study was published in the journal ZooKeys.

#6395. Two teeth found in a Thai coal mine reveal a giant ancient rodent that weighed almost seventy pounds

Two teeth from a Thai coal mine point to a new giant rodent of about 66 pounds that lived some 34 million years ago, long before South America's giants.

Two teeth lay in a clay band inside the main coal seam of the Krabi lignite mine in southern Thailand. A Thai-French expedition between Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources and French research institutions collected them, and they belong to a giant rodent weighing about 66 pounds (30 kilograms).

Researchers from Thailand, France and Canada have now named the animal Yakamys sirindhornae. A molar and an incisor are all they have, so that weight is a loose summary, not a measurement.

The molar and the incisor turned up close together in the same fossil-bearing layer. The team links them provisionally to one animal because both are exceptionally large and come from the same horizon.

The clay band sits at Bang Mark Pit, part of the Krabi lignite mine, which the Electricity Generating Authority of Thailand manages and where it gave permission to work.

The Department of Mineral Resources holds them in Bangkok as TF 2942 and TF 2943. Mammal fossils from the pit and a magnetic reversal in the rock, Chron 13r, date the layer to the late Eocene. That means 35.1 to 33.7 million years ago.

Yaowalak Chaimanee of CNRS and the University of Poitiers is first author of the paper. Five co-authors from Poitiers, Montpellier, McGill and Thailand’s Department of Mineral Resources worked with her. They chose the molar as the holotype, the specimen that anchors the species name.

The tooth is 0.46 inch (11.56 millimeters) long and 0.44 inch (11.27 millimeters) wide. Its crown stands 0.31 inch (7.85 millimeters) high. Contact marks on two sides show that it had erupted and touched its neighbors.

R. Lebrun of the Montpellier evolution institute ISEM scanned it on an EasyTom 150 micro-CT machine, at 9.03 micrometers.

The model is headed to MorphoMuseuM, an open 3D archive. A lone tooth from the Hudson Bay region did similar work for woolly mammoths in Canada, moving their range farther east.

Hulgana had been considered the largest Asian member of the family. Its molars are less than half as long and wide. The nearest match is Manitsha tanka, an Oligocene rodent from South Dakota, with a molar of about 0.32 by 0.35 inch (8.2 by 8.9 millimeters).

The second tooth is a fragmentary left lower incisor, 0.44 inch (11.23 millimeters) across. The lab set it in epoxy, cut it lengthwise, polished it, etched the surface with phosphoric acid for 30 seconds and then coated it in palladium.

A Hitachi S-4000 scanning electron microscope then showed enamel about 235 micrometers thick, under 0.01 inch. Hunter-Schreger bands, sheets of enamel rods that cross each other, were up to five rods wide. Ischyromyidae, an extinct family of very early rodents, have that pattern.

Yak means giant in Thai, and mys means mouse or rat in Greek. Princess Maha Chakri Sirindhorn receives the species name for backing science and paleontology in Thailand.

Seven published equations based on living rodents gave the mass. Virginie Millien of McGill University, a co-author here, wrote the incisor equations with a colleague in 2010. Molar equations came from a 2024 paper by Boivin and colleagues.

Results ran from 47 to 104 pounds (21.4 to 47.3 kilograms). The mean was 70 pounds (31.6 kilograms), the median 63 pounds (28.6 kilograms).

The authors took the midpoint and rounded it to 66 pounds, a value they wrote “should not be interpreted as a precise point estimate.”

Adding each equation’s error widens the spread to about 24 to 152 pounds (10.8 to 69.0 kilograms).

Later giants in South America weighed far more, though their numbers have also been revised, with Josephoartigasia monesi first put above 2,200 pounds (1,000 kilograms) and then cut to about 770 pounds (350 kilograms).

Phoberomys pattersoni fell from as much as 1,634 pounds (741 kilograms) to about 617 pounds (280 kilograms) at most.

Age is the other half of the argument. The authors say an early rodent line had grown exceptionally large by the late Eocene. South America’s giant caviomorphs, the group of the capybara, the largest rodent alive, diversified well after that.

Teeth from South China suggest that mammals grew larger before their teeth specialized. A tooth from Chile put a capybara relative in the Atacama 8.8 million years ago.

Most ischyromyids known from Asia were small and came from China and India, so Krabi adds Southeast Asia to the map.

The team also holds a very large unpublished rodent incisor from the Pondaung Formation of Myanmar, from the late middle Eocene. Nobody has identified it yet.

One molar and one incisor were too little for a formal family-tree analysis. The authors could not test whether similarities with the genus Hartenbergeromys reflect kinship or convergence.

Lake clay surrounded the teeth, but the sediment alone “does not demonstrate a semi-aquatic lifestyle,” the paper says. A lakeside life like a capybara’s stays only a possibility.

Size on islands, a common route to rodent gigantism, does not fit either, since nothing suggests Krabi was an island then.

More complete skull and limb material would be needed to test those ideas. Until it turns up, the species consists of one molar and a fragmentary incisor.

The full study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

Archaeologists found a small cemetery full of high-status burials, two of which may be the graves of Germanic chieftains.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists excavating in northeastern France have unearthed a small fifth-century cemetery containing the graves of two Germanic chieftains and two warhorses. The burial ground is providing new information about the transitional period after the fall of the Roman Empire.

The burial complex was discovered near the city of Colmar, just a few miles from the Rhine River, which forms the border between France and Germany. This area had a Gallo-Roman village from the first to the third centuries, and archaeologists found several ancient houses, hearths, wells and craft areas, according to a Nov. 6 translated statement from the French National Institute for Preventive Archaeological Research (Inrap).

Archaeologists also uncovered a rare fifth-century cemetery at the site, which was used from about A.D. 450 to 500, a critical time period in Western Europe because of the collapse of the Roman Empire. While scholars have debated for centuries about why the empire fell, one key issue was the repeated occupation of Rome in the fifth century by Germanic tribes known as the Goths and the Vandals.

Several of the burials included gold-and-garnet accessories on weapons and clothing.

Archaeologists discovered 11 adult graves, three graves of children and two horse burials at the site, according to the statement. In two of the female burials, archaeologists found silver bird-shaped brooches, glass bead necklaces and a bone comb, suggesting that these may have been high-status women.

But two of the male burials, in particular, stood out because of their high-quality grave goods, including a sword with a partially preserved wooden scabbard, a shield, a javelin and a scramasax, a type of Germanic short sword, which was decorated with a gold-and-garnet accessory. The weapons are characteristic of the burials of Germanic chieftains or mercenaries, according to the archaeologists, and two horses were buried nearby with their harnesses.

Two horse burials were discovered in the cemetery.

In addition to the weapons and warhorses, archaeologists noticed evidence on the men's bones that hinted that the individuals were likely warriors. Two people suffered stab wounds that showed no signs of healing, which suggests they died quickly and violently, according to the statement. And another man's right knee bones had completely fused together, which would have prevented him from bending it. This condition, called ankylosis, commonly results from an improperly healed injury.

The archaeologists believe the warrior's grave goods weren't just for show, but further study of the skeletons is planned to confirm whether the injuries seen during the excavation could have been sustained in a conflict.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Few Germanic settlements and cemeteries from the fifth century have been found, so the newly excavated site should provide important information about the upheavals linked to the fall of the Western Roman Empire and how that political collapse affected communities on the edge of the empire.

#6393. For Over a Decade, They’ve Been the Face of the World’s Most Entrancing Treasure Hunt. Have They Finally Solved Oak Island’s Mystery?

There's gold in the water on Oak Island—but a maze of old tunnels is hiding where it’s coming from.

“Hundreds of thousands of dollars and the wits of the cleverest American engineers and college professors have been vainly spent in trying to solve the mystery of the Money Pits of Oak island and its sheltered haven, Mahone bay, Nova Scotia.”

Those words appeared in the pages of Popular Mechanics 100 years ago, in the March 1926 story “Hunting Hidden Treasures.” In the century that followed, the amount of money and wits expended on the mystery of Oak Island has only grown.

Since 2014, the public faces of the Oak Island mystery have been Rick and Marty Lagina, the stars of HISTORY’s long-running series The Curse of Oak Island. Across more than 250 episodes, audiences have followed along with the brothers’ success and setbacks, their obsession and their frustrations. When they began, via an investment in Oak Island Tours in 2006, they were pursuing a quixotic dream inspired by an old magazine article, joining a pantheon of prospectors that included Hollywood stars like Errol Flynn and John Wayne, and at least one U.S. President (Franklin D. Roosevelt, who kept tabs on the developments on Oak Island throughout his life).

Now, heading into their fourteenth season (debuting on November 10 on the History Channel), the siblings from Michigan are striking a more retrospective tone, reflecting on their role in this centuries-long quest for answers and the colleagues they’ve lost along the way (the season premiere pays homage to the late Dan Blankenship, a longtime partner of the Laginas who spent more than 50 years searching Oak Island before his 2019 passing). Now, there’s a question that’s become just as pressing for the two men as the Oak Island mystery itself: “After all these years, what was it all for?”

Ahead of the new season, Rick and Marty Lagina sat down with Pop Mech to reflect on fourteen seasons of television, how treasure-seeking has changed over the centuries, and what keeps them, and audiences, returning to Oak Island and its mysterious Money Pit year after year.

Although the marketing for Season 14 has leaned heavily on a new discovery through which the Laginas’ “lifelong quest has finally paid off,” the brothers kept the details of the coming episodes close to the vest. (Pop Mech was able to preview only the season premiere.) Otherwise, they were as candid and at times as self-effacing as they’ve been throughout fourteen seasons of television.

In fact, Rick is quick to dispel what he feels is the biggest misconception fans of the show often have. “We’re portrayed on some level as experts in every field, and we’re not,” he told us. “That’s why we have such a large tent of people helping us, because we’re not experts in every field, every arena.”

“It’s a very complex mystery,” he adds, “and we need everybody under the tent, if you will.”

That tent doesn’t just include the various experts who appeared on the program over the last decade, but also the centuries of treasure hunters who came before them. “Rick holds those prior searchers in this huge, high regard,” Marty says of his brother, “and thinks about them all the time.”

If one believes the account published in The Yarmouth Herald in 1863, that list of prior searchers stretches all the way back to 1795. That’s when a young farmer named Daniel McGinnis arrived on Oak Island via canoe, propelled by a piece of folklore which claimed that Captain Kidd had buried millions of dollars worth of treasure on the island. As he searched, he came across a depression in the ground that seemed deliberate, and called together a small team to dig on the site. As they excavated to a depth of 30 feet, they found remnants of a previous presence at the site (some accounts say flagstones, others oak platforms), and that led them to think they’d discovered the location of the buried treasure—or what’s long been referred to as the “Money Pit.”

In the early 1800s, the Onslow Company reportedly paid a visit to the same site, and they dug deeper into the Money Pit than McGinnis ever dared to go, roughly 80 to 90 feet deep. The Onslow Company found further indications that the pit was deliberately dug to store something, though their evidence was far more destructive. Their dig set off a booby trap that caused the Money Pit to flood with seawater up to the 33-foot level. The Onslow Company was unable to bail out the excavation site at the time. To make matters worse, Marty would note, later attempts only exacerbated the problem.

“There was almost certainly a flood tunnel that caused the initial booby trap,” he told us, “And people will come up to you and they’ll say, well, why don’t you shut off the water this way or shut off the water that way. The problem is there’s been so much pumping over the years by other people that the water is coming in from other places.”

Marty, who possesses an extensive engineering background in both petroleum and renewable energy, is both enamored with and exasperated by what’s been left behind by the treasure hunters who preceded him.

“From an engineering standpoint, I’m always astonished, absolutely astonished and in rapt admiration for what those people were able to do with picks and shovels,” Marty says of those earlier excavators. “I mean, you can’t believe it. If you were out there, and you saw these hand hewn timbers come up from 180 feet down. They had nothing. They had horses, you know? I mean, it’s just really amazing.”

Impressive as that work was for its time, it left modern-day diggers with consequences of their own.

“One of our scientific consultants, Ian Spooner, is a PhD geologist. He calls it Chutes & Ladders,” Marty says, before quickly adding, “He actually calls it Snakes and Ladders, because that’s the Canadian thing.”

“We have so many interconnected passages now that have been made by other people that we have to decipher all that,” he laments, “And every time a timber comes out, I mean, almost every time, you have to say, is this an original worker’s timber or is this a searcher’s timber? And we have to run the scientific analysis on that.”

In the show’s ninth season, water samples from the site turned up trace amounts of gold, a discovery that showed just how badly booby traps and centuries of earlier digging had muddied the trail.

“If you followed [the show], you know there’s gold in the water, which has kept us coming back for years,” Marty continued, “Now it’s there, it’s real, it’s coming from a source. And if the water was just moving geologically, like I’m used to in my prior business, we could trace it back, but the problem is it’s all interconnected, so it’s difficult.”

Have past attempts to solve the mystery actually further obscured Oak Island’s secrets? Did stories stoking the hunger for treasure actually, if unintentionally, contribute to the partial destruction of the Nova Scotia island?

If so, it’s a guilt that Pop Mech partially shares.

At one point in our conversation, Marty cuts in to jokingly ask, “By the way, can I do a quick commercial for Popular Mechanics?” to which this author, never afraid of a little self-promotion, gleefully assented. “Growing up, I loved that magazine. Absolutely loved that magazine,” he says, “And Rick will attest, we kind of had a hard time getting our hands on actual magazines. But I mean, I would read those from cover to cover.”

“There is one connection to Popular Mechanics too, aside from our interest in the magazine,” Rick chimed in to add, “There was an article in Popular Mechanics about Oak Island.”

As it turns out, there was more than one. But if Rick recalled an Oak Island story from one of the magazines he and Marty read cover to cover, it was likely the one published at the exact mid-point between 1926’s “Hunting Hidden Treasures” and today.

Fifty years ago, the September 1976 issue of Popular Mechanics ran with the cover story “7 Great Quests of Man,” and the mystery of Oak Island’s treasure was discussed alongside such cryptic quandaries (and just plain cryptids) as Bigfoot, the Loch Ness Monster, ancient aliens, and Noah’s Ark.

But if such outlandish company makes the Oak Island mystery feel like a fantasy, the work the Laginas have done over fourteen seasons has pulled things back into the realm of reality. While a literal pot of gold at the end of this proverbial rainbow would be a satisfying conclusion, Rick says that the true value of these excavations extends beyond the potential payday.

“When you talk about story, the science and technology has pushed the timeline of what happened on Oak island, or at least when something started to happen on Oak Island, to me, has been pushed back, literally, into the latter part of the 13th century,” he noted, “We have core samples from wells, we have carbon dates from old walls, we have archaeo-astronomical alignments. I don’t see any other explanation that some of these structures, including Nolan’s Cross, given the alignments contained within them, were of that time frame. So what happened long, long ago, well before Europeans were supposed to be on this continent, to me, that’s a story in and of itself.”

Perhaps, in that sense, the treasure has served as the profit motive, the lure that funded centuries of expeditions, which may finally be uncovering the site’s true history.

“Marty has always said that the mystery of Oak Island has endured because of treasure, because of that component, and he’s absolutely right,” Rick concluded. “But at this point, I think the treasure and the story are somewhat aligned in terms of importance, and I hope that we can push forward on both agendas.”

The new season of The Curse of Oak Island premieres on the History Channel November 10 at 9/8c.

#6392. Simple fungi can recognize shapes, like circles and crosses, when looking for wood to eat

Daily Wonder, Pink Oyster Mushroom A fungus has no brain, no eyes, and no nerves. Yet a wood-rotting fungus, given a cross of wood blocks to grow on,…

A fungus has no brain, no eyes, and no nerves. Yet a wood-rotting fungus, given a cross of wood blocks to grow on, attached more of its threads to the outer blocks than to the inner ones.

Given a circle to grow on, it showed no such pattern and left the center bare. The researchers suggested the difference may be a form of pattern recognition.

Yu Fukasawa of Tohoku University in Japan led the 2024 study with colleagues at Tohoku and at Nagaoka College.

The fungus they used lives on forest floors and builds its networks by sending thick strands of thread, called cords, from one piece of dead wood to the next.

Its name is Phanerochaete velutina, and Fukasawa’s team had earlier found that it remembers the direction to a piece of wood.

“You’d be surprised at just how much fungi are capable of,” Fukasawa said. “They have memories, they learn, and they can make decisions. Quite frankly, the differences in how they solve problems compared to humans is mind-blowing.”

Even so, the team phrased its own conclusion as a question, not a verdict.

The mushroom in the video above is a pink oyster, not the fungus in this study. Pink oysters, named for their salmon-pink caps, grow on dead hardwood and are farmed on straw as food.

The study’s fungus grows as a thin crust on wood, with no cap or stem. Both break down dead wood with a network of threads.

Fukasawa’s team cut beech wood into cubes less than half an inch (1 cm) on a side, weighed them, and let the fungus grow into them for six weeks.

The team then set nine cubes on each tray of damp soil, in a circle or in a cross, with 2 inches (5 cm) between neighboring blocks. Each tray was about 9.5 inches (24 cm) square, and there were ten of each shape.

Everything but the shape was the same from tray to tray. The trays stayed in the dark at 68°F (20°C) for 116 days, nearly four months.

Once a week the team misted them with sterile water and moved them around the incubator. A camera 18 inches (46 cm) above the trays photographed each one monthly.

At the end, the researchers counted the cords attached to each block, then dried and weighed the blocks again to see how much wood the fungus had broken down.

After 116 days, cords ran from block to block across every tray, though a few blocks ended up with no cord attached at all.

In the cross, the four blocks at the ends of the arms had more cords than the four middle blocks and the one at the center. The count ran from zero cords on some blocks to nine on others.

In the circle, no position in the ring had reliably more cords than another. The cross result was the opposite of what the team had predicted.

They had expected the center block, the one with four neighbors, to be the most connected, and instead the blocks at the ends of the arms were.

The team suggested the outer blocks may have worked as outposts, where the fungus absorbed water and nutrients from the soil. The inner blocks, with fewer cords, may have become little more than a path for cords passing through.

The more cords a block had, the more of its wood the fungus had broken down. Blocks in the circle lost between 18% and 65.5% of their dry weight, and blocks in the cross lost between 16.7% and 62.7%. Overall, the cross blocks lost a little less than the circle blocks did.

The researchers also reran the analysis without the extreme blocks, the ones with no cords or with nine. Without them, the difference between the two shapes faded, while the link between cords and decay remained.

The fungus also spread roughly the same amount of thread over the soil in both shapes. So the cross blocks didn’t decay less because the fungus grew less. The network was built differently, and the wood decayed differently.

The recognition argument rests on that difference. In a human brain, different images activate different groups of neurons, and that contrast in activity is what lets the brain recognize an image.

A network of fungal threads that builds itself one way for a cross and another for a circle may be doing something similar, Fukasawa’s team wrote.

Every block started the same way, with threads growing outward in all directions. Then the fronts from neighboring blocks met and fused into one body.

In the circle trays, the merged fungus kept growing outward, and by day 34 a large bare patch had formed at the center.

Fukasawa’s team compared this to fairy rings, the circles of mushrooms that widen year after year because the fungus beneath them grows outward from its edge. Why the fused network left the center empty is something the team can’t yet explain.

One possibility they raised is crowding: fungal growth is known to stop once the threads get dense enough, and the threads inside the ring may have reached that point.

Whether the fungus is conscious is irrelevant, the team wrote, because cognition can run without consciousness even in a brain.

Slime molds, which also have no brain, have already solved a maze and linked food sources with networks about as efficient as a real railway.

The team raised one possible explanation, and it involves rhythm. The amount of calcium at each growing tip rises and falls in a cycle, and so do the flow of material and the electrical activity through the fungus.

When separate colonies fuse, those rhythms tend to synchronize, and synchronized rhythms may be how the network carries information about where things are.

The rhythm idea is a hypothesis, and this experiment didn’t measure it. The team also can’t yet say whether the tray lids affected the empty center of the ring.

The lids were loose and came off every week, so the researchers doubt the middle ran short of oxygen. The way to settle it is a tray with no lid, and that’s the experiment they said would be worth running.

The full study was published in the journal Fungal Ecology.

#6391. The Grand Canyon’s drinking water comes from a single spring connected to over six miles of hidden caves

Researchers mapped over six miles of caves beneath the Grand Canyon, revealing how groundwater flows and why its drinking water faces pollution risks.

For decades, the twelve different water spigots used by visitors in Grand Canyon National Park have drawn their water from Roaring Springs, a cave-fed spring on the North Rim.

In an August 2025 study, researchers at Northern Arizona University (NAU) described over 6 miles (10 kilometers) of cave passages behind the spring. They mapped them with a handheld lidar scanner.

The 3D maps reveal the passages that carry water through the limestone below the North Rim. That system is fast and vulnerable to contamination from the surface.

The park’s water supply has served more than 6 million visitors a year from that single cave spring. Its water is almost entirely snowmelt from the Kaibab Plateau.

Built starting in 1965, the 12½-mile (20-kilometer) Transcanyon Waterline carried that water toward the South Rim and its 800-plus historic buildings.

The aging pipe had at least 85 major breaks between 2010 and mid-2026, according to the National Park Service. A single break often tops $25,000 to repair.

A replacement project shifts the South Rim intake to Bright Angel Creek near Phantom Ranch. On August 29, 2026, a flash flood destroyed a water intake pump and other infrastructure.

The Bright Angel Creek and Roaring Springs intake areas “sustained significant damage,” the park reported in a September 2026 update. Roughly 40 percent of the old pipeline between Phantom Ranch and the North Rim was also damaged.

The South Rim has been under Stage 4 water restrictions while the park arranged to truck in about 200,000 gallons (757,000 liters) a day. Pumping from Bright Angel Creek to a new treatment plant could begin by November 16.

Blase LaSala, a Ph.D. student in ecoinformatics at NAU’s School of Informatics, Computing, and Cyber Systems, led the mapping. He worked with NAU professor Temuulen “Teki” Sankey, a remote sensing expert.

With park staff and volunteers, the team scanned Roaring Springs Cave, Muav West Cave and Redwall East Cave. The handheld scanner uses near-infrared laser light and records up to 300,000 points per second.

The crews documented more than 6.3 miles (10.2 kilometers) of passages in 25 days. The caves extend beyond 0.6 miles (1 kilometer) from their entrances and 1,300 feet (400 meters) below them.

In Muav West Cave, the lidar maps agreed 98 percent with a traditional survey, which covered about half the distance in the same time.

“I had no idea how large and long these caves are,” Sankey said. “Grand Canyon’s caves have never been mapped in 3D like this.”

Karst forms where water dissolves soluble rock such as limestone, opening caves, conduits and sinkholes.

The caves lie in the Redwall and Muav limestones, karst layers some 2,300 feet (700 meters) beneath the plateau surface. Water travels through these limestone layers via steep fractures and underground conduits.

Abe Springer, an NAU professor and co-author, also worked with the park on dye tracing tests. Dye dropped into surface sinkholes reached springs about 12 miles (20 kilometers) away in as little as a week.

From the 3D models, the authors conclude that today’s groundwater follows near-vertical cracks and the tilt of the rock layers. They link those patterns to regional faulting and uplift.

In Redwall East Cave, bubble trails and other features sit above the stream passage. They suggest that today’s flow may reuse pathways carved by an older aquifer.

“It’s like looking at a black box,” LaSala explained. “You see what comes in and what comes out, but it’s very hard to quantify what’s going on in there.”

The researchers describe karst aquifers like this one as both vulnerable to contamination and challenging to model.

Runoff from burned areas or E. coli bacteria entering sinkholes linked to Roaring Springs Cave could force the park to halt its pumps, NAU warns.

The Dragon Bravo Fire, which started on July 4, 2025, burned 149,399 acres (60,460 hectares), including 71,129 acres (28,785 hectares) of the park.

The park’s burned area emergency response listed protection of the drinking water system among its treatments.

The fire also changed conditions on the Kaibab Plateau, where the snowmelt that feeds the spring begins. The NAU team now has to account for those effects.

“It’s a new twist to our study,” Sankey noted.

A new grant from Grand Canyon National Park will expand the mapping across the park. The university scheduled that work to start in early 2026.

LaSala and Sankey plan to use airborne lidar and decades of satellite data to map sinkholes on both sides of the canyon. They will also track how snowmelt has accumulated over the last 40 years.

“Understanding where the water sinks is critical for the infrastructure, the animals, the plants and the rest of the ecosystems that rely on these springs,” LaSala said. “They’re like oases.”

The study was published in the journal Scientific Reports.

#6390. Nov. 9, 1939: The birth of Carl Sagan

Nobody did more to popularize astronomy than American astronomer Carl Sagan, who was born Nov. 9, 1939, in New York. The landmark 1980 television series Cosmos: A Personal Voyage, which he cowrote and narrated, has been viewed by more than half a billion people. He also wrote popular science books, including The Dragons of Eden, Pale Blue Dot, and the novel Contact, which was turned into a motion picture.

But Sagan was no slouch scientifically. He predicted that Venus’ temperature should be above the melting point of lead due to a runaway greenhouse effect. He also imagined that Jupiter’s moon Europa might have an underground ocean.

As a member of the imaging team for NASA’s Voyager probes, Sagan hatched the idea for Voyager 1 to take the image that would become known as the Pale Blue Dot. In it, Earth is seen from a distance of 3.7 billion miles (6 billion kilometers). He later wrote, “Look again at that dot. That’s here. That’s home. That’s us. On it everyone you love, everyone you know, everyone you ever heard of, every human being who ever was, lived out their lives … on a mote of dust suspended in a sunbeam.”

Michael E. Bakich is a contributing editor for Astronomy magazine. With degrees in astronomy and planetarium education, he has led many eclipse tours, published several books on observing, and logged thousands of hours at the eyepiece.

#6389. Jackery’s FridgeGuard Brings Basic Automated Backup Power at an Affordable Price

Our tests show that during short blackouts, this automated backup power system gets the job done.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Not every home power backup solution has to be an expensive and complicated system. Certainly, a portable power station can be affordable, but it usually has to be set up when the power goes out, which isn’t convenient if you’re not at home. What if you could meet in the middle with something affordable but also automated? That’s the aim of a device like Jackery’s FridgeGuard, an automated appliance backup device that costs less than $800.

It’s named FridgeGuard because Jackery, like competitors Bluetti and BioLite (whose products we also reviewed), is banking on the idea that the appliance most people care about powering when the lights go out is the refrigerator. It makes sense; you’ve got the most to lose with spoiled food during an extended blackout. But in truth, you can use this type of backup with any alternating-current-powered device, whether that is a fish tank, automatic pet feeder, garage freezer, or even essential medical equipment. And since this is designed to be always-on, you don’t have to think about it very much once you set it up.

Out of the box, the Jackery FridgeGuard is smaller and lighter than the competition. It’s a few inches shorter than those from Bluetti and BioLite, and only weighs 23 pounds—the others weigh more than 40 pounds. That makes the task of placing this out of the way, either mounted on a cabinet or sitting flat on top of a cabinet, a bit easier. It also has two airflow vents that you can remove to clean or replace filters, which is a nice feature to have in a kitchen, where air particles can be heavier from cooking.

Cutting down on the size keeps the price point lower, but this comes at another cost. At 1,024 watt-hours of battery capacity, FridgeGuard can’t run a refrigerator for as long as the competition, and with only 800 watts of output (roughly half the amount or more of the others), you can’t run as many things from it. There’s also only one outlet, as opposed to two, so if you want to power more than one thing, you’ll need to attach a power strip.

Of course, this may not matter to people who really are only concerned about keeping their refrigerator running. I tested this out on my own full-size French-door, bottom-freezer model, and I was able to run it for 11 hours. That’s enough time for most people experiencing a blackout after a severe storm. If you find that’s not enough, you can always add the FridgeGuard battery pack and double that capacity to 2,048 watt-hours.

There are some other hidden cost-cutting measures, too. Jackery includes attachable feet if you want to stand it vertically, but wall mounts are optional ($29), and if you want to recharge it using a portable solar panel, you’ll need to purchase a proprietary adapter that costs $89. Competitors include wall mounts, and solar inputs are built into their units.

Despite some cost cutting with its hardware, FridgeGuard doesn’t skimp on smart features within the app. If you're away from home, you get notifications when the power goes out and when the FridgeGuard is starting to get low on power. If you live in a region with variable utility rates, you can set it to only recharge from grid power when the rates are at their lowest (your electric company can tell you when that is).

Conversely, you can also use it to save a bit of money by using a time-of-use (TOU) mode that powers the fridge from the battery during high-rate hours and grid power only during the low-rate hours. It would take many months of testing to see how much money you could really save using this mode, but the potential is there.

Some may worry about daily discharge and recharge, but FridgeGuard runs on a lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) battery that offers up to 6,000 recharge cycles, which is 16 years if you were to do it every day. In the end, TOU mode may be worth it.

If all you want is automated backup power for your refrigerator (or another essential appliance or device) for a few hours, Jackery’s FridgeGuard is the simplest and most economical way to go. It’s easy to set up and the epitome of instant automation. If you frequently experience blackouts longer than 12 hours, spending a bit more on a system from Bluetti or BioLite may suit your needs better, but if not, Jackery has built a good product for you.

#6388. A rare giant moa egg is returning to New Zealand after spending sixty years in an American collection

Colossal Biosciences announced plans to return a rare giant moa egg, discovered in New Zealand in 1966.

A giant moa egg found in New Zealand on January 14, 1966, spent about six decades in a private American collection. On June 12, 2026, it resurfaced at a public auction run by Artemis Gallery in Louisville, Colorado.

Colossal Biosciences, a Dallas-based biotechnology company whose de-extinction projects include the moa, bought the egg. On October 20, 2026, it announced plans to return it to Aotearoa, the Māori name for New Zealand.

Fewer than 40 sufficiently complete moa eggs are known in public collections worldwide. Only eight keep at least 90 percent of their shell.

The egg measures about 8.7 by 6.7 inches (22 by 17 centimeters). That is roughly 1.5 times the length of an ostrich egg and nearly double its volume.

It has been reconstructed from many fragments, and more pieces still need to be reattached.

The egg may have come from a human burial site from the Moa Hunter period, around AD 1300. Further research is needed to confirm that origin.

Colossal made the announcement at the opening of the 11th International Meeting of the Society of Avian Palaeontology and Evolution. The meeting ran from October 19 to 23 at the Christchurch Town Hall and opened with a pōwhiri, a Māori welcome.

Sir Peter Jackson, the filmmaker and a partner in Colossal’s moa program, contacted the company on learning the egg was being sold abroad. Colossal offered to rescue it at its own expense and fly it home privately.

“Every New Zealander grows up knowing the moa and feeling its loss,” Jackson said in a statement.

Once restored, the egg “will very likely become only the ninth known nearly intact moa egg,” Jackson noted.

Colossal plans a repatriation ceremony in December. The egg will be handed to Professor Te Maire Tau, a Māori historian and tribal leader in the Canterbury region.

“When we launched the moa program we made a clear commitment that indigenous leadership would guide the science and every decision surrounding the project,” explained Ben Lamm, the CEO and co-founder of Colossal.

“We are honored to help return it home,” Lamm stated.

The remaining fragments will be reattached under the guidance of Ngāi Tahu researchers.

Non-destructive imaging, or sampling for DNA and isotopes, could confirm the egg’s species and origin. Ngāi Tahu will decide whether and when to do this, following tikanga, or Māori customary practice.

Kyle Davis is a Ngāi Tahu archaeologist and an expert in cultural heritage.

“To see an egg of this rarity return to Te Waipounamu is extraordinary. It carries information about the moa species that birthed it, the landscape it came from and potentially the people connected to it,” Davis said.

Te Waipounamu is the Māori name for New Zealand’s South Island, where the egg is headed.

The moa de-extinction program behind the purchase began in 2025 as a joint initiative of Colossal, the Ngāi Tahu Research Centre, Jackson and Canterbury Museum.

Fossil eggshell preserves ancient DNA from extinct moa, elephant birds and emus, a study of fossil eggshell by Murdoch University researchers showed in 2010. Moa shell carried roughly 125 times less bacterial DNA than moa bone.

A team led by Leon Huynen recovered DNA from the inner and outer surfaces of moa eggs. Sequences from 69 eggshells matched seven moa species.

Several thin-shelled eggs belonged to the heaviest moa, in the genera Dinornis, Euryapteryx and Emeus. They were the most fragile bird eggs measured to date, the team reported in a 2010 study of moa eggs.

Sex-specific DNA on the outer surfaces of Dinornis and Euryapteryx eggs suggests that the lighter males incubated them. Even so, breakage would have been common if they sat on the eggs in the usual way.

The same DNA revealed two distinct lineages within Euryapteryx, whose eggs differed in shell thickness.

Each moa egg “holds information we can get nowhere else,” pointed out Beth Shapiro, Ph.D., Colossal’s chief science officer.

The Canterbury Museum lists nine described moa species, in six genera and three families. In the coastal moa, females could reach 4.9 feet (1.5 meters) tall, while males were about the size of a turkey.

People reached New Zealand more than 600 years ago, and moa disappeared within 100 to 300 years of their arrival.

Frequent hunting of the birds and their eggs drove those losses, a 2025 modeling study by Curtin University and University of Adelaide researchers suggests.

Moa could only have survived alongside people if no-take harvest zones had covered more than half of New Zealand’s land.

Dr. Paul Scofield, senior curator of natural history at Canterbury Museum, is a collaborating scientist on Colossal’s moa work.

“Moa are central to the natural and cultural history of Aotearoa, and this egg has far greater scientific and cultural value here than it could ever have in a private collection overseas,” Scofield remarked.

The information was obtained from Colossal Biosciences.

#6387. A high-fiber diet may clear away plastic in the gut

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Mice that ate lots of fiber had far less particles accumulate in the body

A diet that includes high-fiber foods, like these vegetables, might come with a surprise benefit. Fiber could help carry nanoplastics out of the body, suggests a new study in mice.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Here’s a new reason to eat your beans and greens.

A high-fiber diet may help sweep plastic particles from the gut, researchers report October 15 in Nature Communications. In mice that ingested plastic, eating loads of fiber daily kept the particles from piling up in the intestines. The finding hints at fiber’s power to protect the body from environmental garbage, says Eddy Y. Zeng, an environmental scientist at South China University of Technology in Guangzhou.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Researchers have long known that fiber can improve our health, in part by lowering cholesterol, keeping blood sugar levels in check and easing food through the gut. But now, Zeng says, his team’s results suggest an additional benefit.

We live in a world littered with plastic, much of it too small to see. These micro and nanoplastics, shed by disposable water bottles, fast food containers and other worldly junk, can make their way into our bodies. It’s not completely clear what such shards do to our health, but we have some hints. Scientists have linked plastic particles in people’s arteries to increased risk of heart attack and stroke. And mice that ingest tiny bits of plastic can show signs of organ injury.

Zeng’s team thought dietary fiber might provide some defense. Fiber forms a complex network of polymers that could trap ingested plastics like flies in a spider web, he says.

The researchers put mice on low-, medium-, or high-fiber diets, then fed them plastic particles. Over the next 24 hours, the medium- and high-fiber groups of mice cleared more particles from their bodies than their low-fiber counterparts, the team discovered. That’s important, Zeng says, because these particles can do damage. After a week of daily plastic feedings, his team saw gut tissue damage — but only in the low-fiber group. Experiments in test tubes suggest that fiber physically wraps around and sticks to plastic particles.

It’s too soon to say if dietary fiber does the same in humans. Zeng’s study was performed in mice and not tethered to realistic fiber numbers. Though mice in the high-fiber group ate far more fiber than what what’s recommended for people, he thinks the findings are worth pursuing in follow-up studies.

And even if fiber doesn’t end up purging plastic from people’s guts, Zeng says, it probably wouldn’t hurt for us to add a little more to our diets.
