#6385. Mysterious gas on Mars suggests magma below

Something is leaking from the ground near one of Mars’ largest volcanoes, and scientists think it’s a sign that active magma is buried below.

In a study published Nov. 4 in Science Advances, researchers report detections of hydrogen chloride (HCl) gas within 6 miles (10 kilometers) of the planet’s surface near the volcano Alba Mons. Notably, the detections came during aphelion, when Mars is farthest from the Sun and HCl is typically absent from its atmosphere. The location and out-of-season timing combined with the site’s unique geology likely point to volcanic outgassing — gas escaping from magma as it rises toward the surface — the authors argue.

“It seems that we are showing that there may still be more heat inside Mars than we thought, enough heat to have still fluid magma at depth,” co-author Daniel Mège, a professor at the Space Research Centre of the Polish Academy of Sciences, tells Astronomy.

The detection adds to mounting evidence, including recent detections of marsquakes, that the martian interior is not the dead world scientists once assumed. While scientists know volcanism influenced the planet’s evolution, it has remained unclear whether it continues today.

There’s no question that igneous activity shaped Mars into the planet we see today. Between 3.7 billion and 3 billion years ago, eruptions flooded the planet’s surface with vast lava plains. Later volcanic activity built some of the solar system’s largest volcanoes, including the roughly 16-mile-high (25 km) Olympus Mons — the tallest — and the 4.2-mile-high (6.8 km) Alba Mons, the largest by surface area. Though it rises just 4.2 miles (6.8 km), Alba Mons sprawls roughly 870 by 620 miles (1,400 by 1,000 km).

Those colossal peaks formed not through shifting plate tectonics like on Earth, but through stagnant-lid tectonics. Mars’ outer shell is a single rigid plate, meaning magma repeatedly erupted at the same sites, piling lava to towering heights over millions of years.

Many of these giants, including Olympus and Alba Mons, sit atop Tharsis, a volcanic plateau roughly 3,000 miles (5,000 km) across. Some lava flows at Tharsis are relatively young, dating back only tens of millions of years, yet there has been no definitive evidence for ongoing volcanic activity at the plateau or on the planet as a whole. Nevertheless, the case has been slowly building.

Before its mission ended in 2022, NASA’s InSight lander recorded more than 1,300 marsquakes. Quakes alone don’t prove volcanic activity. “Marsquakes can happen for multiple reasons, only one of which is faulting or other tectonic activity around volcanoes,” says R. Aileen Yingst, a senior scientist at the Planetary Science Institute who studies Mars geology and was not involved in the study. For example, some of the marsquakes InSight detected were caused by meteoroid impacts. And a cooling and contracting crust can cause seismic activity without magma.

Most of the quakes, though, were traced to a system of young volcanic fissures — long, parallel cracks where the martian crust was once pulled apart by rising magma — called Cerberus Fossae. Deposits of volcanic ash at Cerberus Fossae date to as recently as 53,000 years ago. Some scientists argue the large number of marsquakes in this setting could hint that magma is still moving below. In 2022, researchers proposed that a 2,500-mile-wide (4,000 km) active mantle plume lies beneath the Elysium Planitia region that surrounds Cerberus Fossae. On Earth, such columns of hot solid rock rise from deep in the planet’s interior, melting rock and creating magma, which could explain both the marsquakes and the ash deposits.

Orbiters searching for evidence of active volcanism on the martian surface have yet to turn up anything conclusive, the authors say. Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), the gas most often used to track volcanoes on Earth, has never been detected on Mars at concentrations that would point to magma. But that absence doesn’t mean Mars’ magma has gone quiet. Measurements at volcanoes on Earth show that SO₂ dominates during eruptions but drops sharply between them, when HCl becomes the more abundant gas. “[A]s long as we do not observe an active lava flow, or lava fountain, or explosion on Mars, we do not expect SO₂ emissions to be very high,” Mège says. Mars is also about 2.5 times richer in chlorine than Earth, and some martian volcanic meteorites are “up to four times richer” in chlorine than sulfur. “All this suggests that HCl is the best gas to look for on Mars if we want to identify active magma at depth that is not being erupted,” Mège explains.

The detections in the study come from the Atmospheric Chemistry Suite (ACS), a set of three infrared spectrometers aboard the Trace Gas Orbiter, a joint mission of the European Space Agency and Russia’s space agency, Roscosmos. The orbiter began science operations in 2018. ACS’s spectrometers analyze the sunlight filtering through the martian atmosphere, picking out the wavelengths each gas absorbs to reveal what’s in the air and at what altitude. In 2020, ACS made the first detection of HCl on Mars. It appeared planetwide during the warm, dusty season near perihelion, reaching concentrations of 4 to 5 parts per billion. Researchers attributed the presence of that HCl to chemical reactions involving dust, ice, and water vapor in the atmosphere during the warm season, not to volcanic activity.

What’s different about the new finding is that they detected HCl not at perihelion, but near aphelion, when the gas is otherwise absent from Mars’ atmosphere. The HCl was also localized above an interesting geological location: the region around the sprawling, low-profile volcano Alba Mons, located on the northern edge of Tharsis. After two tentative detections in one Mars year, a dedicated search two Mars years later turned up six more, mostly northeast of the volcano. The gas hugged the lowest 6 miles (10 km) of the atmosphere at concentrations up to 1.5 parts per billion.

The team ruled out atmospheric processes for the HCl and considered three possible ground sources: volcanic activity, mud volcanism, and the breakdown of chlorine-bearing salts called perchlorates. Mud volcanoes — likely inactive for billions of years — are widespread across Mars’ northern lowlands, so they alone couldn’t explain why the gas showed up in only one isolated place. And even if mud volcanism were active and releasing the HCl, it would likely still point to magma beneath the surface. Perchlorates are likewise found across the northern lowlands, which rules them out on the same grounds. “[I]f this mechanism were involved, HCl would be detected throughout the northern hemisphere, it would not be local,” Mège says. That leaves localized volcanic activity, which fits with models of the planet’s formation suggesting HCl should be among the most abundant gases in its volcanic emissions.

To gather more data, the team turned to high-resolution images from the High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment (HiRISE) camera aboard NASA’s Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and the Colour and Stereo Surface Imaging System (CaSSIS) aboard the Trace Gas Orbiter. They were looking for features near Alba Mons that could explain the seepage. They found a grouping of several narrow fissures that had not previously been identified. Many were just tens of centimeters wide, and some extended for up to 6.21 miles (10 km) long. Some were ringed by dark halos, suggesting material may have recently been ejected from within. The fissures were so thin that seasonal dust and ice activity should have already covered them up unless something was actively keeping them open. The authors did not confirm that the HCl came from the fissures, but they suggest the cracks may run from the icy ground near the surface all the way down to magma. Gas rising through them could escape directly or become trapped in the frozen ground, seeping into the atmosphere over time as the ice turns to vapor.

The case isn’t closed. The team didn’t catch gas escaping from any specific fissure. And although the cracks hadn’t been described before, they appear in older orbital images, with no visible changes between then and now. The authors stop short of a firm conclusion, saying only that ongoing volcanic activity is the best explanation for what they found. “What we can say today is: when we consider all the alternatives, it is the best explanation,” Mège notes. The next step is to keep watching. Future searches could reveal more hidden pockets of gas, and with them, more signs that Mars’ interior is still stirring. Ultimately, “to confirm the source,” Mège says, “we would need someone or some robot to check, with a very multidisciplinary payload.”

If there is still magma beneath Alba Mons, the implications reach beyond geology. Mars is smaller than Earth, so it should have shed its internal heat faster. “If it’s the case that Mars is still volcanically active, then the thermal models of Mars would probably need to be revisited,” Yingst explains. And where magma meets groundwater, hydrothermal systems – the kind of environment where life on Earth may have first emerged – usually follow. If conditions stayed stable long enough, Mège says, life could have arisen there. And “if these stable conditions continue until now, then these living organisms may still be there, somewhere below the surface.”

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer at Astronomy, based in Chattanooga, Tennessee, fueled by an unending curiosity about the universe. A former classroom teacher, he has a knack for breaking down complex concepts for a wide audience.

Neuroscientists say people can be "trained" to recognize when they're dreaming — in other words, lucid dreaming may be an acquirable skill.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

During dreams, bizarre scenes you encounter can seem as tangible as reality; you feel as though you're really flying through the sky or being chased through a jungle of bright-purple trees. But in special cases, people realize they're in the midst of a dream as it's unfolding.

Called lucid dreaming, this phenomenon occurs when we suddenly regain our capacity for metacognition, or thinking about our own thoughts, in the middle of a dream. Lucid dreamers can sometimes even control the content or trajectory of their dreams. Now, researchers claim that they've found a way to "train" people to lucid dream by having them meditate and complete virtual-reality-augmented exercises while they're awake.

In a study involving a few dozen participants, the scientists found that repeating this training twice a week for a month significantly increased how often participants experienced lucid dreaming. They say the approach could have practical applications as an intervention for people with nightmares, anxiety or post-traumatic stress disorder — but those applications are theoretical, for now.

If you could learn how to lucid dream, would you? Let us know in the poll below, and add your thoughts in the comments.

#6383. Researchers designed a stiff new solid that keeps heat from escaping better than soft foams and aerogels

A solid crystal film with organic layers blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics, a record for dense solids.

The best heat blockers are mostly made of air. Inside foam, it sits trapped in tiny pockets, which is why foam insulates so well and also why it squashes so easily. Now, engineers and chemists have made a solid crystal film that is stiff and has no air pockets at all.

It blocks heat nearly as well as still air, while staying stiffer than most plastics.

According to the team, no fully dense solid had ever been measured blocking heat this well at room temperature. The result suggests stiffness and insulation don’t have to be traded against each other.

Jun Liu, an engineer at North Carolina State University, led the work with physicist Dali Sun. Chemists at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and colleagues in China also took part.

So far the stiff crystal film exists only in the lab. It is a layer far thinner than a human hair on silicon wafers, and it contains lead.

In most materials, stiffness and heat flow rise together. Strong bonds hold diamond together, and it is extremely rigid, and it carries heat very well. Plastics are made of loosely stuck chains, which makes them softer and poorer at passing heat along.

“Because, in general, stiff materials are good at conducting heat, and materials that are not stiff are good at insulating against heat,” Sun said.

That’s why most insulation is soft. Foams and aerogels get close to air by being mostly air. However, they give up almost all their stiffness to do it.

Better insulation is one way to save energy in buildings, but a coating that has to hold its shape on a circuit or a solar panel can’t be that fragile.

The stiff film belongs to a family of layered crystals called inorganic-organic perovskites that stack thin sheets of lead and iodine between layers of organic, carbon-based molecules.

In earlier work, Liu’s group found that swapping some of the carbon-carbon chains in the organic layers with benzene rings – stiff, six-sided rings of carbon atoms – made the crystals both stiffer and worse at carrying heat.

This time the team used molecules carrying two rings joined by a double bond. The rings make the layer rigid. They also vibrate mostly at high frequencies, which barely overlap with the vibrations of the lead-iodide sheets, so heat has trouble crossing from one layer to the next.

The longer molecules also jumble the way the sheets stack. That disorder slows the passage of heat even more.

The team compared four versions. The one with a plain carbon chain carried about five times the heat as the best version, which used a molecule called azobenzene ethyl ammonium.

To test the films, the researchers coated each one with a thin layer of metal. A short laser pulse heated the surface, and a second beam tracked how fast that heat drained away into the film below.

At room temperature, the best film carried heat only about 60 percent better than still air. That’s less than half as well as typical plastics, and one spot on one sample came in lower still.

The team got its best results from films about 6 millionths of an inch (150 nanometers) thick. Thinner and thicker films did worse, and only films in a narrow band of thicknesses stayed near the record.

Measurements at several spots on several samples gave consistent results, so the team doesn’t think it was a fluke of one sample.

For the second test, the team pressed a tiny vibrating probe against the film to measure how much it resisted bending. The azobenzene film came out stiffer than most plastics and far stiffer than foams and aerogels.

The films are made by spinning a liquid onto a surface and then heating it. The authors wrote that the method can be adapted to coat large or flexible surfaces cheaply. This is in contrast to earlier, ultralow-heat films that needed a high-vacuum chamber.

In an interview with Earth.com, Liu picked out two early targets for this technology. “Electronics and spacecraft would be the first series of applications, for the near-room-temperature thermal insulation in the form of thin film coating,” he said.

The team also sees it as a coating for use near room temperature, based on how it held up when heated.

The researchers see other possible roles too, such as shielding parts in fuel cells and solar collectors, or slowing the heat that spreads when a battery fails. None of those uses has been tested.

Like the materials in many experimental perovskite solar cells, the film is built around lead.

“Yes, the current formula has lead in it and there needs to be environmental considerations if the exact composition will be used,” Liu told Earth.com.

He called the tested film an example of a design idea, and he pointed to related crystals made without lead as the route to practical use. Handling lead safely is already a question for perovskite solar recycling.

The team also spelled out limits of the design idea. A near-twin molecule, with the two rings joined by carbon atoms instead of nitrogen, didn’t jumble the layers nearly as much and missed the record.

The team’s model accounts for that gap only loosely, and it can’t yet predict which molecule will work before someone makes it.

Nobody has shown whether a lead-free crystal keeps the same trick. By the team’s own estimate, a molecule whose rings twist more easily could push the film’s heat flow close to that of air itself. Making one is the next test.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6380. A whale buried for 9.5 million years had unexpected company

Scientists discovered ancient brittle star fossils beside whale bones, revealing how marine animals gathered around carcasses millions ago.

Brittle stars gather around dead whales on today’s seafloor, sometimes at much higher densities than on the surrounding seabed. Yet no fossil had ever placed them at a whale carcass.

Studies of fossil whale carcasses have mostly reported clams, snails, and animals that eat bone.

Now fossils from beside a beaked whale skeleton in Denmark suggest that brittle stars joined these gatherings 9.5 million years ago.

If that reading holds, it’s the first fossil record of a brittle star tied to a whale fall. That’s the term scientists use for a sunken whale carcass and the community of life it feeds.

The clues are tiny skeletal plates from a species new to science, now named Ophiura huebnerjenseni. The fossils are loose pieces rather than whole animals, so they can’t show what the brittle stars ate.

Ben Thuy, curator of paleontology at Luxembourg’s National Museum of Natural History, led the study.

Thuy worked with Mette Elstrup and Trine Sørensen of Museum Sønderjylland in Denmark. The fourth author, Lea Numberger-Thuy, works at the Luxembourg museum and at a dinosaur park in Germany.

The Gram Clay Pit in southern Denmark exposes about 23 to 25 feet (7 to 7.5 meters) of clay that built up on the floor of an ancient North Sea. Geologists call these layers the Gram Formation.

The pit is famous for its fossil clams, snails, and animals with backbones, including whale skeletons and giant megalodon vertebrae. Sea urchins, sea stars, and their relatives have been far scarcer there.

Scientists call that group of spiny-skinned animals the echinoderms. Before this study, only one echinoderm species had been reported from the Gram Formation.

Brittle stars are echinoderms too, with long, thin, flexible arms built from many small skeletal pieces.

The North Sea has plenty of them today, yet none had been found in these old clays. Thuy and Numberger-Thuy had already searched for them in clays of a similar age at Groß Pampau in northern Germany, without success.

The new fossils came from sediment collected in 2018, during the excavation of a beaked whale‘s lower jaw and four vertebrae from its backbone.

The bones were found about 21 feet (6.5 meters) below the top of the exposed clay. That level dates to roughly 9.5 million years ago.

Five sediment samples came from around the skeleton. The team dried each one, soaked it in water, and washed it through screens, then washed the leftovers a second time with a detergent-like chemical.

Under a microscope, the researchers picked out the smallest fossils one by one. The best brittle-star pieces were then photographed with a scanning electron microscope.

For comparison, they also processed a sample packed with tiny fossils. It came from 2 to 4 inches (5 to 10 centimeters) below a fossil log that was dug up in 2023.

“Only three samples taken directly beside the whale bones contained brittle-star remains. Samples from the same layer farther from the skeleton, and other comparison samples, yielded none,” Thuy said.

The three samples held 33 skeletal pieces in all. Most were plates from the sides of the arms, along with one piece of an arm’s inner backbone and one plate from the central disc of the body.

The arm plate chosen as the reference specimen for the species came from a sample taken 2 to 8 inches (5 to 20 centimeters) from the whale’s jawbones. Its shape placed the animal in the genus Ophiura, which still lives in the North Sea.

The closest living match there is Ophiura albida. The fossil plates differ from it in two ways: they have a slanted upper edge, and they lack the faint spurs that O. albida plates carry.

A cluster of fossils beside a skeleton doesn’t automatically mean the animals lived there, so the team considered other explanations.

“We considered whether currents had simply concentrated the plates around the bones, or whether local chemical conditions had helped preserve them,” Thuy added.

“However, sea-urchin fragments of comparable size and mineral composition occurred in every sample studied. This makes a preservation-only explanation less likely and supports the interpretation that the brittle stars lived on or close to the whale carcass.”

Scientists divide a whale fall’s life into stages. In the early stage, the carcass enriches the seabed around it and feeds animals that take advantage of any sudden meal.

In the deep sea, later stages can follow. One of them supports life that runs on sulfur compounds released as the bones decay.

Fossils around the Gram whale included clams that filter food from the water and meat-eating snails, some of them scavengers.

The team found no clams of the kind that live off chemical energy with help from bacteria. The bones had no animals cemented to their surfaces and showed no signs of burrowing.

“We found no evidence for the later sulfide-based community stages that can develop at deep-sea whale falls,” Elstrup said.

“The discovery therefore adds a rare fossil perspective on how animals responded to a large food source on an ancient shallow-water seabed.”

Ophiura huebnerjenseni honors Holger Hübner and Thomas Jensen, who founded the heavy metal festival Wacken Open Air. It joins a long line of species named after musicians, but this one comes with a geological link.

“The clay that accumulated on the bottom of the ancient North Sea not only preserved the remains of a 9.5-million-year-old brittle star, it also turns Wacken Open Air into the muddy battlefield renowned by metalheads worldwide,” Numberger-Thuy said.

Brittle stars have been found before beside the carcasses of ichthyosaurs, ancient sea reptiles, in rocks from the Early Jurassic. A fossil whale fall had never produced one.

The researchers can’t yet say whether this species lived only at whale carcasses.

They favor the idea that it lived on the surrounding seabed and gathered at the carcass in numbers large enough to leave a fossil trace.

Living brittle stars at shallow whale falls also come from the nearby seafloor. Finding plates of this species in ordinary Gram mud, far from any bones, would support that idea.

For now, the only place Ophiura huebnerjenseni has been found is the mud right beside one whale.

The full study was published in the journal Neues Jahrbuch für Geologie und Paläontologie – Abhandlungen.

#6379. Drugs like Ozempic may help reverse chronic kidney disease

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Semaglutide helped repair blood vessels and reduce inflammation in the kidneys, a study finds

A patient undergoes hemodialysis, a process that filters waste from blood when the kidneys can’t. A new study shows how the popular weight loss drug semaglutide can help repair damaged kidneys.

Maria Symchych-Navrotska/iStock/Getty Images Plus

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ozempic’s key ingredient fixes faulty filters in the kidney.

The well-known weight loss drug repairs and restores blood vessels that power people’s waste disposal systems, researchers report October 1 in Nature Medicine. Those actions mean the ingredient, called semaglutide, can add another notch to its list of health benefits: treating chronic kidney disease.

In patients with the condition, semaglutide also increased blood flow and tamped down inflammation, the team found. The study reinforces the GLP-1 drug’s known anti-inflammatory effects, while also suggesting that it may play a direct role in protecting the kidney’s blood vessels, says Susan Quaggin, a nephrologist at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine in Chicago who was not involved in the work.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Chronic kidney disease affects an estimated 674 million people worldwide, with some of the most common causes being diabetes and high blood pressure. As the disease progresses, the kidneys slowly lose their ability to filter out waste from blood and excrete it as urine. This causes other health complications, as well as a sharply increased risk of dying from a heart attack or stroke.

Patients with diabetic chronic kidney disease who took semaglutide were less likely to wind up in kidney failure, or die from a heart attack or stroke, than those taking a placebo, researchers reported in 2024 in the New England Journal of Medicine. That trial was stopped early, as the drug was so effective at preventing death that doctors no longer considered it ethical to keep giving participants the placebo.

For the new study, some of those same researchers then looked at a subset of 106 participants to find out how the drug worked. The team collected kidney tissue samples before and after the participants took semaglutide, and compared them with samples from participants given the placebo. Semaglutide use led to striking visible changes in the tissues, including increased blood flow, reduced scarring and reduced blood vessel stiffness, a measure of vessel health.

Increased blood flow is important because it increases filtration, which is the kidneys’ main job, says Peter Nguyen, a nephrologist at Houston Methodist Hospital who was not involved in the study.

Researchers also looked at levels of a protein, called albumin, in patients’ urine. High levels can be an early sign that the kidneys’ filters aren’t working well. While those levels didn’t change much in those on the placebo, they dropped in patients taking semaglutide ― a sign the filters weren’t quite as leaky any more.

The team then looked under the hood for genetic clues to how semaglutide appeared to heal the kidneys. Within the glomerulus, the tiny blood vessels responsible for the kidney’s filtering action, genes relating to metabolic stress were turned off, Katherine Tuttle, a nephrologist at the University of Washington’s Providence Medical Research Center in Spokane, and colleagues found. Within these same cells, inflammatory genes were also turned off, while repair genes were switched on.

The researchers also looked at a subset of genes responsible for cells “talking” to each other within the glomerulus. Before semaglutide, the blood vessels and immune cells were “chattering” with each other, sending lots of inflammatory signals, Tuttle says. After semaglutide, the immune cells went quiet, silencing the messages that ramp up harmful inflammation. These changes in gene activity point to a healthier kidney that’s less stressed and inflamed, and that has had repair processes flipped on.

With semaglutide treatment, Tuttle says, patients’ damaged kidneys showed clear signs of repair.

#6377. Celestron Origin’s Mosaic Mode brings wide-field astrophotography to the biggest smart telescope

Almost any galaxy or nebula that the Celestron Origin Intelligent Home Observatory can find will fit in its field of view in a single shot. But there is a short list of exceptions.

For instance, the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the nearest major galaxy to our own and a popular first target, stretches about 3° from end to end. And the iconic North America Nebula (NGC 7000), which lies just 2,600 light-years away in Cygnus, spans roughly 2°. Both of these objects spill out of the field of view of the Origin Mark II, which, with its 6-inch (152 mm) f/2.2 Rowe-Ackermann Schmidt Astrograph (RASA) optics, captures a field of 1.32° by 0.75°.

Celestron’s answer is Mosaic Mode, a free update that brings automated mosaic imaging to the Origin smart telescope. In the Origin app, users draw a box around their target. Origin then divides that area into overlapping tiles, slews to each position, captures the data, and stitches the results into a single wide-field image.

Celestron Innovation Specialist Eric Kopit estimates that 90 percent or more of what Origin can see fits within its field of view. “The vast majority of objects” — most galaxies, globular clusters, and planetary nebulae — “are really small,” Kopit says. “But the objects most people want to start with are bigger.”

The ease of imaging with smart telescopes has brought a wave of newcomers into the hobby, he says, and those showpieces are usually what they reach for. Mosaic Mode ensures their reach does not exceed their grasp.

Mosaic Mode changes the rhythm of an Origin session. The telescope’s standard experience is built around watching an image take shape on your phone, tablet, or smart TV in near-real time. A mosaic is closer to an overnight project. Large targets can take hours, so Kopit says users can set the telescope to turn itself off once it’s done. Users can still watch the tiles come in, but it isn’t a requirement.

Those long capture times also made mosaic image stitching a challenge to bring to life. Each tile is shot at a different point in the night, and conditions can change from one moment to the next. A passing cloud might dim one tile and leave its neighbors untouched.

Targets with a wide range of brightness, like Andromeda, presented their own challenge. “One tile is a bright core, others are faint dust lanes,” Kopit says.

Early versions of the software had trouble blending exposures that were so different, but a recent firmware update reworked the processing. According to Celestron’s release notes, the new version produces fewer visible seams, better preserves faint nebulosity, aligns tiles more accurately, and better rejects frames corrupted by external light sources.

Mosaic Mode follows another software addition to Origin’s feature set aimed at users who want to push their images further.

With dithering, the telescope nudges itself slightly between exposures so the target lands on different pixels in each frame. Hot pixels and other sensor defects stay put on the chip, so once the frames are aligned to the stars, those defects end up scattered. Stacking software can then recognize them as outliers and toss them out.

Astrophotography dithering is a technique advanced imagers have relied on for years, and Origin owners had been asking for it.

“We had it on our roadmap, and people wanted it,” Kopit says.

Both Mosaic Mode and dithering work on every Origin, not just the Mark II that Celestron introduced in October 2025. The two generations share the same optics and electronics. The only difference is the camera, which owners can replace.

Camera sensors improve quickly, largely because Sony develops them for other industries. Astronomy gets to borrow the results, meaning a telescope with a fixed camera falls behind rather quickly.

“Modularity was always the vision,” Kopit says. “It can continue to take on new features so that you can keep the rest of the system.”

The Mark II’s camera uses Sony’s IMX678 sensor, an 8.4-megapixel chip with 2.0-micrometer pixels. The original Origin used the 6.4-megapixel IMX178, with 2.4-micrometer pixels.

Those smaller pixels matter more than you might expect on a telescope this fast. At f/2.2, Kopit says, Origin’s resolution is limited more by pixel size than by its 6-inch (152 mm) aperture. With a 335 mm focal length, the Mark II samples the sky at about 1.2″per pixel, compared with about 1.5″ on the original camera.

Sensors with larger pixels used to be commonly preferred in astrophotography for their increased sensitivity, but newer designs have changed that. Kopit sees room for more gains as pixels keep shrinking. First-generation owners can buy the new Origin 678C camera and install it themselves or have Celestron handle the upgrade.

Celestron first sketched the idea for Origin in 2011, before the technology existed to support it. The original goal wasn’t deep-sky astrophotography, but rather helping people see galaxies and nebulae the way they see the Moon and planets through an eyepiece.

“The idea is to aid the eye,” Kopit says. “For us, it’s turning imaging into a visual experience.”

In practice, that means users experience very little waiting. After the app connects, Origin focuses itself, uses Celestron’s StarSense technology to recognize the sky, and aligns in about a minute. When users tap a target in the SkySafari-powered planetarium view, the telescope begins taking 10-second exposures, stacking each new frame onto the last. Because the fast optics pour so much light onto a sensitive sensor, even the first exposure can reveal detail, and this view rapidly sharpens as the telescope stacks more exposures.

Thanks to this speed, capturing ten or more objects in a night can be a realistic observing plan. The app also offers audio presentations on more than 200 popular targets along the way. When users end the session, the final stacked image saves to the device, acting as a digital souvenir of the night.

The Origin app keeps its core controls up front and tucks advanced settings into deeper menus. A first-time user never has to touch them, which makes Origin an intuitive entry point into astrophotography.

Those venturing deeper into the app will find an option for equatorial mode, which uses an optional wedge to reduce field rotation, along with support for the StarSense Autoguider. This ability for users to choose the depth of their experience speaks to the different kinds of people attracted to Origin.

Celestron always expected Origin would be alluring even to experienced imagers — not just beginners. What surprised the company, however, was how many veteran astrophotographers have made it their primary rig. Many of those buyers already own a full imaging setup, Kopit says, but Origin is far easier to get running on a given night.

Kids sit at the other end of the spectrum. These young users often want to look through a telescope but struggle to see anything in an eyepiece. On a tablet screen, they can see it.

“With kids particularly, it opens up the hobby,” Kopit says.

Mosaic Mode is available now through the app and the latest Origin firmware. Kopit says more features are on the way.

#6376. Bees make a natural plastic that starts breaking down in soil within months

Solitary bees make natural plastic that breaks down in soil, offering clues for designing less persistent synthetic materials.

A plastic wrapper may be useful for a few minutes, then stay in the environment for centuries. But a small bee makes a plastic-like material that starts breaking down in soil within months.

The bee, Colletes inaequalis, uses it to cover the inside of its underground nest. The material helps protect the young bee growing inside.

Researchers studied these nests in Tennessee. In fresh nests, plastic made up 73% of the lining’s weight, but four months later, that share had fallen to 40%.

Now the team wants to learn how the bee makes a material that is tough but still breaks down. The answer could help scientists make better plastics for everyday use.

Jonathan Coote, an assistant professor at Virginia Tech, led the study.

Laura Russo, who studies bees at the University of Tennessee, first told him about the material while he was a doctoral student there.

Coote kept studying it during his later research at the University of Minnesota. After joining Virginia Tech in 2025, he made it his main research focus.

Scientists identified the chemical makeup of the bee’s plastic more than 45 years ago. But for years afterward, few people studied it further.

Most bees live alone rather than in hives. This species, common in the eastern United States, digs tunnels in the ground and builds small rooms for its young.

The female covers each room with a thin, clear layer, which gives these insects the name cellophane bees. She adds pollen and nectar, lays one egg, and closes the room.

The young bee spends more than 90% of its life inside. The lining likely protects it and its food from water and fungus.

The lining contains silk and a natural plastic made by the female.

A gland connected to her stinger releases tiny, ring-shaped molecules, which join into long chains as she spreads them over the walls.

The bee’s material resembles polyethylene, a plastic widely used in packaging.

Polyethylene contains long chains of carbon atoms held together by strong bonds that are hard to break, even in industrial compost.

Only about 9% of the world’s plastic was recycled in 2022. Nearly a third is poorly managed and ends up in the environment, where it can break into tiny pieces called microplastics.

Scientists have tried making similar plastics with weaker links in their chains. Water or enzymes, natural substances that help chemical reactions happen, can break these links.

These materials are called polyesters, and the bee’s plastic belongs to this group. “This is a polyester that mimics polyethylene,” Coote said.

Even with weaker links, most lab-made versions barely break down.

Their chains pack closely together and keep water out, making the weaker links hard to reach.

The best-studied version lost only 18% of its weight after 280 days in industrial compost. It did not break down at all under milder conditions.

The bee’s nests offered a clue that its material was different. More than 10,000 nests can share one site, and bees may return to the same ground for decades.

Yet the old plastic linings do not seem to pile up. Something appears to break them down.

The team first tried to dissolve the bee’s plastic to study its chains. After two days in a solvent heated to 302°F (150°C), the material still held its shape and size.

This suggested that the chains were linked together like a net.

About 60% of the plastic also formed tightly packed areas called crystals, arranged like those in polyethylene.

Usually, these tightly packed areas make plastic harder to break down. So the bee’s material seemed to have the same features that cause trouble in lab-made plastics.

The researchers collected fresh nests in March 2023 in Hamblen County, eastern Tennessee.

They returned in July and October 2023 and February 2024, digging seven to 12 inches (17 to 30 centimeters) down to find them.

After four months, the linings could still bend and hold their shape. By about seven months, when the young bees had become adults, cracks had appeared.

By 11 months, the linings crumbled when handled roughly. They had not vanished, but they were falling apart.

At first, the lining was about 73% plastic and 27% silk by weight. After four months, plastic made up only 40% of the remaining lining.

Silk usually breaks down fairly quickly, so the team was surprised to find the plastic breaking down even faster.

Later, the balance changed less, suggesting both materials were then breaking down at roughly the same pace.

Tightly packed regions accounted for about 60% of the plastic initially and nearly 100% of the remaining plastic after four months. By 11 months, their share had fallen to 39%.

This suggests the looser parts broke down first. The tightly packed parts appear to have broken down later.

The answer may lie in the plastic’s tiny building blocks. Most are rings with 18 carbon atoms, while some have 20 or 22.

Mixing these sizes may spread the weaker links unevenly along the chains. That could leave more links where water and enzymes can reach them.

The tightly packed areas are also small and less orderly, which could help. Microbes in the nest may also play a part.

Another idea involves an enzyme in the bee’s saliva. It might help build the plastic, then help break it down later.

The researchers rinsed the linings three times and collected the liquid. They added a chemical that this kind of enzyme can break apart.

Liquid from both a new lining and a four-month-old lining broke down the chemical. This suggests enzymes could keep working in the nest for months.

But the test used only one new nest and one older nest. More tests are needed to find out what those enzymes actually do.

The team still does not know which explanation matters most. Each nest provides only a few milligrams of lining, so some tests ran just once or twice, and all the older nests came from one site.

“The goal is to be able to answer that and then engineer it into something that we can make at scale. I don’t see a future where we have these massive bee farms making all of our plastic products,” Coote said.

If the spacing of the weaker links is the key, scientists could try copying it. They want a useful plastic that can break down in soil after its job is done.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

The chicken-shaped, black-glazed vase has an abecedarium ‪—‬ an inscription with the 26 letters of the Etruscan alphabet in order.

What it is: A bird-shaped ceramic inkwell

This small terra-cotta vase, which is shaped like a cockerel or young male chicken with human feet, was discovered in central Italy and was made by the ancient Etruscans. The potter inscribed the Etruscan alphabet on the body of the chicken, giving modern researchers clues to a language that has never been fully deciphered.

The vase stands just over 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is in the collection of the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The dark-black ceramic, known as bucchero, was made through a unique firing method that prevented the kiln from getting enough oxygen, which caused the clay to absorb carbon. Bucchero is considered the trademark Etruscan ceramic, and it was produced from the seventh to the fourth centuries B.C. by this pre-Roman society. It is unclear where the cockerel vase was originally found, but it may have been discovered in a grave in one of the many cemeteries that surround Viterbo, which was originally an Etruscan town about 50 miles (80 kilometers) northwest of modern-day Rome.

According to The Met, the vase may have been a portable inkwell used by an ancient Etruscan who was learning how to write. The cockerel's head was the stopper, and it was loosely attached to the body by a cord through a set of loops. The inscription on the body of the vase is known as an abecedarium ‪—‬ the sequential list of letters in an alphabet.

The Etruscan alphabet is well known, since it was adopted from a regional version of the Greek alphabet in the early eighth century B.C. There were 26 letters in the Etruscan alphabet, but one of them in this abecedarium is incorrect. A close look at the end of the alphabet shows that someone inscribed an S twice; the second one should look more like an X, according to The Met.

The terracotta cockerel vase was one of several ancient Etruscan artifacts that helped experts partially decode the mysterious ancient language, as it preserved the order of the letters in the early alphabet, archaeologist Gisela Richter wrote in a 1930 catalog of The Met's classical artifacts.

Thanks to the adoption of the Greek alphabet, it's possible to fully sound out the Etruscan language. But although more than 10,000 Etruscan inscriptions have been found, the language is still only partially understood because those inscriptions are short and any lengthy Etruscan literature that once existed has been lost.

#6374. When rain returns after a drought, groundwater reserves don’t always get caught up before the next drought

Most groundwater refills faster than it drains in a drought, but in about a quarter of places, the next drought hits before recovery ends.

When a drought breaks, the rain returns first, then the soil moisture, the plants and the rivers. Groundwater usually comes last, and in some places the next drought arrives before it has caught up.

A new global analysis suggests that, in most places, groundwater refills faster than it drains during a drought. But across about a quarter of the places studied, water levels tended to slip back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That matters because groundwater supplies roughly 35 percent of all the fresh water people withdraw, and it’s the reserve many communities rely on when rivers run low.

Hydrologist Sandra Hauswirth led the work with three colleagues at Utrecht University in the Netherlands. Their results come from a computer model rather than direct measurements.

It estimates how deep you’d have to dig to reach water, a level called the water table, month by month from 1960 to 2019.

This model divides the world’s land into squares about 0.6 mile (1 kilometer) across. It was developed at Utrecht’s Department of Physical Geography, and it tracks both the rain that soaks into soil and the water people pump out of it.

Checked against real wells, the model gave useful estimates at about 80 percent of wells shallower than about 200 feet (60 meters). For deeper wells, the figure was about 70 percent.

For every square and every calendar month, the team worked out how deep the water table usually was and how much that depth normally varied.

A drought started when the groundwater dropped so far below its usual level for that time of year that only about 16 percent of months would qualify. It ended when the water rose back above that line.

Droughts lasting two months or less were left out, because monthly data can’t capture them reliably. For the rest, the team measured how fast the water fell, how fast it rose again, and what it did in the six months afterward.

Climate did more than anything else to set the pace of recovery. Places where a lot of rain soaks into the ground, such as the Amazon and Southeast Asia, recovered quickly. Their droughts also tended to be shorter and more frequent.

Dry regions recovered slowly. The slow places included Australia, the Middle East and Central Asia, southern Africa, southern South America and the U.S. Midwest.

During drought recovery, the groundwater at a typical location rose about 0.7 inches (1.8 centimeters) a month. In the fastest places it climbed as much as about 3 feet (1 meter) a month.

Those raw speeds partly reflect how much a water table swings in an ordinary year. So the team also compared each place with its own normal range, and the split between wet and dry regions became sharper.

Average speed told only part of the story. Two places could recover at the same average rate and still behave very differently during a drought.

Hauswirth hadn’t expected recovery to vary so much within a single region. In an interview with Earth.com, she said, “I was surprised to see that the groundwater recovery pattern was not necessarily homogeneous within a region and could vary quite a bit locally.”

To capture those differences, the team sorted every location by how its droughts unfolded. About 57 percent were resilient: on average, the water came back faster than it had dropped. Another 26 percent were unstable, slipping back into drought before they had fully recovered.

That makes the unstable group the second largest. The researchers described its behavior as even more critical than that of the vulnerable group, where the water fell quickly and climbed back slowly.

The unstable group covered about 15 percent of places, and only around 2 percent were stable, with the fall and the rise at about the same speed.

Unstable places weren’t clustered in one part of the world, and they weren’t limited to heavily pumped areas. Their droughts were shorter, milder and more frequent than in any other group, often with little time to refill in between.

Terrain set the vulnerable places apart. In every region the team examined up close, they turned up at higher elevations, where the ground stores less water and the water table swings more widely.

In Europe, some may be linked to limestone country, where water drains through cracks and caves.

The close-ups included California, Spain, India and the North China Plain, all places known for heavy groundwater use. In Spain, the vulnerable and unstable spots shared similar pumping patterns. In California, pumping appeared to affect more of the categories.

Sorting places this way, Hauswirth said, made it clear that local features “are an important part of the drivers and should not be underestimated.”

For water managers in vulnerable regions, her advice starts with knowing where the water comes from. Where possible, she said, they should map how much of local demand and supply is covered by groundwater.

That “could help us better understand when groundwater resources are overexploited,” she told Earth.com, and when a wet spell could help restore levels, possibly by cutting back on pumping.

The authors name their own blind spots. They filtered out places where water tables have fallen steadily for decades, often from heavy pumping, because a long decline makes single droughts hard to pick out. Those places may be underrepresented in the results.

Every number here is also a model’s estimate. This model performed well against real wells, but global groundwater models have both overestimated and underestimated water levels in the past.

And because the team averaged 60 years together, the results can’t show whether recovery is speeding up or slowing down.

“I want to dive deeper into how these recovery patterns have changed over time, as the current work has mainly focused on the spatial pattern,” Hauswirth said.

Next, the team wants to pair the four categories with projections of a warmer climate. That could show which places are at risk of shifting from resilient toward vulnerable or unstable.

The full study was published in the journal Environmental Research: Water.

#6373. After LINK mission failure, Swift reenters atmosphere

Editor’s note: This story was originally published Aug. 24, 2026. Swift reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4, 2026, ending its nearly 22-year mission. See the most recent updates at the end of this story.

NASA announced Aug. 19 that the Katalyst Space LINK spacecraft built to boost the aging Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory will still rendezvous with the telescope but won’t raise its orbit, after an attitude-control failure sidelined LINK during on-orbit commissioning.

The Swift Boost Mission was a quick-turnaround rescue attempt designed to save the Swift observatory from an early demise. Thanks to increased atmospheric drag from the effects of solar maximum, NASA predicts the space telescope will reenter Earth’s atmosphere later this year, cutting short the extended run of a spacecraft that has delivered a number of breakthroughs in understanding gamma-ray bursts — the highest-energy explosions in the universe.

NASA contracted Katalyst Space Technologies, a startup based in Flagstaff, Arizona, in September 2025 to attempt the rescue, giving the company less than a year to go from concept to execution. Katalyst designed and built the LINK spacecraft for the express purpose of rendezvousing with Swift in orbit, docking with the telescope, and boosting it to a higher altitude for a few more years of science.

LINK launched July 3 on a Northrop Grumman Pegasus XL rocket but quickly ran into trouble, losing control of two of its three reaction wheels over the last weekend of July. Reaction wheels are spinning flywheels that use angular momentum to let a spacecraft point itself precisely without burning propellant. Three of them, angled correctly, can hold a spacecraft steady on every axis; NASA’s Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, set to launch Aug. 30, carries six for redundancy. LINK carries only the minimum three, and losing two sent it tumbling at nearly nine degrees per second, compromising communications with ground controllers. Katalyst spent the following weeks firing LINK’s electric propulsion thrusters to slow the spin, eventually taming it to about 1.47 degrees per second by early August — but for a while, it was an open question whether the mission could continue at all.

RELATED: Is NASA’s Swift Boost Mission spinning away?Katalyst uploaded a flight-software fix Aug. 11 that reestablished LINK’s attitude control. But at that point, the timeline was even tighter. Swift had decayed to an orbital height of 216 miles (347 kilometers), just 31 miles (50 km) shy of the point where an orbit-raising mission would become much more difficult. Then came the Aug. 19 announcement from NASA that the spacecraft would still attempt rendezvous and proximity operations — closing in on and flying near Swift to test the maneuvers any future servicing mission would need — but would make no attempt to boost the telescope’s orbit. Without that boost, Swift is still expected to meet a fiery end before the end of the year.

Neither NASA nor Katalyst has said how LINK’s mission will end — whether the spacecraft will dock with Swift and remain there through the telescope’s final days or drift off on its own.

The Swift Boost Mission was framed from the start as a long shot, and NASA’s messaging hasn’t shifted now that it’s fallen short. “This is not the outcome we were working toward, but it does not change why this mission was worth attempting,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman in the Aug. 19 announcement.

“We knew this was a high-risk, high-reward mission — a first-of-its kind attempt, developed on an unprecedented timeline driven by the Sun’s activity,” said Shawn Domagal-Goldman, director of NASA’s Astrophysics Division. “We were all hoping for more science from Swift. But we knew the takeaways from this mission would be worthwhile either way, and we have gained so much through the series of accomplishments up to this point.”

The agency plans to lean on its other missions to help cover the gap in gamma-ray burst monitoring once the 21-year-old Swift telescope is lost, as well as file away whatever lessons LINK’s rendezvous can teach us about robotic servicing for missions that follow.

Update Sept. 15, 2026: On Sept. 4, NASA announced that LINK had made its closest approach to the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, closing to within roughly 8 miles (13 kilometers) of the space telescope. That’s as close as the two spacecraft will come, NASA says, now that the agency is no longer planning to boost Swift’s orbit, thanks to lingering attitude-control problems aboard LINK.

In the days following the rendezvous, Katalyst put the robotic servicer through the paces: raising its orbit, aligning it with Swift’s path, unfurling all three robotic arms, and firing all three xenon thrusters at once on Aug. 30. With no further approach planned, Katalyst expects LINK to deorbit later this month.

With the boost off the table, Swift’s team switched its ultraviolet/optical and X-ray telescopes back on Aug. 26, months after powering them down to reduce draft and slow Swift’s decay. A third instrument, the Burst Alert Telescope, should follow in the coming weeks. NASA anticipates the gamma ray observatory will reenter and burn up before the end of the year.

Update Sept. 29, 2026: On Sept. 25, LINK deorbited and reentered Earth’s atmosphere, concluding the mission. LINK was not successful in its attempt to capture and boost Swift’s orbit, but the team collected useful data across 85 days of LINK’s operation that will help inform future missions.

Update Nov. 9, 2026: The Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory reentered Earth’s atmosphere Nov. 4 at 7:39 a.m. EST, according to NASA, coming down over Indonesia’s North Sumatra region. While some components may have survived the journey and made it to the surface, NASA expected most of the spacecraft to disintegrate completely.

Brooks Mendenhall is a staff writer for Astronomy and is based in Chattanooga, Tennessee.

#6372. Kershaw and Civivi Pocket Knives Are on Sale for Black Friday—These Are the Deals Our Gear Editors Trust

Add to your EDC rotation with these picks from Kershaw, Civivi, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Black Friday is a great time to stock up on hobby supplies or even get a jump on holiday shopping. Or you could do both at the same time. One hobbyist category I’m always scoping is pocket knives. Like most EDC enthusiasts, no matter how many pocket knives I acquire, there’s room for more. Right now there are a lot of great deals from two of PopMech’s most tested (and beloved!) brands—Kershaw and Civivi.

Between the extensive testing I’ve done, along with intel from Test Editor Justin Park, I’ve rounded up some of the best deals on pocket knives: There are sleek EDC options from Kershaw and Civivi, as well as standout brands like Gerber and Victorinox. If you don’t think you'll use a pocket knife much, I implore you to try one of these—you don’t have to be in the field to reap the benefits of a reliable pocket knife.

This cleverly-designed Kershaw doubles as a bit and driver set. Its 8Cr13MoV-steel blade has excellent edge retention and deploys quickly thanks to the thumb stud. The driver swings out of the handle, which also holds the two flathead and two Phillips bits.

I’m a big fan of narrow knives. They remind me of the sleek stiletto blades popular with mobsters, but with modern functionality. The Gerber Pledge hits those old-school notes with better materials like an oxide-coated blade and textured handle. Its barely-there design fits comfortably in your pocket as well.

The Leek’s blade comes to an extremely fine point, ideal for dressing game and gutting fish—like a paring knife built for the outdoors. The blade features assisted opening, meaning easy one-handed deployment, and the stonewashed blade bolsters durability.

The Incindie’s hollow blade not only looks cool but keeps the knife lightweight and offers some grip when slicing. The G10 handle also helps with grip—a lot of my knives have this fiberglass blend material, and it wears in well.

The No. 09 is as functional as it is elegant. The carbon-steel blade is easy to maintain, and the beechwood handle adds a touch of polish. Its rotating collar lock keeps you safe, and the nail indent allows easy blade deployment.

The Blur has a very fine edge that’s easy to sharpen and maintain. A thumb stud makes deployment easy, and the liner lock keeps it in place. The blade itself has a Cerakote coating for extra corrosion resistance.

I love a small pocket knife because they’re so practical, but adding a cat face makes them even more fun to use. Civivi’s Purr is a sub-2-inch blade made of durable Nitro steel with jimping on the spine. Add a grippy G10 handle, and you have an excellent, unique EDC.

The slim profile of the Guile makes it look like a gentleman’s pen knife: easy to slip into the chest pocket of a shirt or jacket. The 14C28N steel blade has excellent edge retention and corrosion resistance, and jimping on the spine for leverage.

The blade deploys with either the thumb hole or the flipper edge on the front.

You can’t go wrong with the classic Swiss Army knife. It’s a knife plus 20 other tools in a small 4.5-inch package. It’s the ultimate multitasker, and the brand has a limited warranty for some peace of mind.

This is a gift-worthy pocket knife you’ll probably want to keep for yourself. The combo of a wooden handle with a Damascus-steel blade marries craftsmanship with practicality.

The Yonder is on the smaller side, with a closed length of just 3.75 inches—excellent for daily compact carry.

Hollowed handles keep a knife lightweight and give it a unique look. The Noctic's skeletal handle is made of Micarta, which helps with grip and develops a patina over time. It also has a finger choil to keep your digits out of the way when slicing.

Jimping (the groove along the spine of the blade) provides leverage when cutting, and the frame lock keeps the blade secured.

This EDC flipper is an excellent choice in an all-black colorway. Its textured handle bolsters grip, and its stonewashed finish adds durability. The blade steel offers excellent corrosion resistance and a hardness level that won’t crack or break.
